proposals.name: RMR-D: rhythmic masking release by delayed captors. The B stream is frozen across D, and the response is rhythm identity.
proposals.one_paragraph: The listener identifies which of two rhythms (SSLL or SLSL) is played by high B tones (1000 Hz). The target tones are hidden among identical B distractor tones on the same 200-ms grid. Every distractor, and only the distractors, gets a low A captor (420.4 Hz, 15 st below) at onset delay D. When A and B group, as at D = 0, distractors are heard as dyads, the lone B tones stand out, and the rhythm is easy (rhythmic masking release; Turgeon et al. 2002, 2005). When D breaks grouping, all B tones sound alike and accuracy falls toward the no-captor floor. So grouping helps here, and performance must fall with D: the exact mirror of Micheyl et al. (2013) Exp. 3, using their tones, rate, frequency separation and D values. Two properties built into the stimulus answer the reviewer objections. (1) Nothing the listener judges involves D. The judgment is categorical rhythm identity with fixed 400/800-ms intervals, so there is no pedestal and no Weber's law. (2) For a given random seed, the B waveform is sample-identical at every D. The A stream is identical up to a rigid time shift, which a random trial-onset jitter hides. Any strategy that uses one stream alone therefore gives the same accuracy at every D. A fall with D can only come from the A-B relation, which is the definition of cross-stream grouping. A capture control (Exp. 2) keeps the D = 0 dyads physically identical while pulling A into its own sequential stream. That gives a grouping-specific dissociation that loudness or other local-acoustic accounts cannot produce. The design uses constant stimuli and short fresh trials, and a mixture analysis turns bistability from a nuisance into a measured quantity: the objective probability of grouping, π(D).
proposals.stimulus:
TONES: copy Micheyl et al. (2013).
- B = 1000 Hz; A = 420.4 Hz (15 semitones below B; ratio 2.378, not a low-integer ratio).
- 100-ms tones including 20-ms raised-cosine ramps, random starting phase, 44.1 kHz, diotic.
- Nominal 60 dB SPL per tone. Every tone, A and B, is roved independently over ±5 dB (uniform). This is Micheyl's ±4 dB A rove widened, so a "louder event = dyad" cue is unreliable.

TIME GRID: 200-ms slots (5 Hz, equal to Micheyl's SOA). All B tones, targets and distractors alike, start exactly on slot onsets. Distractors must NOT be jittered off the grid. If they were, "the on-grid tones" would become a single-stream cue to the target.

TARGET RHYTHMS (B tones with no captor):
- R1 "SSLL": inter-onset intervals 400, 400, 800, 800 ms.
- R2 "SLSL": inter-onset intervals 400, 800, 400, 800 ms.
- Both have 4 tones per 2.4-s cycle and the same set of intervals. Only the order differs, so tone count, density and the interval distribution are equal.
- Each trial plays 2 cycles plus a closing tone: 9 target tones over 4.9 s.
- The cyclic starting rotation is random (4 rotations of R1, 2 of R2, equated for first-interval statistics).

DISTRACTORS:
- B tones placed on the non-target slots, each slot filled independently with probability p.
- Start with p = 0.55 (about 4.4 distractors per 2.4-s cycle, about 3.5 B tones/s overall).
- Pilot p upward if the no-captor floor exceeds 0.62.

CAPTORS: each distractor B tone gets one A tone starting D ms after its onset, with A lagging B as in the lab's tcoh/tsync code. Confirm that this matches the sign used in Micheyl 2013 Exp. 3. Target tones never get a captor.

CONDITIONS:
- D = 0, 10, 20, 35, 50, 71 and 100 ms. This covers all five of Micheyl's values plus 10 and 20, so the range below 40 ms, where fusion is expected to collapse, is sampled densely.
- A no-captor condition (B-only; the floor).

FROZEN SEEDS: 30 seeds. A seed fixes target identity, rotation, distractor slots and all roves. Each seed is played once in each of the 8 conditions. So item difficulty is matched exactly across D, and the B waveform within a seed is identical sample for sample in all 8 conditions.

ONSET JITTER: the start of each trial is jittered uniformly over 0 to 200 ms after the ready cue. This makes the rigid A-stream shift invisible to absolute timing.

GEOMETRY NOTE: at D = 100 a captor ends exactly when the next slot begins. The main claims therefore rest on D ≤ 71, and D = 100 is kept only to line up with Micheyl.

EXP. 2 (capture / dissociation; optional, about 15 min). Held at D = 0, three conditions:
- (a) as in the main experiment;
- (b) "on-frequency fillers": extra 420.4-Hz tones at every slot midpoint (+100 ms) with no B. These turn A into a dense sequential stream (cf. Bregman & Pinker 1978; Darwin, Hukin & al-Khatib 1995);
- (c) "off-frequency fillers": the same fillers at 250 Hz, about 9 semitones below A (cf. Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010 off-frequency captors).
The dyads themselves are physically identical in all three conditions.

Optional overlap control: an offset-aligned captor (duration 100−D, offsets aligned) at D = 35, to separate onset asynchrony from overlap (Turgeon et al. 2005 Exp. 3 logic).
proposals.task_and_measure:
TRIAL AND RESPONSE: single interval, two alternatives. After each sequence the listener presses one of two keys: "pairs" (SSLL) or "alternating" (SLSL). There is feedback on every trial. There is no adaptive track; this is the method of constant stimuli.

PRIMARY MEASURE: d'(D) = z(H) − z(F), where H = P("R1" | R1) and F = P("R1" | R2). This is free of response bias and on the same scale as Micheyl's yes/no d'. Pc is also reported.

PRIMARY TEST: a monotone decline of d' with D.
- Planned contrasts: D = 0 vs 35, 50 and 100 (the same pairs Micheyl found credible, opposite sign predicted).
- Ordered trend test.
- GLMM: correct ~ D (categorical) + block + previous-trial D + (D | listener), logit link.

MODEL-BASED MEASURE, per listener:
Pc(D) = Pfloor + (Pmax − Pfloor) · π(D), with π(D) = 1 − Φ((D − D50)/σ).
- Pfloor is fixed from that listener's no-captor trials on the same seeds.
- Pmax is free, with a lapse bound.
- Outputs: D50, the delay at which grouping is lost on half the trials; σ, the steepness (a step versus a gradual decline); and π(D), the objective probability that the trial was organised as grouped.

SECONDARY: a 4-min subjective block at the end. On Micheyl Exp. 1-style sequences (12 A + 12 B, 2.4 s, at the same D values), the listener reports "one or two streams" at the end of each sequence. There are 6 repetitions per D, plus Farkas et al. (2016)-type catch trials: synchronous 1-semitone sequences (expected one stream) and alternating 15-semitone sequences (expected two streams). This relates the objective π(D) to the subjective P(one stream | D) in the same listeners.
proposals.why_grouping_helps_and_falls_with_D:
Why grouping helps: the target B tones and the distractor B tones are physically identical. The only property that tells them apart is whether a B tone is bound to a concurrent A tone. At D = 0, temporal coherence binds each distractor to its captor (Elhilali et al. 2009; Shamma et al. 2011). The distractor is then heard as a dyad with a different timbre, and the lone B targets stand out as the rhythm. This is the logic of rhythmic masking release.

Why accuracy falls with D: as D grows, A and B lose coherence. The captors segregate into their own stream, and the B stream again sounds like one undifferentiated irregular sequence. Accuracy then falls toward the no-captor floor. Doing the task without binding would require cross-stream order judgments, and those are poor across segregated streams (Bregman & Campbell 1971; Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010, where on-frequency captors raised synchrony and order thresholds to about 43-50 ms).

Quantitative anchors:
- Turgeon et al. (2005, Exp. 1): Pc 0.99-1.00 at 0 ms, falling monotonically with asynchrony (F(4,32) = 81.2); 75% thresholds 32-37 ms; no-captor control Pc 0.53-0.56.
- Turgeon et al. (2002), brief noise bursts: full fusion at 0 ms, partial at 10-20 ms, none at 20-40 ms.
- Christiansen & Oxenham (2014): a grouping-helps benefit (CMR) that was significantly reduced at 40-60 ms offsets.
- Micheyl et al. (2013): listeners L6 and L8 improved abruptly between D = 0 and 35 ms.

So the expected curve is the mirror image of Micheyl's rising d'. It is likely steep, with D50 in the range of roughly 20-45 ms. That expectation is why D is sampled densely below 40 ms.
proposals.confounds_and_controls:
Objections answered by the design itself:

1. Weber's law or a pedestal. The decision variable is rhythm identity. The rhythms are built from 400/800-ms intervals that are the same at every D. No interval is ever compared with D or with D plus a change, and there is no staircase on a time variable. This is unlike tcoh (D vs D+δ) and unlike tsync, where the probe sits D/2 from each rhythm, so a within-stream anisochrony pedestal of D/2 grows with D.

2. Single-stream strategies.
- For each seed, the B waveform is sample-identical in all 8 conditions.
- The A stream is identical up to a rigid shift of 100 ms or less, which the 0-200-ms trial-onset jitter makes uninformative.
- So any observer using A alone or B alone, ideal or human, has a function of D that is exactly flat. A single-stream strategy can only add a D-independent floor; it cannot create a slope.
- The floor is measured directly: no-captor trials use the same seeds. Pc there should be about 0.55; Turgeon reports 0.53-0.56.
- The captors' timing is set by random distractor positions, not by the target rhythm. The only constraint is that captors never fall on target slots. Listening for the A stream's silent slots is therefore a masked-rhythm task in its own right, and it too is flat across D.

3. Local acoustics.
- A and B are about 7 ERBs apart, so peripheral masking or suppression is negligible at 60 dB.
- There are no beats at 15 semitones (Micheyl's L7 problem occurred at small separations).
- Harmonicity is constant across D (cf. Micheyl, Kreft et al. 2013).
- Loudness summation in the D = 0 dyad: every tone is roved independently by ±5 dB. Exp. 2 holds the dyads physically fixed at D = 0 and changes only sequential context. The grouping account predicts on-frequency fillers < off-frequency fillers ≈ no fillers. A loudness or acoustic account predicts no difference.
- D changes onset asynchrony and temporal overlap together, exactly as in Micheyl 2013. The optional offset-aligned condition at D = 35 separates them (Turgeon 2005 found both matter).

4. Item effects: frozen seeds, so every D gets exactly the same 30 patterns.

5. Learning and memorisation.
- Listeners train to a criterion at D = 0 first.
- All 8 conditions are interleaved in every block, and each seed's 8 presentations are spread across blocks by a Latin square.
- Block is a covariate.
- Pc in the no-captor condition is tracked across blocks as a built-in check for memorised seeds; it should stay at the floor.

6. Trial history: previous-trial D is a GLMM covariate (Snyder et al. 2008), with at least 2 s of silence between trials.

7. Instructions and attention: the instructions are identical at every D and never mention grouping (Billig et al. 2018 found that intention shifts perceptual organisation). The task is active at every D (Lu et al. 2017).

8. Sign of D: A lags B in the main experiment, the direction listeners tolerate better (Wojtczak et al. 2017). This is stated in the paper. If time allows, one extra condition at D = 35 with A leading tests the asymmetry.
proposals.bistability_handling:
Is it bistable? Plausibly yes, but as a mixture across trials rather than as switching within a trial.
- Auditory streaming is genuinely bistable (Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006).
- In Micheyl et al. (2013) Exp. 1, synchronous tones 15 semitones apart were reported as two streams on about 76% of trials, with large and even reversed individual differences.
- In Micheyl Exp. 3, L6 and L8 showed step-like jumps between D = 0 and 35 ms.
- Billig & Carlyon (2016) showed that objective performance follows the momentary percept (d = 1.80), even with the stimulus fixed.
- On the other side: no study has measured switching dynamics as a function of A-B onset delay, and dominance phases last about 4-9 s (Rankin et al. 2015). A trial of about 5 s therefore mostly samples the first percept, which is biased toward grouping (Hupé & Pressnitzer 2012).

What this means for the measure, and how the design handles it:
1. Staircases are the wrong tool. Under a mixture, the psychometric function is shallow and capped below 100%, so tracks wander. This is a plausible, though unproven, reason the tpair and tsync thresholds were noisy or hit ceiling. Constant stimuli with fixed trial counts per D replace them.
2. The mixture model makes π(D), the probability a trial was grouped, the reported quantity. A per-listener steepness σ tests "step-like versus graded" directly. A steep individual function combined with a graded group mean is the bistability signature, consistent with Denham & Winkler (2006): build-up can be an artefact of averaging.
3. Trials are short, single-interval and of identical length at every D. That holds the effect of build-up constant and avoids the reset that a 2I gap causes (Cusack et al. 2004). Short trials also give a grouping-helps task its widest range, because the first percept favours grouping.
4. The 4-min subjective block gives P(one stream | D) in the same listeners, so the objective and subjective functions can be compared.
5. A continuous one-vs-two report over long sequences as a function of D would be a new result in itself. It is set aside for a later or EEG session, not this visit.
proposals.session_plan:
One visit of about 50-55 min. Recruit 14-16 naive listeners to end with at least 12 analysable. Exclusion is pre-registered: Pc at D = 0 in the main blocks below 0.70, which would remove a listener like Micheyl's near-chance L3.

0-5 min: consent, questionnaire (including percussion or musical training, a covariate per Ehrlé & Samson 2005), headphone check, calibrated volume. This reuses the tsync PROTOCOL, audio engine and underflow checks.

5-13 min: training.
- (a) R1 and R2 played alone, labelled, 4 demonstrations each.
- (b) 8 target-only identification trials with feedback; criterion 7/8.
- (c) 16 trials at D = 0 with distractors and captors, with feedback; criterion 12/16, at most 2 rounds.
- (d) 8 mixed-D practice trials.

13-45 min: main experiment. 6 blocks × 40 trials, each block holding 7 D values × 5 trials plus 5 no-captor trials, all randomised. That is 240 trials, 30 per condition, using 30 frozen seeds each played in all 8 conditions. Each trial takes about 4.9 s of sound, about 1.2 s to respond, and 0.5 s of feedback, with at least 2 s of silence between trials, so about 7.6 s per trial and about 30.5 min in total, plus 5 × 30-s breaks.

45-50 min: subjective block. Micheyl Exp. 1-style 2.4-s sequences at 7 D values × 5 repetitions, plus 6 catch trials, reporting one or two streams at the end. About 41 trials × 5.5 s ≈ 4 min.

50-52 min: debrief and strategy questionnaire.

Exp. 2 (capture dissociation): 3 conditions × 40 trials at D = 0, about 15 min. Run it in a short second visit, or in the same visit for listeners who move faster, or in the second week of the window.

Pilot before the window: 3 listeners, about 1 h each. Go/no-go criteria:
- Pc at D = 0 at least 0.85;
- no-captor Pc at most 0.62;
- Pc at D = 0 minus Pc at D = 100 at least 0.15.
Adjust the distractor probability p first. If D = 0 fails at 15 semitones, fall back to 9 semitones (A = 594.6 Hz).
proposals.expected_effect_and_power:
Expected values:
- Anchors: Turgeon 2005 Pc 0.99-1.00 at 0 ms vs 0.53-0.56 without captors, thresholds 32-37 ms. The ceiling is discounted for pure tones 15 semitones apart.
- Predicted Pc at D = 0: 0.85-0.95 (d' about 2.1-3.3).
- Predicted floor and Pc at D = 100: 0.55-0.65 (d' about 0.25-0.75).
- Predicted D50: about 20-45 ms.
- Predicted Δd' from 0 to 100 ms: about −1.5 to −2.8. Micheyl 2013 found +0.95 (MAP +1.10, 95% CR [0.03, 2.05], n = 7) in the opposite direction, so the expected effect is about 1.5-3 times larger in magnitude.

Power:
- With a Pc difference of 0.15 or more and a between-listener SD of the difference of 0.12 or less, dz ≥ 1.25. With n = 12 and two-sided α = .05, power exceeds 0.97.
- The smallest effect detectable with 80% power is dz ≈ 0.89 at n = 12 and ≈ 0.75 at n = 16.
- Within a listener, 30 trials per D gives a binomial SE of about 0.08. Pc of 0.90 vs 0.60 differs at p < .01, so individual curves (graded vs step) can be interpreted, which Micheyl's staircase-free but n = 7 design could only partly do.
- Expected precision of per-listener D50 from the mixture fit (210 captor trials) is about ±8-12 ms. This is an estimate to be confirmed by simulation with the pilot's Pmax and Pfloor before running.
- Exp. 2 effect sizes are untested (no published RMR capture data were verified). Treat it as a directional test: 40 trials per condition detects a Pc difference of 0.15 or more at n = 12.
proposals.risks:
1. The D = 0 ceiling may be low with pure tones 15 semitones apart. Turgeon's near-ceiling result used interleaved harmonics in a shared spectral region, and Micheyl Exp. 1 found synchronous tones heard as two streams 76% of the time. Mitigation: the pilot go/no-go criteria; fall back to 9 semitones (the alternating vs synchronous difference was still credible there in Micheyl Exp. 1), changed in both arms.

2. The no-captor floor may be too high: the rhythm may be audible through the distractors. Raise p toward 0.7. Never jitter distractors off the grid.

3. A curve that saturates by about 20 ms would compress the function. Denser D values below 40 ms already allow for this. If D50 is under 10 ms, add 5 ms and drop 71.

4. A D-flat strategy learned from feedback (for example, "the target is where the low tones are silent") would raise the floor at every D. It cannot produce a slope, but it shrinks the range. Monitor Pc at D = 100 by block, and add test blocks without feedback if it drifts upward.

5. The task is new with these tones: there is no published pure-tone RMR at 100-ms durations, and Darwin & Ciocca (1992) and Hukin & Darwin (1995) show grouping windows depend on the task. D50 could exceed 50 ms. That is still a valid result, and D = 71 and 100 cover it.

6. Exp. 2 fillers might act through distraction rather than capture. The off-frequency filler condition controls for this, although Micheyl 2010 Exp. 1 found off-frequency captors are not perfectly neutral.

7. Cost: new stimulus and trial code. The tsync audio, logging, calibration, protocol and analysis scaffolding carry over; the stimulus generator and mixture fit are new. Estimate 3-5 days of coding, including an ideal-observer simulation that checks the B-only and A-only information against the design.

8. Verdict on tsync: frankly, it is not worth keeping as the primary measure. Its zero-pedestal probe is a good idea, and Christiansen & Oxenham (2014) show a synchronous test after an offset context is publishable. But three problems remain:
- (a) The ending sits D/2 off each stream's rhythm, so each tone can be judged against its own stream. The within-stream displacement pedestal (D/2 vs D/2 ± δ/2) grows with D. A single-stream anisochrony strategy therefore predicts rising thresholds with D, the same prediction as grouping (Hirsh et al. 1990; Ehrlé & Samson 2005).
- (b) The ending deviates further from the context as D grows, so reset or distraction effects are confounded with D. The single D0_late control (50 ms) matches neither the geometry nor the D-scaling. Haywood & Roberts (2013) found no single-deviant reset after alternating inducers, so reset is possible but not established; a reviewer will raise it and the design cannot answer it.
- (c) 2I staircases under a mixture of percepts give noisy, censored thresholds, at about 40 min for 6 tracks.
Treat the existing tsync and tpair data as pilots, and reuse the infrastructure.

The tcoh curve may be partly rescued as a side analysis. Wojtczak et al. (2012) found that isolated pairs with the high tone leading show flat thresholds from 0 to 40 ms, so a matched isolated-pair pedestal control in the same listener would test whether the ≈0.4·D growth is Weber or context. It cannot be the headline experiment.

proposals.name: Percept-tracked deviant detection (PTDD): concurrent one/two-stream report plus fixed-size cross-stream timing deviants in long Micheyl-type A-B sequences, with D effect expressed as P(integrated | D) and percept-contingent d'
proposals.one_paragraph: Treat A-B organisation as a latent, possibly bistable state and measure it directly, rather than fitting a staircase to a mixture of states. Each trial is a 20-s Micheyl-type sequence: B = 1000 Hz, A 9 semitones below, 100-ms tones, 5 Hz, A lagging B by a fixed D. With the left hand the listener continuously reports "one stream (chords)" or "two streams (two melodies)". With the right hand they press for rare, fixed-size deviants: the B tone of one pair is displaced by ±Δ while A stays put. This copies Billig & Carlyon (2016) Exp. 2, where detection was much better during integrated reports (t(11) = 4.15, d = 1.80; 12 listeners, 48 sequences, about 30 min). The D effect is read out in three linked ways. (1) P_int(D), the fraction of time reported integrated, plus time to first segregation and phase durations; this is the bistability result. (2) Percept-contingent d': at the same D, the integrated and segregated stretches are physically identical, so Weber's law and pedestal effects cannot produce the integrated-minus-segregated difference. (3) A mixture test. The grouping account says D lowers overall d' only by lowering P_int, so d'(D) = P_int(D)·d'_I + (1−P_int(D))·d'_S with d'_I and d'_S constant across D. A pedestal account says d' also falls with D within each state. The headline ARO figure is overall d' falling with D (predicted roughly 2.3 to 1.2), shown beside Micheyl's rising 1.48 to 2.43, with P_int(D) underneath to explain it. VERDICT ON tsync: drop it as the main measure, but keep its code. Its core logic, a synchronous test event after a context with lag D, is not stupid: it has a published JASA precedent in Christiansen & Oxenham (2014). Three problems sink it. Its ending moves further off rhythm (by D/2) as D grows. Its 2.4-s contexts mostly sample the grouping-biased first percept (Hupé & Pressnitzer 2012). And a 2I-2AFC staircase run on trials that are a mixture of two organisations gives noisy or ceiling thresholds (cf. Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010, about 44-50 ms against a 100-ms cap). That is what the lab saw in tpair and tsync. It also costs about 40 min for 6 single tracks. The tone synthesis, A rove, audio scheduling, staircase (for the Δ calibration) and level code in /Users/eminent/Res/SeqSFG/tsync/ can be reused directly.
proposals.stimulus:
Base geometry, the same as /Users/eminent/Res/SeqSFG/tsync/configs/tsync_main.json except where noted.
- Tones: B = 1000 Hz. A = 594.6 Hz (9 semitones below), changed from 15. Pure tones of 100 ms with 20-ms raised-cosine ramps, SOA 200 ms (5 Hz) in both streams.
- Levels: B at 60 dB nominal. A at 60 dB, roved independently per tone by ±4 dB (Micheyl 2013). Fixed system volume, 48 kHz, diotic over the MacBook headphone output.
- Delay: A lags B by D = 0, 20, 35, 50 or 100 ms. 0, 35, 50 and 100 are Micheyl anchors, and his credible contrasts were 0 vs 50 and 0 vs 100. 20 samples the 10-40 ms partial-fusion zone (Turgeon et al. 2002). At D = 100 the result is a perfectly alternating ABAB sequence.
- Sequence: 100 A-B pairs, about 20 s, with no break or change at the end.
- Deviant: the B tone of one pair is shifted by +Δ or −Δ (sign random 50/50); A and all other tones are unchanged. Δ is fixed per listener at 0.75 × that listener's B-alone threshold (see the session plan), clipped to 8-25 ms.
  - Without A, the shift is only a within-stream anisochrony: B-B intervals of 200±Δ and 200∓Δ.
  - With A, it also changes the A-B relation from D to D±Δ. At D = 0 this is the Elhilali cue: 2-4 ms synchronous vs 10-20 ms asynchronous or B alone.
- Deviant count and placement: 2-6 per sequence (mean 4), never in the first 5 pairs (1 s), at least 12 pairs (2.4 s) apart. At least one early (1-6 s) and one late (14-20 s) per sequence, so build-up position is a factor (Thompson et al. 2011; Billig & Carlyon 2016 found only 2% of early deviants in segregated phases).
- Response window: 150-1500 ms after the deviant B onset.
- Control sequences, both 20 s:
  - B-alone sequences with the same deviants. These give the within-stream floor, d'_floor.
  - Report catch sequences (Farkas et al. 2016). Integrated catch: A = 500 Hz (an octave below), synchronous. Segregated catch: A = 420.4 Hz at a mismatched SOA of 250 ms.
- Inter-trial interval: 4 s of silence, inside the 2-5 s used by Billig & Carlyon (2016) and Rankin et al. (2017).
- Order: the D order is carryover-balanced (a Williams design for 5 conditions, repeated), and previous-trial D is logged (Snyder et al. 2008).
- Bridge block (Micheyl 2013 Exp. 1 protocol): 2.4-s sequences of 12 + 12 tones at 9 and 15 semitones × D = 0, 35, 100 ms, with a single one/two report at the end of each.
proposals.task_and_measure:
The task is a dual task.
- Left hand: two keys, "1 = one stream (a sequence of chords or two-note events)" and "2 = two streams (a high melody and a low melody you could follow separately)". Listeners press as soon as the first percept forms and again at every change. Key-state timestamps are logged on the audio clock.
- Right hand: press space whenever "something in the rhythm or timing jumps".
- Instructions stay neutral: "do not try to hold either organisation; report what you hear". This matters because intention shifts organisation (Billig, Davis & Carlyon 2018) and so does volitional control (Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006). There is no feedback in the main blocks.

Measures:
(1) Organisation, the bistability outcome:
  - P_int(D): fraction of reported time integrated, in 50-ms bins from 1 s to 20 s. Binomial GLMM on bins or beta GLMM on per-sequence proportions, with D as a factor and random intercepts and slopes per listener.
  - Latency to the first switch from the initial percept: a Cox model with listener frailty. Hupé & Pressnitzer (2012) and Denham et al. (2013) say the first phase is where stimulus parameters matter most.
  - Durations of later phases, fitted as log-normal (Rankin et al. 2015), modelled separately for integrated and segregated phases versus D.
(2) Percept-contingent sensitivity:
  - Each deviant takes the reported state at its onset (primary analysis). In a sensitivity analysis, deviants within 1 s after a switch are dropped and the report trace is shifted 0.5 s to allow for report lag.
  - Hits are modelled with a logistic GLMM: state × D + position (early/late) + shift sign + previous D + block, with (1 + state | listener).
  - False alarms are presses outside every window, computed per 1.35-s pseudo-window and per state. This allows d' and criterion c per state and per D, which is needed because listeners are more conservative when segregated (Billig & Carlyon 2016: t(11) = 8.93).
(3) Objective P_int: with h_I and h_S estimated at each D, solve P(hit | D) = π·h_I + (1 − π)·h_S for π_obj(D). π_obj(D) should agree with the reported P_int(D), which gives a report-independent check.
(4) Headline curve: overall d'(D), all states pooled, minus the B-alone floor. This is the falling curve that mirrors Micheyl Exp. 3.
(5) Mixture/mediation test: compare a model where D acts only through state against one with D slopes inside each state (likelihood-ratio test, plus an equivalence bound of ±0.5 d' per 50 ms of D within state). Report the proportion of the total D effect on d' that is mediated by the reported state.
proposals.why_grouping_helps_and_falls_with_D: When A and B are grouped into one stream of two-tone events, the deviant changes the internal timing of a single event. In fused chords at D = 0 this is an across-channel onset asynchrony. Elhilali et al. (2009) found thresholds of 2-4 ms with synchronous context, against 10-20 ms with asynchronous or B-alone context. Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham (2010) showed that once A is captured into its own stream, synchrony and order thresholds jump to about 43-50 ms (captor effect η² ≈ 0.66-0.78). When A and B are segregated, the only usable cue is anisochrony within the B stream, about 12-16 ms at a 200-ms IOI (Hirsh et al. 1990), which is the B-alone floor. So d'_I is greater than d'_S. Billig & Carlyon (2016) found exactly this pattern in time with reported percept, beyond what the stimulus parameters predict (adding percept to the model: χ²(1) = 77.4; pseudo-R² .22 to .36). Temporal coherence (Elhilali et al. 2009; Shamma, Elhilali & Micheyl 2011) predicts that as D grows, coherence falls and the integrated state becomes rarer and shorter. Rankin et al. (2015) predict mainly shorter dominance of the stronger, integrated percept. Overall d' then falls because the deviants increasingly land in segregated phases. Micheyl 2013's segregation-helps task rises with D through the same P_int, so the two experiments are mirror readouts of one latent variable. D = 100 is a useful diagnostic. There the merged ABAB is isochronous, a privileged reference where B displacement is easy for a timing-acuity mechanism. A pure pedestal account therefore predicts d' recovers at D = 100 (U-shape). The grouping account predicts that d' at D = 100 is low except in the rare integrated phases.
proposals.confounds_and_controls:
Weber and pedestal effects:
- Primary inference is the integrated-versus-segregated contrast at a fixed D. It compares physically identical stimuli, so a reference-asynchrony effect cannot produce it.
- D affects d' through state only if the within-state D slopes are null (the mixture test). This directly decides between the tcoh '0.4·D' Weber reading and the grouping reading.
- Δ is applied with a random sign, so the deviant reference is D±Δ, symmetric around D.
- Wojtczak et al. (2012) found isolated high-leading pairs (this direction: A low lags) roughly flat over 0-40 ms standards, and Wojtczak et al. (2013) found a plateau from 20 to 100 ms. So large within-state pedestal slopes are not expected, but the test does not assume it.
- The raw across-D curve keeps a sync-versus-async step (Zera & Green 1993b). It is reported as descriptive only.

Single-stream strategy: a listener who monitors only B gets d'_floor at every D and in every state. The B-alone sequences measure that floor directly. Any integrated-over-segregated advantage shows that cross-stream information is being used. If a listener has no state contrast and sits at floor, that is diagnostic of this strategy; report it rather than exclude.

Local acoustics:
- Spectral overlap, loudness and roughness differ across D but are constant within D, so the within-D contrast is unaffected.
- The A level rove (±4 dB) stops level-based cues to pair timing.
- The deviant is the only within-sequence change, and it is brief and unpredictable. Rankin et al. (2017) found that only perturbations between or at the A/B frequencies promote segregation, and Haywood & Roberts (2013) found no single-deviant reset after alternating inducers. Still, check the percept trace for deviant-locked switches as a reactivity control (switch hazard 0-2 s after deviants versus after matched non-deviant times).

Reports driven by the wrong cue:
- 'Two streams' could be used to mean 'two onsets'. Training demonstrates a 1-semitone alternating trill (asynchronous but one stream), and the report catch sequences are scored (exclude a listener below 75% correct on catches).
- Micheyl's pitch-separation caveat is handled by holding the separation constant across D.

Bistability nuisances:
- Previous-trial D is a covariate, with a Williams order (Snyder et al. 2008).
- Inter-trial interval is 4 s.
- Stable individual biases (Denham et al. 2014) are handled with random slopes and per-listener curves.

Attention: the active task is the same at every D, which matters given that coherence effects depend on attention (Lu et al. 2017).

Learning:
- D is interleaved within blocks, and block is a covariate.
- Δ is fixed after calibration, so drift shows up as a block effect.
- Practice comes before the data, and dual-task cost (about −0.59 d′; Billig & Carlyon 2016) should be the same across D.

Lead direction: A lags B, matching tcoh and tsync. This is the tolerant direction (Wojtczak et al. 2017), so it may push the integration window to larger D. State the direction explicitly; counterbalancing it is deferred to the JASA study.
proposals.bistability_handling:
Is this bistable, as in ABA paradigms? Plausibly yes, but it is not yet shown for this stimulus. Supporting evidence:
- ABA streaming is bistable, with spontaneous switches and volitional control (Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006; Moore & Gockel 2012; Denham & Winkler 2006).
- Phase durations average about 4-9 s, log-normal, CV about 0.8 (Rankin et al. 2015).
- In Micheyl 2013, synchronous 15-semitone tones were reported as two streams on about 76% of trials, with idiosyncratic and even reversed individual curves. Listeners L6 and L8 jumped abruptly between D = 0 and 35 ms. That looks like a threshold or mixture, not graded binding.
- No study has measured switching dynamics as a function of A-B onset delay, so that measurement is itself a new result.

Implications already built into the design:
(a) A staircase (as in tcoh, tpair and tsync) tracks a mixture of states and drifts or hits ceiling. Use fixed stimuli and condition on the state.
(b) Short 2.4-s trials mostly sample the first percept, which is biased toward integration and lasts longer (Hupé & Pressnitzer 2012). Use 20-s sequences, which hold about 2-5 phases, so both states occur at intermediate D. Then model the first phase and later phases separately.
(c) Treat the state as data: continuous report, state-conditioned d' and c, and an objective π_obj(D) checked against the reported P_int(D).
(d) Validate the reports with catch sequences (Farkas et al. 2016) and keep instructions neutral (Billig et al. 2018).
(e) The bridge block (short sequences with an end report) shows the first-percept regime at 9 and 15 semitones, so the long-sequence P_int can be related to Micheyl Exp. 1.
(f) Expect stable individual biases (Denham et al. 2014): report individual P_int(D) curves and the D at which P_int = 0.5 (D50) per listener. These map onto Micheyl's large individual differences.

A predicted result that would be new: D mainly shortens integrated phases and the first-phase latency, with smaller effects on segregated phases. This follows the generalised Levelt II prediction of Rankin et al. (2015).
proposals.session_plan:
One visit, about 48 min. 16 naive listeners recruited, so that 12-14 remain after exclusions.

Before data collection: pilot 3 listeners (lab members are acceptable) on days 1-2.
- Go criteria, pooled: P_int(D=0) ≥ 0.6, P_int(D=100) ≤ 0.3, and at least 25% of deviants at intermediate D falling in each state.
- Fallbacks: if D = 0 is not integrated enough, use 6 semitones; if D = 100 is not segregated enough, use 12 semitones.

Session timeline:
- 0-5 min: setup, fixed volume, self-reported hearing.
- 5-9 min: organisation demos and report-only practice, 6 × 10-s sequences: octave synchronous (one), 1-semitone alternating trill (one, though asynchronous), 15-semitone rate-mismatched (two), plus 9-semitone sequences at D = 0, 35 and 100 with "either is fine, just report".
- 9-14 min: Δ calibration using the existing tsync staircase code. B-alone 12-tone sequences, 2I-2AFC, 3-down-1-up on the displacement of the last B, about 40 trials. Set Δ = 0.75 × threshold, clipped to 8-25 ms.
- 14-18 min: dual-task practice, 4 sequences (D = 0, 100, 35, B-alone) with deviant feedback.
- 18-42 min: main experiment, 5 blocks of about 4.5 min with 30-60 s breaks. Each block has every D twice (10 sequences), 1 B-alone sequence, and blocks 3 and 5 add one catch each.
  - Totals: 50 D sequences + 5 B-alone + 2 catch = 57 sequences × 24 s (20 s sound + 4 s inter-trial interval) ≈ 23 min.
  - Yield per listener: about 1000 s of report data, about 200 deviants (about 40 per D, of which about 13 early and 13 late), and about 20 B-alone deviants.
- 42-46 min: bridge block, 2.4-s sequences with an end-of-sequence report: 9 and 15 semitones × D = 0, 35, 100 × 6 repetitions = 36 trials at about 5 s each, about 3.5 min.
- 46-48 min: questionnaire (years of musical and percussion training; Ehrlé & Samson 2005) and debrief.

Logistics: 16 × 50 min ≈ 13.5 h, which fits easily in the two-week window at 2-3 listeners a day.

Code: reuse /Users/eminent/Res/SeqSFG/tsync/ (stimulus.py, audio.py, staircase.py, levels.py, logbook.py). New pieces needed:
- 20-s sequence generation with deviant insertion
- key press and release logging on the audio clock
- a block scheduler with Williams-design D order
- the analysis pipeline (percept time series, state-conditioned SDT, GLMM, Cox and survival models).

EEG is optional and should come later. At an intermediate D the paradigm supports percept-locked responses (Gutschalk et al. 2005; Billig et al. 2018), but motor responses complicate it.
proposals.expected_effect_and_power:
Integrated versus segregated d' within D:
- Billig & Carlyon (2016) found d_z = 1.80 with n = 12, using 50-ms deviants in ABA- sequences.
- If the true effect here is half that (d_z = 0.9), a paired test at α = .05 has about 80% power with n = 12 and about 93% with n = 16.

Organisation, P_int(D):
- In Micheyl 2013 Exp. 1 at 9 semitones, alternating minus synchronous P(two streams) was 0.23 with 2.3-s sequences. Build-up over 20 s should widen this.
- Working assumption (to be checked in the pilot): P_int ≈ 0.75, 0.6, 0.45, 0.35 and 0.15 at D = 0, 20, 35, 50 and 100.
- With 10 sequences per D, the per-listener SE is about 0.07, so the D effect on P_int should be very well powered (d_z > 1.5).

Headline d'(D):
- Assume d'_I ≈ 2.5-3 and d'_S ≈ 1, with Δ calibrated near the B-alone floor and Elhilali's roughly 5× synchrony advantage.
- The mixture then predicts overall d' of about 2.4 at D = 0 falling to about 1.2-1.3 at D = 100, a change of about −1.1.
- That is equal and opposite to Micheyl's +0.95 (1.48 to 2.43). Micheyl resolved 0 vs 50 and 0 vs 100 credibly with only n = 7; n = 12-16 with about 40 deviants per D should do at least as well.
- Dual-task cost (−0.59 d′ in Billig & Carlyon) is absorbed into these values.

Mixture and mediation test:
- Within-state D slopes need deviants in both states at the same D, so mainly at D = 20-50: about 120 deviants per listener, about 60 per state.
- The group SE of a within-state slope is roughly 0.15-0.2 d' per 50 ms.
- Treat it as an equivalence test (±0.5 d' per 50 ms) and label it confirmatory only if the pilot variance supports that; otherwise call it exploratory.

Phase durations and first-switch latency versus D: exploratory. About 50 sequences × 2-5 phases each gives 100-250 phases per listener.
proposals.comparability_with_micheyl_2013:
Kept the same as Micheyl 2013:
- B = 1000 Hz with A below it, 100-ms tones, 20-ms ramps, 200-ms SOA, A level rove ±4 dB
- the D anchors 0, 35, 50, 100 ms (20 added)
- d' at fixed levels instead of thresholds
- hierarchical or mixed-model inference
- individual curves reported.

Deliberately different:
(1) Grouping helps the task here, whereas segregation helped in Micheyl, so the predicted slope over D has the opposite sign.
(2) 9 semitones instead of 15. Micheyl's own Exp. 1 shows that synchronous 15-semitone tones are mostly heard as two streams (0.76), which compresses the range for a grouping-helps task. Synchronous and alternating differed credibly only at 9 and 15 semitones. 9 semitones (594.6 Hz) is also the off-frequency captor frequency used by Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham (2010).
(3) 20-s sequences with a concurrent report, rather than 2.4-s sequences.
(4) A timing deviant rather than a 4-dB level increment.

The bridge block (2.4-s sequences, end-of-sequence report, 9 and 15 semitones at D = 0, 35, 100) reproduces the Micheyl Exp. 1 condition, linking the two separations and the two sequence lengths.

For ARO: plot the falling d'(D) next to Micheyl's published rising curve (1.48 to 2.43), and state that they come from different listeners. Under both, show P_int(D) as the common latent variable.

For JASA: a second session running Micheyl Exp. 3's level-increment task at 9 semitones in the same listeners would give within-listener crossing functions. This is the matched-task template of Micheyl & Oxenham (2010). The prediction is that each listener's D50 from P_int marks both the fall in our task and the rise in theirs.
proposals.risks:
1. Naive listeners may find the dual task too hard. Billig & Carlyon's listeners managed it, at a cost of about 0.59 d′.
   - Fallback A: report-only blocks plus separate detection-only blocks. Percept contingency is lost, but P_int(D) remains.
   - Fallback B: a probe report. After each response window the listener answers "one or two just now?", which costs about 2 s per deviant.

2. At 9 semitones, organisation may barely depend on D, or barely switch. The pilot go/no-go criteria cover this, with fallbacks to 6 or 12 semitones. If D = 0 and D = 100 are each near-monostable, the percept-contingent analysis rests on 20-50 ms, which is where it is needed anyway.

3. Listeners may use 'two streams' to mean 'I hear asynchrony'. Mitigated by demos (the alternating trill is one stream), catch sequences, and the objective π_obj(D) check, which does not depend on the report.

4. Ceiling or floor. If d'_I sits near ceiling at D = 0 (Billig reported a maximum of 4.4), the state contrast shrinks. Calibrating Δ on the B-alone floor addresses this; the pilot should check that d'_I < 3.5.

5. Report lag blurs state labels. This biases the state contrast toward zero, so the test is conservative; the sensitivity analyses address it.

6. The deviant might itself trigger switches. Test with deviant-locked switch hazard. Reset after alternating context is not established (Haywood & Roberts 2013).

7. MacBook output is not calibrated in SPL. Levels are nominal (the tsync levels module already flags this); timing within a synthesized sequence is sample-accurate.

8. The raw d'(D) curve still contains a sync-to-async pedestal step (Zera & Green 1993b). Reviewers must be pointed to the within-D state contrast and the mixture test as the actual inference.

tsync, frank verdict: not worth keeping as the primary measure. Its logic is defensible: Christiansen & Oxenham (2014) used a synchronous test burst after offset context and published it in JASA. And the 'reset' critique is not established for alternating contexts (Haywood & Roberts 2013). But four problems remain:
- the ending's displacement grows with D
- 2.4-s contexts sample mostly the grouping-biased first percept
- a 2I-2AFC staircase across a bistable mixture produces exactly the noisy or ceiling thresholds the lab has already seen
- it takes about 40 min for 6 single tracks with no information about organisation.

Reuse its code. The D0_late control and the existing tsync data can be presented as a pilot showing why a state-aware measure is needed.

proposals.name: trmr: pure-tone rhythmic masking release with lagged A captors, at Micheyl 2013's tones and D grid (constant stimuli, single interval)
proposals.one_paragraph: On each trial a 1000-Hz B stream carries one of two target rhythms, "steady" or "gallop". Extra B "distractor" tones, identical to the targets, are scattered irregularly among them and hide the rhythm. Each distractor gets a 420.45-Hz A "captor" that starts D ms after it. When D = 0, each distractor fuses with its captor into an A+B event, so only the bare B targets remain and the rhythm is easy to hear. As D grows, temporal coherence between captor and distractor is lost, the distractors fall back into the B stream, and the rhythm is masked again. Grouping helps here and performance falls with D, which mirrors Micheyl et al. (2013) Exp. 3. The listener judges which rhythm was played, and that judgement does not depend on D. The B waveform is bit-identical across D because the seeds are yoked, and the A waveform only shifts in time. So anything one channel can do on its own (B alone, A alone, or a timing Weber law) is flat across D. Only binding A with B can produce a fall. The precedent is rhythmic masking release (Turgeon et al. 2002, 2005): fusion is full at synchrony, partial at 10-20 ms and absent by 20-40 ms. The 2005 study used brief tones, 18 naive listeners and constant stimuli, with Pc 0.99-1.00 at 0 ms and 0.53-0.56 without captors. The task is easy to explain ("steady or galloping?"), it uses single-interval trials of about 2.9 s, and each D gets 48 fixed-level trials, so one ~44-min visit yields a full Pc/d′ function of D. About 70% of the code can come from tsync (audio engine, calibration, Qt runner, logbook, simulated listeners). Frank verdict on tsync: its logic is not stupid. Christiansen & Oxenham (2014) published the same "synchronous test after offset context" design in JASA. But it should not be the primary measure for this deadline. Retire the paradigm and keep its code.
proposals.stimulus:
Tones: B = 1000 Hz and A = 420.45 Hz (15 semitones below), the same as Micheyl 2013. Each tone is 100 ms with 20-ms raised-cosine ramps, at 48 kHz, diotic (MacBook built-in headphone output). B is 60 dB SPL. A is 60 dB SPL, roved ±4 dB uniformly per tone so loudness cannot serve as a cue. Micheyl's 1-2 A "decoy" increments are dropped.

Target rhythms (B tones without captors), 7 tones in a 2.4-s span:
- STEADY: onsets 0, 400, 800, 1200, 1600, 2000, 2400 ms.
- GALLOP: onsets 0, 267, 800, 1067, 1600, 1867, 2400 ms (inter-onset intervals alternate 267 and 533 ms; same count, same mean rate).
Add a random global offset of 0-100 ms.

Distractors: 6 B tones per trial. This number is the difficulty knob; it is tuned in the pilot within 4-8 and then frozen. Their onsets are drawn uniformly over [100, 2500] ms by rejection sampling under two rules:
(i) at least 150 ms between any two B onsets;
(ii) the next B onset comes at least 220 ms after a distractor, so a captor at D = 100 still leads the next target by at least 120 ms and cannot capture it.

Captors: one A tone per distractor, starting at distractor onset + D, with A lagging B as in Micheyl. Total sound is about 2.9 s.

Conditions (6), interleaved: D = 0, 20, 35, 50 and 100 ms, plus CTRL-random. D = 35, 50 and 100 are Micheyl's values; 20 is added because Turgeon 2002 and Micheyl's listeners L6 and L8 put the steep part below about 35 ms. Micheyl's 71 ms is dropped because it was not credibly different from its neighbours. In CTRL-random there are the same number of A tones with the same rove, placed at random under the same spacing rules but uncoupled from any distractor (at least 150 ms from every B onset). It sets the floor for "A present, no binding".

Yoking: each B pattern (targets, distractors, offset) and each A-rove draw is used once in every one of the 6 conditions, in different blocks. The B channel is therefore identical across conditions, and the A channel differs only in its timing.

Verification battery, which must pass before any listener runs (using the tsync verify/sim machinery):
- On 10,000 simulated trials, ideal observers that see only B onsets or only A onsets reach Pc ≤ 0.62. The B-only observer uses inter-onset-interval histograms plus the autocorrelation at 400 ms; the A-only observer uses the gap pattern.
- The B buffer's SHA is identical across D for yoked seeds.
- No A onset falls within 120 ms of a non-partner B onset.

Subjective add-on (Micheyl Exp. 1 protocol): regular sequences of 12 A + 12 B tones, 2.4 s long, at D = 0, 35 and 100 with 15 semitones, plus a catch condition of D = 0 at 1 semitone, which should be heard as one stream. D = 100 at 5 Hz is pure alternation and serves as the two-stream catch.
proposals.task_and_measure:
Main task: one interval per trial and a two-alternative identification: "Was the hidden beat STEADY or GALLOPING?" Keys are ← (steady) and → (gallop), read by physical position as in tsync. Feedback is given on every trial (550 ms). Silence between trials is at least 1.5 s after feedback.

Dependent variables per listener and condition:
- Pc.
- d′ = z(H) − z(F), with "gallop" as the signal and a log-linear correction. This puts it on the same axis as Micheyl's d′.

Primary pre-registered test: the paired difference Pc(D0) − Pc(D100) > 0 across listeners. Secondary: a monotonic trend over D.

Model: GLMM with logit(correct) ~ D (factor) + block + previous-trial condition + (D | listener). Per listener, fit a logistic in D whose lower asymptote is fixed at that listener's CTRL-random Pc, giving D50 and a slope. Compare the D50s with the subjective 20-44 ms one/two-stream boundary (Christiansen, Jepsen & Dau 2014) and with the 0→35 ms jumps of Micheyl's L6 and L8.

Subjective block: after each 2.4-s sequence, the listener answers "one stream or two?" This gives P(two streams | D) per listener, which is correlated with the objective D50.

Talk figure: our d′ falling with D next to Micheyl's published d′ rising from 1.48 to 2.43, on the same D axis and with the same tones.
proposals.why_grouping_helps_and_falls_with_D:
The rhythm can only be recovered if the listener knows which B tones are distractors. On its own, the B channel holds 13 identical tones at irregular times. That pattern is the same for both answers in distribution and literally identical across D, because the seeds are yoked. On its own, the A channel is a random pattern that only shifts in time with D. The only information about which tones are distractors is the cross-frequency relation "this B has an A partner". At D = 0, temporal coherence binds each distractor to its captor into one A+B event (Elhilali et al. 2009; Shamma, Elhilali & Micheyl 2011), so the lone B targets stand out as the rhythm. This is rhythmic masking release (Turgeon et al. 2002, 2005).

As D grows, the onset asynchrony breaks the binding. Turgeon 2002 found partial fusion at 10-20 ms and none at 20-40 ms. Turgeon 2005, with tones, found 75% thresholds of 32-37 ms. Christiansen & Oxenham (2014) found that a fixed offset of 40-60 ms abolishes a grouping-dependent masking release (CMR). Once the binding breaks, distractors and targets merge into one irregular B stream and Pc falls toward the CTRL-random floor.

Because every single-channel strategy is invariant to D by construction, any fall with D has to come from processing A and B together. That is the "grouping helps" signature, opposite in sign to Micheyl 2013 Exp. 3, where binding A to B hurts detection of the B increment.
proposals.confounds_and_controls:
Weber / pedestal: none. The judged quantity is rhythm identity, which is the same at every D, and no timing judgement is scaled by D. This removes the tcoh problem, where the threshold grew as about 0.4 × D.

Single-stream strategies: the B channel is bit-identical across D (yoked seeds), and the A channel is a pure time shift. Both are therefore flat in D by construction. The ideal-observer battery caps their absolute value at Pc ≤ 0.62, and CTRL-random measures it empirically in each listener.

Local acoustics:
(a) Peripheral masking of a B distractor by a simultaneous A could weaken distractors at small D. But A is 15 semitones (1.25 octaves) below B, A is roved ±4 dB, and upward spread from a 60-dB 420-Hz tone onto 1000 Hz is small. A masking account would also follow overlap, which falls linearly from 100% to 0% over 0-100 ms. Grouping predicts a steep fall by 20-35 ms. The shape of the curve, (Pc0 − Pc35)/(Pc0 − Pc100), separates the two accounts, as Turgeon 2005 Exp. 3 did when it separated asynchrony from overlap.
(b) Spurious capture of targets by a captor at large D is prevented by the spacing rule (next B at least 220 ms after a distractor).

Context and sequence: all conditions share the same sequence length and have no anomalous ending event. The tsync risk of a reset at the context-probe boundary (Roberts, Glasberg & Moore 2008; Haywood & Roberts 2013) is therefore absent.

Carry-over: D is randomised within blocks, balanced as 8 trials per condition per block, and the previous trial's condition is a GLMM covariate (Snyder et al. 2008).

Learning: feedback could teach listeners to match "B followed by A at lag D" at intermediate D, which would flatten the curve over the session. Block is a covariate, and a first-half vs second-half × D interaction is pre-registered. Training is mostly at D = 0 and on the clean rhythms, so it teaches the rhythm categories, not lag matching.

Instructions: the same neutral wording for every condition, because intention shifts organisation (Billig, Davis & Carlyon 2018).

Direction of D: A lags B, as in Micheyl. Listeners tolerate a low-tone lag more than the reverse (Wojtczak, Mehta & Oxenham 2017), so the main conditions keep Micheyl's direction for comparability. A B-lags-A probe is noted as a JASA-stage extension, not part of the visit.
proposals.bistability_handling:
Is it bistable? Plausibly yes, at the level of the trial-to-trial percept:
- Auditory streaming is genuinely bistable (Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006; Moore & Gockel 2012).
- At 15 semitones, synchronous A/B tones were reported as two streams on about 76% of trials, with large and even reversed individual differences (Micheyl 2013 Exp. 1).
- Micheyl's L6 and L8 jumped abruptly between D = 0 and 35 ms. A step, not a ramp, is what a mixture of two discrete states predicts.
- Billig & Carlyon (2016) showed that objective performance follows the momentary percept (d = 1.80).

Within a 2.4-2.9-s fresh-start trial, however, switches should be rare. Phase durations are about 4-9 s (Rankin, Sussman & Rinzel 2015), and the first percept is biased toward grouping and has inertia (Hupé & Pressnitzer 2012). So each trial samples one state, and a condition's Pc is a mixture: Pc(D) = p_bound(D)·Pc_bound + (1 − p_bound(D))·Pc_floor. No study has measured switching as a function of A-B onset delay, so this remains an inference.

What that implies, and how the design follows from it:
(1) Staircases are the wrong tool. They assume a smooth monotonic psychometric function, while a mixture produces plateaus and lapse-like trials. This is a plausible reason the tpair and tsync tracks were noisy or hit ceiling. Use fixed-level constant stimuli instead, with a per-listener mixture/logistic fit: p_bound(D) as a logistic with D50, the floor fixed at CTRL-random, and a lapse term.
(2) Use short fresh trials with at least 1.5 s of silence between them, so each trial sits in the first-percept regime. That regime is the one most sensitive to stimulus parameters (Denham et al. 2013), and it maximises the D = 0 anchor for a grouping-helps task.
(3) Report individual curves and D50s, because individual switching biases are stable traits (Denham et al. 2014).
(4) Run a cheap 2-min subjective block of P(two streams | D = 0, 35, 100), with catch trials of the kind Farkas et al. 2016 recommend. It answers the user's bistability question directly, links to Micheyl Exp. 1, and lets objective D50 be correlated with subjective organisation.
(5) Do not use concurrent continuous reporting during the main task. It costs about 0.59 d′ (Billig & Carlyon 2016) and would push the visit over budget. Percept-conditioned analysis is a JASA-stage or EEG follow-up.
proposals.session_plan:
One visit, about 44 min (shorter for fast responders):
1. Consent, questionnaire (musical and percussion training), sound check: 4 min.
2. Familiarisation: 4 examples of each rhythm with B only and no distractors, then 4 examples at D = 0 with distractors and captors, then 2 at CTRL-random ("this is hard; guess"). About 2 min.
3. Training: 20 trials with feedback, 12 at D = 0 and 8 mixed across conditions. Criterion: at least 9 of the 12 D = 0 trials correct, with up to 2 repeats. About 2.5 min. Listeners who fail are paid and excluded by a pre-registered rule.
4. Main: 6 blocks × 48 trials = 288 trials, 8 per condition per block, randomised, giving 48 trials per condition. One trial ≈ 0.4 s ready + 2.9 s sound + about 0.9 s response + 0.55 s feedback + 1.5 s silence ≈ 6.2 s. Each block is about 5 min, with 30-s rests, so about 32 min in total. An optional 7th block (56 per condition) can be run if the clock allows.
5. Subjective block: 32 trials (D = 0, 35, 100 at 15 semitones, plus D = 0 at 1 semitone, 8 each), about 2.5 min.
6. Debrief: 1 min.

Listeners: recruit 16 naive listeners and aim for at least 12 completers after exclusions.

proposals.expected_effect_and_power:
Anchors from the evidence:
- Turgeon 2005, brief tones, 18 naive listeners: Pc 0.99-1.00 at 0 ms, 0.53-0.56 with no captors, 75% thresholds of 32-37 ms. Its captors shared a spectral region and F0 with the distractors.
- Micheyl 2013 Exp. 1: 15-semitone synchronous pure tones fuse less (P(two streams) ≈ 0.76).
- Christiansen & Oxenham 2014: a grouping effect that is reduced but not abolished at 40-60 ms unless context surrounds the target.

Planning assumptions (conservative): Pc(D0) ≈ 0.85 (d′ ≈ 2.1), Pc(D35) ≈ 0.68, and Pc(D100) ≈ Pc(CTRL) ≈ 0.60 (d′ ≈ 0.5). That gives an expected Δd′ ≈ −1.5, larger than and opposite to Micheyl's +0.95 (1.48→2.43; 0 vs 100 ms credible interval [0.03, 2.05] with 7 listeners).

Per listener, with 48 trials per condition, the SE of Pc(D0) − Pc(D100) is sqrt(.85·.15/48 + .6·.4/48) ≈ 0.087. An individual effect of 0.25 is therefore about 2.9 SE, so most individual curves can be read on their own (Micheyl's could not: L3 was near chance and several listeners showed weak trends).

Group, assuming a between-listener SD of the effect of about 0.15: d_z ≈ 1.6, giving t(11) ≈ 5.7 at N = 12, with power > 0.99.

Pessimistic case (effect halved to 0.12, SD 0.12, d_z = 1.0): power ≈ 0.90 at N = 12 (two-sided α = .05) and about 0.97 at N = 16.

The GLMM uses all 288 trials per listener, and the per-listener D50 is estimable when the drop is at least 0.15.

The pilot go/no-go thresholds were chosen so that the pessimistic case still clears them.
proposals.risks:
1. The D = 0 anchor may be weaker than in Turgeon. Their captors and distractors shared a spectral region and F0, while ours are pure tones 15 semitones apart. Mitigation: the distractor-count knob in the pilot. Even without timbral fusion, coincidence detection at D = 0 is very precise (Zera & Green 1993 floor), and the task only needs that. If D = 0 Pc stays below 0.75 after 2 iterations, use the fallback.

2. The curve may saturate early, falling to the floor by 20-35 ms so that 50-100 sit flat. This is not a failure: it is the predicted contrast with Micheyl's later rise, and D = 20 and 35 are in the grid to catch it.

3. The fall may instead be shallow and extend past 100 ms, because 100-ms tones still overlap partly at D ≤ 100 (Turgeon 2005: overlap matters; Neilans & Dent 2015: humans fuse partly overlapping tones). Mitigation: the curve shape is analysed, and D = 100 is equal to perfect alternation (no overlap) as an anchor.

4. Information may leak into a single channel (rhythm recoverable from B or A alone). The ideal-observer battery and CTRL-random catch this, and any such leak is constant across D by construction, so it lowers sensitivity but cannot fake a D effect.

5. Learning of lag-matching with feedback over the session; a block × D analysis is pre-registered.

6. A new, unpublished pure-tone RMR with 100-ms tones. Turgeon 2005's exact parameters and intermediate Pc values come from figures or archived text and some could not be verified, so do not cite specific intermediate numbers.

7. Code slip. The generator and verification battery are new, but everything else comes from tsync. Budget one week, with the hard go/no-go date of Nov 26.

8. MacBook output: recalibrate both frequencies with tsync's calibrate command and keep the device-match guard.

9. Previous-trial carry-over (Snyder 2008). Modelled as a covariate rather than removed.

10. Wojtczak 2017's lag-tolerance asymmetry may raise D50 for A-lags-B. Accepted for comparability with Micheyl.

VERDICT ON tsync: do not keep it as the primary measure.
- Its core logic is legitimate: Christiansen & Oxenham 2014 used a synchronous test after offset context, and Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010 showed capture raising synchrony thresholds to about 44-50 ms. It is not stupid.
- But the re-synchronised ending moves each stream's last tone by D/2 in opposite directions: 50 ms at D = 100, which is 25% of the 200-ms inter-onset interval and about 3-4 times the 6-8% single-stream anisochrony threshold (Hirsh et al. 1990). So a salient rhythm violation co-varies with D.
- D0_late shifts both tones in the same direction, so it does not match that violation.
- A deviant at the context-probe boundary risks resetting the organisation, although Haywood & Roberts 2013 found single-deviant resetting only after constant-frequency inducers, so this is possible but not established.
- The two-interval trials (2 × 2.4 s) and one staircase per condition give 6 noisy thresholds in about 40 min, with no within-listener reliability, in a regime where bistability makes staircases a poor tool.

Keep its infrastructure, which becomes about 70% of trmr, and drop the paradigm.

verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the full text. A was 1000 Hz and B was 6 or 15 semitones above it (one Exp. 1 figure caption says 6 and 9). Tones were 100 ms with 10-ms ramps at 60 dB SPL. Five captors came before and two after the target A, with 50-ms gaps; off-frequency captors were 9 semitones below A (594.6 Hz). The staircase was 3-down-1-up with Δt capped at 100 ms; Exp. 2 interleaved two tracks starting at 100 ms. Listeners: 6 in Exp. 1, 8 in Exp. 2 (4 of them from Exp. 1), 4 per sub-experiment in Exp. 3. Each listener did about 3 × 2-h sessions (about 6 h). This total covers the whole study; the colleague's 'Exp. 1 took about 6 h' is imprecise. With on-frequency captors, mean thresholds were about 43 ms (Exp. 1, 6 semitones), about 50 ms (Exp. 1, 15 semitones; the authors note this may be ceiling) and about 44 ms (Exp. 2, 15 semitones). No-captor and off-frequency means are not given in the text, only in Figs. 2-3, so the colleague's 'a few ms' is unverified as a number. Captor-condition η² was 0.657 in Exp. 1 and 0.777 in Exp. 2. Caveat: the captors here are an on-frequency A sequence, not a lagged A–B context, so whether a D-lagged context does the same thing is untested.

verified.citation: Billig AJ, Carlyon RP (2016). Automaticity and primacy of auditory streaming: concurrent subjective and objective measures. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 42(3):339-353
verified.corrected_claim: Matches the full text. Tones were 50 ms with 10-ms ramps; within-triplet gaps were 75 ms and between-triplet gaps 200 ms, giving a 500-ms period. A was roved over one octave around 800 Hz, with B 4 or 8 semitones above. Sequences were 35, 37 or 39 triplets (17.5–19.5 s). The deviant B was 50 ms late, placed early (triplet 6), middle or late, with 0–3 deviants per sequence. The same 12 listeners did both experiments. Exp. 1: 96 objective + 32 subjective trials, about 90 min. Exp. 2: 48 trials, about 30 min. Integrated vs segregated detection: t(11) = 4.15, p = .002, d = 1.80. Deviants falling in segregated phases: 2% early, 41% middle, 64% late. Adding the percept improved the logistic model, χ²(1) = 77.40, and adjusted-count pseudo-R² rose from .22 to .36. Listeners were more conservative when segregated (t(11) = 8.93). The dual-task cost was Δd′ = −0.59. Maximum d′ was 4.4, and more than a third of early d′ scores were within 0.5 of it.
verified.relevance: Verified, and the most direct answer to the bistability question: objective performance tracks the momentary percept beyond what the stimulus parameters predict.

verified.citation: Pressnitzer D, Hupé JM (2006). Temporal dynamics of auditory and visual bistability reveal common principles of perceptual organization. Curr Biol 16(13):1351-1357
verified.corrected_claim: The abstract confirms that auditory streaming is bistable. Percepts alternate spontaneously, and the temporal dynamics and susceptibility to volitional control resemble visual plaids. Subject-specific biases did not correlate across modalities. Specific phase-duration numbers were not checked.
verified.relevance: Verified support for treating one vs two streams as bistable, with listener-specific biases that could underlie the large individual differences in Micheyl et al. (2013).

verified.citation: Micheyl C, Hanson C, Demany L, Shamma S, Oxenham AJ (2013). Auditory stream segregation for alternating and synchronous tones. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 39(6):1568-1580
verified.corrected_claim: Matches the full text. Tones were 100 ms with 20-ms ramps; B was 1000 Hz and A was 1, 3, 6, 9 or 15 semitones below. There were 24 tones per sequence (2.3 s synchronous, 2.4 s alternating). Exp. 1 at 15 semitones: P(two streams) ≈ 0.97 alternating vs ≈ 0.76 synchronous, with 7 listeners and 28 presentations per condition. L7 showed a reversed trend, possibly from beats. Exp. 2 task: a 4-dB increment (60→64 dB SPL) on one B tone, not among the first four, with p = .5. A distractors were roved ±4 dB, and 1–2 A tones also received a 4-dB increment as foils. Exp. 2 had 8 listeners with 104–216 trials per condition (more than 200 in 86% of cases) in blocks of 51–52 trials, after ≥100 practice trials. Exp. 3 had 7 listeners at 15 semitones with D = 0, 35, 50, 71 and 100 ms. Group d′ was about 1.48 at 0 ms and 2.43 at 100 ms. Only the 0 vs 100 ms (MAP 1.10) and 0 vs 50 ms (MAP 0.65) differences were credible. L6 and L8 jumped sharply between 0 and 35 ms, L3 was often near chance, and L1, L2 and L5 showed weaker trends. Per-condition trial counts for Exp. 3 are not reported separately; the trial numbers come from Exp. 2.
verified.relevance: Verified counterpart study. It sets the stimulus family, the D grid and the fixed-level d′ approach to mirror.

verified.citation: Christiansen SK, Jepsen ML, Dau T (2011). Modeling auditory grouping based on a temporal coherence analysis. Proceedings of Forum Acusticum 2011, Aalborg, pp. 2673-2678
verified.corrected_claim: The DTU Orbit record confirms the authors, venue and pages. The abstract reports one stream when asynchrony was 'less than 20–44 ms' and two streams for larger asynchronies. The organisation depended on absolute asynchrony across a range of tone-repetition rates. Tone durations, rates and per-listener boundaries were not available, and the full text was not retrieved. The peer-reviewed follow-up is Christiansen, Jepsen & Dau (2014, JASA 135:323, doi 10.1121/1.4845675), whose Exp. (ii) covers grouping by onset/offset synchrony; its numbers were not checked. Cite that paper rather than the proceeding.
verified.relevance: A plausible place for the integration/segregation boundary in D (about 20–44 ms) to guide the D grid. The evidence comes from subjective reports, so treat it as a guide only.

verified.citation: Vliegen J, Moore BCJ, Oxenham AJ (1999). The role of spectral and periodicity cues in auditory stream segregation, measured using a temporal discrimination task. J Acoust Soc Am 106(2):938-945
verified.corrected_claim: Matches the abstract. In ABA ABA sequences, B fell either at the midpoint between A tones or slightly delayed. A was 300 Hz (pure tones) or had F0 = 100 Hz (complex tones). Conditions were pure tones, unresolved harmonics (>10th) with a fixed passband varying only F0, and same F0 with a shifted passband. Five intervals from 1 to 18 semitones were tested. Shift thresholds rose with interval in all conditions, most when spectrum differed.
verified.relevance: Verified canonical integration-helps paradigm with a pedestal-free reference, but the grouping variable is not time, so it does not apply directly to D.

verified.citation: Roberts B, Glasberg BR, Moore BCJ (2002). Primitive stream segregation of tone sequences without differences in fundamental frequency or passband. J Acoust Soc Am 112(5):2074-2085
verified.corrected_claim: Matches the abstract. Complex tones had unresolved harmonics (F0 = 100 Hz), 60-ms duration and a 40-ms intertone interval, at 70 dB SPL in pink noise. Listeners picked which of two sequences had the irregular rhythm, made by a progressive B delay. Passbands were 1250–2500, 1768–3536 or 2500–5000 Hz, and phases were cosine, alternating or random. Passband or phase differences raised thresholds. In Exp. 2, continuous judgments of long ABA sequences showed segregation driven by the same factors.
verified.relevance: Verified. Progressive delays avoid a single-event pedestal for non-temporal grouping cues, but the cue still rests on A–B timing.

verified.citation: Roberts B, Glasberg BR, Moore BCJ (2008). Effects of the build-up and resetting of auditory stream segregation on temporal discrimination. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 34(4):992-1006
verified.corrected_claim: Matches the abstract. A 2.0-s fixed-frequency inducer was followed by a 0.6-s test of 3 L–H cycles, isochronous or with H delayed, in a 2-interval task. H–L separation was 0–12 semitones. The inducer differed from the L tones in frequency, number of onsets, tone:silence ratio, level or lateralization. Every inducer–L difference pushed thresholds back toward the no-inducer case, i.e. reset segregation and improved discrimination.
verified.relevance: Verified. Any abrupt change between context and probe (such as the re-synchronised tsync ending) can reset grouping and contaminate an integration measure.

verified.citation: Bregman AS, Campbell J (1971). Primary auditory stream segregation and perception of order in rapid sequences of tones. J Exp Psychol 89(2):244-249
verified.corrected_claim: The paper exists; correct DOI is 10.1037/h0031163. PubMed has no abstract, and the full text was not checked here. The summary (order reportable within high and low groups but not across them in rapid 6-tone loops) matches the standard account in the literature, but the stated rate and frequency details are unverified.
verified.relevance: Historical origin of cross-stream order judgments. As the colleague notes, order judgments are unsuitable when D is the variable.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Micheyl C, Kreft H, Shamma S, Oxenham AJ (2013). Temporal coherence versus harmonicity in auditory stream formation. J Acoust Soc Am 133(3):EL188-EL194
verified.corrected_claim: Verified from the abstract. A performance-based test of temporal coherence: listeners discriminated frequency shifts in a regular sequence of target pure tones inside a constant or randomly varying multi-tone background. Targets were temporally coherent or incoherent with the background, and harmonic or inharmonic with it. Temporal incoherence made segregation easier, and inharmonicity helped even when targets and maskers were coherent.
verified.relevance: Missed by the colleague. It is the Shamma/Oxenham group's own objective temporal-coherence test with pure tones. It is a segregation-helps task, so it belongs on the Micheyl 2013 side of the ARO contrast and shows harmonicity as a confound to control (15 semitones is not a harmonic ratio, so less of a concern).

verified.citation: [ADDED] Hupé JM, Pressnitzer D (2012). The initial phase of auditory and visual scene analysis. Philos Trans R Soc Lond B Biol Sci 367(1591):942-953
verified.corrected_claim: Verified from the abstract. At stimulus onset, perceptual organisation is biased toward the grouped (one-stream) interpretation, and this first percept has 'inertia': it lasts longer than later percepts. That is why the probability of segregation builds up over time. In streaming, both the first-percept bias and inertia survived a level-difference manipulation.
verified.relevance: Missed by the colleague. It is the mechanistic reason short sequences like Micheyl's 2.4 s mostly sample the first, grouped percept. It argues for controlling sequence length and placing the probe either inside the first phase (where grouping is near-certain at small D) or late (where alternations dominate).

verified.citation: [ADDED] Snyder JS, Carter OL, Lee SK, Hannon EE, Alain C (2008). Effects of context on auditory stream segregation. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 34(4):1007-1016
verified.corrected_claim: Verified from the abstract. A larger Δf on preceding trials reduced streaming on the current trial. This was not a response bias, and it was weaker but still present with a 5.76-s inter-trial silence.
verified.relevance: Missed by the colleague. If D is randomised trial by trial, the previous trial's D may shift the current trial's grouping. Counterbalance or model the previous-trial D, or use long enough inter-trial intervals.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Haywood NR, Roberts B (2013). Build-up of auditory stream segregation induced by tone sequences of constant or alternating frequency and the resetting effects of single deviants. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 39(6):1652-1666
verified.corrected_claim: Verified from the abstract. Replacing only the FINAL inducer tone with silence reset build-up, while replacing the 4th or 7th did not. A constant-frequency inducer reached its maximum effect after only 3 tones. A single deviant (a longer tone) caused resetting only with constant-frequency inducers.
verified.relevance: Missed by the colleague. A single deviant at the context–probe boundary can reset grouping, which directly threatens tsync's anomalous re-synchronised ending and any probe that departs from the context rhythm.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Darwin CJ, Ciocca V (1992). Grouping in pitch perception: effects of onset asynchrony and ear of presentation of a mistuned component. J Acoust Soc Am 91(6):3381-3390
verified.corrected_claim: Verified from the abstract. A mistuned 4th harmonic (F0 = 155 Hz) contributed less to the complex's pitch only when it began ≥160 ms early, and not at all beyond 300 ms. Effects were larger for 90-ms sounds than for 410-ms sounds.
verified.relevance: Missed by the colleague. It shows that the onset-asynchrony window for 'grouping' depends strongly on the task: 20–40 ms in RMR versus ≥160 ms for pitch integration. So the fusion window for 100-ms tones in an RMR-style task must be piloted, not assumed.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Zera J, Green DM (1993). Detecting temporal onset and offset asynchrony in multicomponent complexes. J Acoust Soc Am 93(2):1038-1052
verified.corrected_claim: Verified from the abstract. Onset-asynchrony detection thresholds in harmonic complexes reached a minimum of about 0.2 ms. Offset thresholds were about 10× larger. For log-spaced complexes, some thresholds were nearly two orders of magnitude larger. Detection relies on comparisons across frequency channels.
verified.relevance: Missed by the colleague. It is the floor for a zero-pedestal synchrony probe: in isolation, asynchrony between widely spaced components is detected at a few ms or better. Any D-context effect on a synchrony probe should be measured against a no-context baseline (cf. Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010 no-captor condition).

verified.citation: [ADDED] Teki S, Chait M, Kumar S, Shamma S, Griffiths TD (2013). Segregation of complex acoustic scenes based on temporal coherence. eLife 2:e00699
verified.corrected_claim: Verified from the abstract. Listeners were highly sensitive to coherent 'figures' in stochastic figure-ground stimuli and tolerated spectral and temporal perturbations. Adaptation-based models could not explain the behaviour, but a temporal-coherence model could.
verified.relevance: Missed by the colleague, and relevant because the lab's EEG project is figure-ground. It shows coherence-based segregation in a different behavioural format. O'Sullivan, Shamma & Lalor (2015, J Neurosci 35:7256, doi 10.1523/JNEUROSCI.4973-14.2015, verified) give an EEG regression approach to tracking coherence that could pair with any D manipulation.

candidate_measures: 1. KEEP, now the primary candidate: rhythmic masking release (RMR) with Micheyl's tones. B-frequency target rhythm plus identical irregular B distractors, with A-frequency captors under the distractors only at lag D; task is 2AFC rhythm identity. The basis is verified: Turgeon 2002 and 2005 confirmed via PubMed. CORRECTION: Turgeon, Bregman & Roberts (2005) already used brief TONES, not only noises, so the tonal version has precedent. The 2002 noise-burst window (full fusion at 0 ms, partial at 10–20 ms, none at 20–40 ms) may not transfer to 100-ms tones; Darwin & Ciocca (1992) show the window can be ≥160 ms in other grouping tasks. Pilot the D grid. The parameters 48-ms bursts and 384/768-ms rhythms are UNVERIFIED and should not be cited.

2. KEEP with stated caveats: constant synchronous-vs-asynchronous probe after a jittered, D-lagged context. The supporting evidence is verified: Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham (2010) found asynchrony thresholds of about 44 ms with on-frequency captors (η² = .78 for the captor effect), and Christiansen & Oxenham (2014) showed jittered synchronous precursors leave CMR intact. Two added risks from verified papers: a single deviant at the context–probe boundary can reset build-up (Haywood & Roberts 2013; Roberts et al. 2008), and the previous trial's grouping state carries over (Snyder et al. 2008). Include a no-context baseline; Zera & Green (1993) show isolated asynchrony thresholds are a few ms or less.
3. KEEP as a reference only: precursor-offset CMR (Christiansen & Oxenham 2014). Fully verified, but it takes ≥1–3 h of training and uses noise bands, so it is not feasible for one 45-min visit.

4. KEEP as a supplementary block: concurrent percept report plus objective task (Billig & Carlyon 2016). Fully verified: t(11) = 4.15, d = 1.80; pseudo-R² .22→.36; dual-task cost Δd′ = −0.59; 48 trials in about 30 min with 17.5–19.5-s sequences.

5. KEEP: fixed-level constant stimuli with d′ per D instead of staircases. Supported by Micheyl et al. (2013), which used 104–216 trials per condition (more than 200 in 86% of cases; verified for Exp. 2), and by the bistability evidence (Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006; Billig & Carlyon 2016). CORRECTION to the colleague's efficiency numbers: Thompson et al. (2011) Exp. 2 had 96 trials of 13.5 s in about 25 min, with at most one deviant per sequence. That was Exp. 2, not 'Exp. 3'.

6. KEEP as a negative or control example: ABA-/AB delay-deviant detection. It carries a D pedestal (Weber growth). Use only with a single-stream (no-A) control of the kind verified in Micheyl & Oxenham (2010): slow/fast no-A ratios of 1.82, 1.35 and 1.20, with the rate effect surviving correction at p = .048.

7. KEEP as an opposite-sign control only: cross-stream order judgment. Bregman & Campbell (1971) exists (DOI 10.1037/h0031163), but its details are unverified here. The logical argument does not depend on them.

8. KEEP, with a corrected source: sampling and sequence-length guidance. The 20–44 ms subjective boundary is confirmed in the Christiansen, Jepsen & Dau (2011) proceeding abstract; cite the JASA 2014 follow-up (doi 10.1121/1.4845675). Hupé & Pressnitzer (2012) give a verified mechanism: the first percept is biased toward grouping and lasts longer than later ones. So short (2.4-s) sequences sample mostly the grouped first phase, and a D × sequence-length interaction is a principled diagnostic that separates grouping from Weber accounts.
