9. NEW (design hygiene from added verified papers): randomise D across trials but model or counterbalance the previous trial's D (Snyder et al. 2008). Make the probe continuous with the context rhythm to avoid resetting (Haywood & Roberts 2013). These apply to options 1, 2 and 4.
evidence.angle_summary:
All 13 cited papers exist, and their PubMed IDs and DOIs resolve: 12 are in PubMed and the Christiansen, Jepsen & Dau 2011 proceeding is in the DTU Orbit repository. I found no fabrication. The core claims hold up against abstracts or full text (PMC for Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010; Christiansen & Oxenham 2014; Micheyl & Oxenham 2010; Micheyl et al. 2013; Billig & Carlyon 2016; and the Thompson 2011 PDF).

Corrections needed:
(a) Thompson et al. 2011. The '2 × 48 trials, about 25 min' design is Exp. 2, the attention-switch experiment: 13.5-s sequences, A roved, at most one 50-ms deviant per sequence. It is not 'Exp. 3'.
(b) Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010. The text gives only the on-frequency captor thresholds: about 43 and 50 ms (order discrimination) and about 44 ms (asynchrony detection). 'A few ms' without captors appears only in the figures. The 1.84 factor means Exp. 2 thresholds were 1.84× smaller than Exp. 1, even though SDT predicted them to be 2.91× larger. The 6-h figure is the whole-study participation per listener. Ear separation removed the captor effect only when the captors and target A were in a different ear from B.
(c) Micheyl & Oxenham 2010. The 4-of-7 individual correlation applies to the integration task only; the segregation task had 2 of 7. The direction of the rate effect was not verified.
(d) Turgeon et al. 2005 used brief tones, not noises, which helps the RMR proposal. The 2002 burst and rhythm parameters (48 ms; 384/768 ms) could not be verified because the PDF host is dead.
(e) Bregman & Campbell 1971: the correct DOI is 10.1037/h0031163. The details are unverified.
(f) Christiansen, Jepsen & Dau 2011: the 20–44 ms boundary is confirmed only from the proceeding abstract. Cite the JASA 2014 follow-up instead.

The colleague's answer on bistability is supported. Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006 show genuine bistability in streaming, and Billig & Carlyon 2016 show objective performance tracking the momentary percept (d = 1.80). The added Hupé & Pressnitzer 2012 explains why Micheyl's short sequences sample mostly the grouped first percept.

I added seven verified papers the colleague missed:
- Micheyl, Kreft, Shamma & Oxenham 2013: an objective temporal-coherence test with pure tones (segregation-helps).
- Hupé & Pressnitzer 2012: first-percept grouping bias and inertia.
- Snyder et al. 2008: the previous trial's context biases streaming, which matters if D is randomised.
- Haywood & Roberts 2013: a single deviant at the context–test boundary resets build-up, which directly undercuts the tsync ending.
- Darwin & Ciocca 1992: the asynchrony window depends on the task (≥160 ms for pitch), so the RMR window must be piloted.
- Zera & Green 1993: the floor for asynchrony detection.
- Teki et al. 2013: coherence-based figure-ground. O'Sullivan, Shamma & Lalor 2015 (also verified) gives an EEG approach to the same question.

No candidate measure rests only on a refuted finding, so all are kept, with the caveats corrected. RMR with tones (Turgeon 2005 precedent) and a jittered-context synchrony probe remain the best integration-helps options with no pedestal.

verified.citation: Turgeon M, Bregman AS, Roberts B (2005). Rhythmic masking release: effects of asynchrony, temporal overlap, harmonic relations, and source separation on cross-spectral grouping. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 31:939-953
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the full text (archived PDF). Correct: Exp. 1 had 18 naive listeners in free field. Tones were 48 ms with 8-ms quarter-sine ramps. Captor SOAs were 0, 12, 24, 36 and 48 ms. Sequences lasted 8.8 s, held 15 target tones at a mean of 1.7 tones/s, and used ITIs of 384 and 768 ms. The task was single-interval 2-rhythm identification with feedback, plus a 1-5 clarity rating. At 0 ms, Pc was 0.99-1.00 at every angle. No-captor controls gave Pc 0.53-0.56 (SE 0.03-0.05). Pc fell monotonically with SOA (F(4,32) = 81.24). At 48 ms, Pc was still above the no-captor control (t(17) = 2.66 and 3.41). Weibull 75% thresholds were 32.42-36.72 ms. Exp. 2 (headphones, 67 dB SPL): Pc fell from at least 0.88 to at most 0.68. Dichotic presentation lowered Pc (F(1,17) = 27.55) and lowered thresholds by 13.8 ms (same F0) or 8.7 ms (different F0). Corrections: (a) the intermediate Pc values (0.97, 0.82-0.92, 0.70-0.78, 0.60-0.65) appear only in Fig. 3 and could not be verified from text. (b) Harmonicity did have a small significant effect on Pc (F(1,17) = 6.22) and a large one on clarity (F(1,17) = 69.21). Source separation had no effect on Pc (F(2,39) = 0.69). (c) Crucial stimulus caveat: distractors and captors were 4-component complexes made of the first four odd vs even harmonics of a 300 or 333 Hz F0. They were spectrally interleaved in the same region, not pure tones more than an octave apart. (d) In Exps. 1-2, asynchrony was confounded with temporal overlap; Exp. 3 addressed this.
verified.relevance: Still the best template for a grouping-helps task with no pedestal, scored by Pc on the method of constant stimuli. However, the near-ceiling Pc at 0 ms depended on D and C sharing a spectral region and an F0. With pure tones 15 semitones apart, synchronous fusion is much weaker (see Micheyl et al. 2013, Exp. 1), so the 0-ms anchor may be well below ceiling. Pilot ΔF before adopting this.

verified.citation: Turgeon M, Bregman AS, Ahad PA (2002). Rhythmic masking release: contribution of cues for perceptual organization to the cross-spectral fusion of concurrent narrow-band noises. J Acoust Soc Am 111:1819-1831
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract (PubMed) matches. Synchrony fully fuses short narrow-band noise bursts across frequency and space. An asynchrony of 20-40 ms produces no fusion; 10-20 ms produces partial fusion, where other cues are critical. Frequency and spatial separation reduced fusion additively but did not abolish it, and onset asynchrony was the dominant cue. Exact Pc values were not checked.
verified.relevance: Replicates the RMR asynchrony function with noise bursts. The 10-20 ms partial-fusion zone is where organisation is ambiguous and should be sampled densely.

verified.citation: Christiansen SK, Oxenham AJ (2014). Assessing the effects of temporal coherence on auditory stream formation through comodulation masking release. J Acoust Soc Am 135:3520-3529
verified.corrected_claim: Correct details: 20-Hz-wide bands, masker at 1 kHz, flankers at 0.25, 0.5, 2 and 4 kHz, each 60 dB SPL. Bursts were 187.5 ms with 20-ms ramps and a 250-ms onset interval; Exp. 1 had 4 precursors plus the target burst. Offsets were 0, 20, 40 and 60 ms; rate conditions were flankers at 200 or 300 ms; a ±30-ms synchronised-jitter condition was included. Procedure was 3I-3AFC, 2-down/1-up. Listeners: n = 7 (Exp. 1), 10 (Exp. 2), 8 (Exp. 3). In Exp. 1, CMR was significantly reduced at 40 and 60 ms and by unequal rates; jitter had no effect. Exp. 3 CMR: t(7) = 14.1 at 0 ms and t(7) = 1.42 (n.s.) at 60 ms. CORRECTIONS: (1) The offset applied only to the precursor bursts. The paper states the final flanker and masker bursts carrying the target 'were always gated on and off synchronously'. So D was NOT a fixed offset throughout the sequence. The design is a synchronous, zero-pedestal test burst preceded by context of varying coherence, i.e. the same logic, and the same rhythm-break at the test burst, as tsync / candidate 4. (2) CMR was reduced but NOT abolished at 60 ms in Exps. 1-2: comodulated vs random t(6) > 4.46 for all Exp. 1 conditions, and t(9) = 2.39 at 60 ms in Exp. 2. Only in Exp. 3 (10 bursts, pre- and post-cursors) was it non-significant. (3) CMR values in dB appear in figures only.
verified.relevance: Verified precedent that a context-only coherence manipulation, with a synchronous target event and a non-temporal (dB) dependent variable, yields a grouping-helps measure that falls with D. This directly vindicates the tsync logic (a synchronous test token after D-offset context). It also shows that the 'anomalous ending' was accepted in a published JASA design. The effect is modest at 60 ms unless context surrounds the target (Exp. 3).

verified.citation: Grose JH, Hall JW (1993). Comodulation masking release: is comodulation sufficient? J Acoust Soc Am 93:2896-2902
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract matches. Exp. 1: onset/offset asynchrony between the on-signal and flanking bands had a marked effect, and CMR could be completely abolished at 50 ms or more. Exp. 2: a streaming paradigm significantly disrupted CMR, but a substantial CMR remained. Exp. 3: the small harmonic-series effect did not appear to reflect parsing.
verified.relevance: Shows that a within-burst asynchrony of about 50 ms removes a grouping-dependent benefit, and that sequential capture only partly disrupts it.

verified.citation: Dau T, Ewert SD, Oxenham AJ (2009). Auditory stream formation affects comodulation masking release retroactively. J Acoust Soc Am 125:2182-2188
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract matches. Detection of a 1-kHz tone in a 20-Hz-wide masker with four comodulated or independent flankers at 1/6-octave or 1-octave spacing. CMR was present for both spacings. Gated postcursor flankers eliminated CMR only for the wide spacing. Controls excluded long-term adaptation and distraction.
verified.relevance: Shows that sequential context alone can switch off a grouping-dependent benefit, even after the target.

verified.citation: Micheyl C, Hunter C, Oxenham AJ (2010). Auditory stream segregation and the perception of across-frequency synchrony. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 36:1029-1039
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the PMC full text. Correct: A = 1000 Hz, B 6 or 15 semitones higher (1414.2 or 2378.4 Hz). Tones were 100 ms with 10-ms ramps at 60 dB SPL. There were 5 captors before and 2 after, with 50-ms gaps (150 ms onset-to-onset). Captors were at 1000 Hz (on-frequency) or 594.6 Hz (off-frequency). The track was 3-down/1-up with Δt capped at 100 ms. Exp. 2 off-frequency vs no captor: F(1,7) = 0.52, n.s. Corrections: (1) Exp. 1 was temporal-order identification (B lead vs lag). (2) Δt STARTED at 50 ms, not 100. (3) On-frequency thresholds: Exp. 1 about 43 ms (6 st) and about 50 ms (15 st), with possible ceiling; Exp. 2 about 44 ms at 15 st, with runs above 70 ms. (4) In Exp. 1, off-frequency captors produced a small but significant elevation relative to no captors (F(1,5) = 8.66). (5) Order thresholds were 1.84 times larger than detection thresholds in the 4 shared listeners.
verified.relevance: The zero-pedestal 'segregation hurts synchrony' result. Use a cap above 100 ms or constant stimuli. An off-frequency context is a usable control, but it is not perfectly neutral.

verified.citation: Wojtczak M, Beim JA, Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ (2012). Perception of across-frequency asynchrony and the role of cochlear delays. J Acoust Soc Am 131:363-377
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the PMC full text. Tones were 40 ms with 10-ms ramps: 250 Hz paired with 1, 2, 4 or 6 kHz, at 85 dB SPL and 20 dB SL, in a half-octave noise. n = 6. Procedure was 3I-3AFC, 2-down/1-up, with standards 0, 10, 20, 30 and 40 ms. Statistics: standard asynchrony F(4,20) = 25.418; LF vs HF lead at 0 ms F(1,5) = 12.665; no effect of frequency separation (F(3,15) = 0.30). Authors: 'Both our results and those of Zera and Green do not follow Weber's law', and 'roughly constant thresholds for larger values of baseline asynchrony'. The 4.9 vs 14.5 ms values are model predictions, not data. Key added detail: 'for the HF-tone leading conditions, thresholds remained roughly the same for all baseline values of asynchrony'. The step from detection to discrimination appeared only when the LF tone led.
verified.relevance: Strengthens the case against a pure pedestal account of tcoh. In tcoh the low A lags the high B (HF-lead), and for isolated HF-lead pairs thresholds were flat across 0-40 ms standards. A threshold that grows about 0.4 x D in sequence context is therefore unlikely to be Weber alone. The matched isolated-pair control is still needed, because tones (75 vs 40 ms), level and context differ.

verified.citation: Wojtczak M, Beim JA, Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ (2013). Effects of temporal stimulus properties on the perception of across-frequency asynchrony. J Acoust Soc Am 133:982-997
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the PMC full text. Tones were 500 ms (250 Hz plus 1-6 kHz) with standards 0, 10, 20, 60 and 100 ms; 3AFC, 2-down/1-up, n = 5. At 85 dB SPL, thresholds rose up to 20 ms, then 'increased less or remained relatively constant' from 20 to 100 ms. The LF/HF asymmetry held only for standards of 20 ms or less. Onset ramps of 10 vs 250 ms mattered at 0 ms (F(1,4) = 52.3) and at 60 ms (F(1,4) = 20.2); offset ramps did not. Thresholds for 500-ms tones were higher than for 40-ms tones (F(1,3) = 12.46). No numeric thresholds are given in the text.
verified.relevance: Extends the near-plateau pedestal function to 100 ms, covering Micheyl's D range.

verified.citation: Zera J, Green DM (1993a). Detecting temporal asynchrony with asynchronous standards. J Acoust Soc Am 93:1571-1579
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract: for onsets, asynchrony in the standard 'greatly increased the difficulty' of detecting one component's asynchrony in harmonic and log-spaced complexes; offsets were little affected. Wojtczak et al. (2012) confirm the secondary summary: detection 'did not depend on the amount of asynchrony between the components'. No numbers were verified; the full text was not accessed.
verified.relevance: The pedestal cost is a step from a synchronous to an asynchronous standard, not proportional growth. D = 0 is qualitatively different from all D > 0.

verified.citation: Zera J, Green DM (1993b). Detecting temporal onset and offset asynchrony in multicomponent complexes. J Acoust Soc Am 93:1038-1052
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract matches. Onset thresholds were as low as 0.2 ms (1-ms rise, displaced component near 2 kHz). Offset thresholds were 0.45-1.3 ms, about 10 times larger. Some log-complex conditions were nearly two orders of magnitude larger. Detection relies on across-channel comparison.
verified.relevance: Floor values for zero-pedestal detection in dense complexes. Onsets dominate.

verified.citation: Bregman AS, Pinker S (1978). Auditory streaming and the building of timbre. Can J Psychol 32:19-31
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the full text (archived PDF). Correct: the cycle was 117 ms silence, A (117 ms), 47 ms silence, then BC (147 ms), with B = 527 Hz, C = 300 Hz and A at 559, 978 or 1713 Hz. BC asynchrony was 0, ±29 or ±58 ms. Exp. 1 (n = 22): richness fell with asynchrony and with a nearer A (F(2,42) = 10.79). Exp. 2 (n = 16): strong AB-separation effect (F(2,30) = 71.27). At the intermediate separation (10.7 st), synchronous BC gave a mean of 4.88 vs 3.23 and 3.81 at ∓50%. At 1 semitone the mean was 1.73. At about 1.7 octaves all means were on the 'two streams' side (combined 5.24). The authors explicitly predicted intermediate AB separation to be 'unstable' and found the clearest asynchrony effect there. Exp. 4 likewise found the largest asynchrony effects where sequential and simultaneous tendencies were 'more balanced'. CORRECTION: the direction asymmetry is that the lower tone C leading B gave more A-B segregation (i.e. B stayed with C). The authors attribute the reverse case to 'good continuation' of the A-B-C frequency movement, not to lead-direction sensitivity. Linking it to the Wojtczak asynchrony-sensitivity asymmetry is not supported. The '40 cycles per trial' detail was not checked.
verified.relevance: Supports the bistability point: asynchrony matters most where sequential and simultaneous grouping are balanced. The measure is subjective only.

verified.citation: Darwin CJ, Ciocca V (1992). Grouping in pitch perception: effects of onset asynchrony and ear of presentation of a mistuned component. J Acoust Soc Am 91:3381-3390
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract matches. The contribution was reduced at a lead of 160 ms or more and absent above 300 ms. Effects were larger for 90-ms than 410-ms sounds. A contralateral captor did not augment the effect.
verified.relevance: Pitch grouping needs asynchronies far beyond 0-100 ms, which rules it out as a measure.

verified.citation: Hukin RW, Darwin CJ (1995). Comparison of the effect of onset asynchrony on auditory grouping in pitch matching and vowel identification. Percept Psychophys 57:191-196
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract matches. About 40 ms removes a harmonic from vowel quality, whereas pitch needs more than about 80 ms, with zero contribution by about 300 ms. The difference is due to the task, not the stimulus.
verified.relevance: Grouping time constants are task-dependent. Event and timbre tasks fit a 20-50 ms window.

verified.citation: Darwin CJ, Hukin RW, al-Khatib BY (1995). Grouping in pitch perception: evidence for sequential constraints. J Acoust Soc Am 98:880-885
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract matches. Four 90-ms precursor tones at the mistuned frequency substantially reduced the pitch shift, and this held with contralateral presentation. A level-reduction control argues against peripheral adaptation.
verified.relevance: Shows sequential capture of a component, with an adaptation control.

verified.citation: Roberts B, Holmes SD (2006) JASA 119:2905; Holmes SD, Roberts B (2006) JEP:HPP 32:1231; Roberts B, Holmes SD (2007) JASA 121:3655; Holmes SD, Roberts B (2011) JEP:HPP 37:1988
verified.corrected_claim: All four abstracts were checked. 2006 JASA: captor efficacy needs neither a common onset nor harmonic relations, extends to about 1.5 octaves, and is equivalent to about 6 dB attenuation; interpreted as broadband inhibition. 2006 JEP: the effect is maintained for noise-band captors and over gaps of 80 ms or more. 2007: contralateral captors are at least as effective. 2011: precursor effects follow adaptation predictions, but for some listeners even the smallest gap largely eliminated the precursor effect. CAUTION: these papers argue that the captor effect is NOT grouping. Citing the 80-ms-gap persistence as evidence that stream capture survives a gap before a test pair (as candidate 4 did) misapplies them.
verified.relevance: Apparent context capture can be inhibition or adaptation, so any context design needs off-frequency, contralateral or energy-matched controls.

verified.citation: Weise A, Schröger E, Bendixen A (2012). The processing of concurrent sounds based on inharmonicity and asynchronous onsets: an ORN study. Brain Res 1439:73-81
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract matches. A partial leading by 40 or 500 ms, mistuned by 3 or 13%. The ORN increased with inharmonicity and DECREASED with longer onset asynchrony (500 vs 40 ms), with no interaction. This was interpreted as sequential integration of the leading partial within about 350 ms. Caveat: the ORN is therefore not a monotonic index of onset-asynchrony segregation, and only two asynchronies were tested, both outside or at the edge of the 0-100 ms D range.
verified.relevance: Weak support for an ORN-based EEG companion measure. The direction of the effect complicates interpretation.

verified.citation: Lipp R, Kitterick P, Summerfield Q, Bailey PJ, Paul-Jordanov I (2010). Concurrent sound segregation based on inharmonicity and onset asynchrony. Neuropsychologia 48:1417-1425
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract matches. In MEG, a third harmonic delayed by 160 ms (or mistuned by 8%) elicited ORNm and P230m. The ORNm looked relatively automatic; the P230m was more attention-sensitive.
verified.relevance: An ORN to an onset-delayed partial exists, but at 160 ms.

verified.citation: Wojtczak M, Mehta AH, Oxenham AJ (2017). Rhythm judgments reveal a frequency asymmetry in the perception and neural coding of sound synchrony. PNAS 114:1201-1206
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract matches. There was no low-frequency timing advantage. Listeners were more sensitive when the high tone followed the low tone than vice versa, with the same asymmetry in EEG. The MMN paradigm is per keywords; details were not checked.
verified.relevance: The direction of D matters. tcoh used the less sensitive, more tolerant direction (high B leading).

verified.citation: Fujisaki W, Nishida S (2010). A common perceptual temporal limit of binding synchronous inputs across different sensory attributes and modalities. Proc R Soc B 277:2281-2290
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract matches. Cross-attribute binding limits were about 2-3 Hz for any combination of visual, auditory and tactile attributes; cross-attribute synchrony judgments reached 4-9 Hz.
verified.relevance: Peripheral. It concerns cross-attribute what-when binding, not across-frequency grouping of tones, so it is weak evidence about 5-Hz sequences.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Micheyl C, Hanson C, Demany L, Shamma S, Oxenham AJ (2013). Auditory stream segregation for alternating and synchronous tones. JEP:HPP 39:1568-1580 - Exp. 1 subjective data and Exp. 3 individual data
verified.corrected_claim: PMC full text. Exp. 1: at 15 semitones, synchronous tones were reported as two streams on most trials (group P_MAP about 0.76, vs about 0.97 for alternating tones). Synchronous results varied across listeners; for one listener P(2 streams) decreased with ΔF. Exp. 3: d' rose from 1.48 (0 ms) to 2.43 (100 ms). Only the 0 vs 100 ms (MAP 1.10) and 0 vs 50 ms (MAP 0.65) differences were credible. Listeners L6 and L8 showed an abrupt improvement from 0 to 35 ms. B was 1000 Hz and A was 15 st below (420.4 Hz). A 4-dB increment fell in one B tone excluding the first four; A tones were roved ±4 dB.
verified.relevance: Central to the bistability question and missed by the colleague. At 15 semitones, synchrony does not reliably bind A and B (about 3 in 4 reports are 'two streams'). Some listeners show step-like rather than graded functions of D. Both point to ambiguous, possibly bistable organisation at D = 0, which limits the dynamic range of any grouping-helps measure at 15 st. A smaller ΔF (e.g. 6-9 st) is worth piloting.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Elhilali M, Ma L, Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ, Shamma SA (2009). Temporal coherence in the perceptual organization and cortical representation of auditory scenes. Neuron 61:317-329
verified.corrected_claim: PMC full text. Psychophysics: A = 1000 Hz, B 0.5, 0.75 or 1.25 octaves higher. Tones were 100 ms with 10-ms ramps and 50-ms gaps; 5 precursor pairs plus a target pair. Asynchrony-detection thresholds were 2-4 ms with synchronous precursors at all separations, and 10-20 ms in controls. In the controls the A-stream gaps were 30 or 70 ms (a different rate), so precursor asynchrony varied from tone to tone rather than being a fixed lag.
verified.relevance: The behavioural basis for the lab's tcoh. Its asynchronous controls were rate mismatches, not fixed-D lags, so tcoh's fixed-lag design is not a replication of that contrast.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Pressnitzer D, Hupé JM (2006). Temporal dynamics of auditory and visual bistability reveal common principles of perceptual organization. Curr Biol 16:1351-1357
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract: auditory streaming shows spontaneous percept alternations with temporal dynamics and volitional control similar to visual plaids. Subject-specific biases did not correlate across modalities.
verified.relevance: Establishes that streaming is bistable over long listening. Per-trial organisation in A-B sequences can flip, which adds variance to any staircase.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Billig AJ, Carlyon RP (2016; online 2015). Automaticity and primacy of auditory streaming: Concurrent subjective and objective measures. JEP:HPP 42:339-353
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract: ABA- triplets. Exp. 2 had listeners perform the subjective and objective tasks concurrently and found superior detection of rhythmically deviant triplets during integrated reports, beyond the shared dependence of both measures on stimulus parameters.
verified.relevance: Direct precedent for conditioning objective performance on concurrently reported organisation, the right analysis if A-B grouping is bistable.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Thompson SK, Carlyon RP, Cusack R (2011). An objective measurement of the build-up of auditory streaming and of its modulation by attention. JEP:HPP 37:1253-1262
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract: ABA triplets of 50-ms tones with 75-ms gaps. Detection of a delayed B (an integration-helps task) was better early in the sequence and at Δf = 4 than at 8 st, mirroring subjective build-up. A competing task in the other ear improved late detection.
verified.relevance: A validated objective integration-helps streaming task. Build-up implies the position of the test event in the sequence matters.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ (2010). Objective and subjective psychophysical measures of auditory stream integration and segregation. JARO 11:709-724
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract: two complementary temporal-gap discrimination tasks with near-identical stimuli, one helped by integration and one by segregation, measured with subjective judgments in the same listeners across ΔF, rate and sequence length. The results were mostly consistent with the hypothesis.
verified.relevance: The methodological template for pairing a grouping-helps and a segregation-helps task on matched stimuli: the exact contrast the ARO/JASA story needs (mirror of Micheyl 2013 Exp. 3).

verified.citation: [ADDED] Billig AJ, Davis MH, Carlyon RP (2018). Neural decoding of bistable sounds reveals an effect of intention on perceptual organization. J Neurosci 38:2844-2853
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract: with HLH- sequences, an MEG classifier distinguished periods of reported integration from segregation (n = 27). Intention shifted both the reports and the neural signatures.
verified.relevance: Shows that percept-locked neural signatures of bistable streaming are decodable, relevant to the lab's EEG option. Intention or attention instructions must be controlled.

candidate_measures: 1. RHYTHMIC MASKING RELEASE (RMR) WITH PURE TONES: grouping helps, no pedestal; keep, with a corrected caveat. Turgeon et al. (2005), verified from full text: Pc 0.99-1.00 at 0 ms, Pc still above the no-captor baseline (0.53-0.56) at 48 ms, 75% thresholds 32-37 ms, 18 listeners. BUT their distractors and captors were interleaved odd/even harmonics of the same F0, sharing one spectral region. Pure tones 15 st apart fuse far less: Micheyl et al. 2013 Exp. 1 found P(2 streams) about 0.76 even for synchronous tones. So the 0-ms anchor will not be near ceiling at 15 st. Pilot ΔF (6-9 st) and tone duration; shorten their 8.8-s sequences; use constant stimuli and Pc. Intermediate Pc values (12-36 ms) are from figures and unverified.

2. SEQUENCE CMR (Christiansen & Oxenham 2014): keep, with corrected description. The D offset was applied to the PRECURSOR bursts only; the target-carrying burst was always synchronous. So this is a context-coherence manipulation with a zero-pedestal test event, scored in dB, the same logic as tsync. It is a verified, published precedent that this logic works and that the rhythm-break at the test burst was acceptable in JASA. CMR was significantly reduced at 40-60 ms but still significant at 60 ms in Exps. 1-2. It was non-significant at 60 ms only with pre- plus post-cursors (Exp. 3), so surround the test event with context. Synchronised jitter left CMR intact. Downside: noise bands rather than pure tones, and two thresholds per D.

3. PEDESTAL-MATCHED CONTROL FOR tcoh: keep, and strengthened. Wojtczak et al. (2012) report that for HIGH-tone-leading pairs (tcoh's direction: high B leads, low A lags) isolated-pair thresholds 'remained roughly the same for all baseline values' from 0 to 40 ms, and that neither their data nor Zera & Green follow Weber's law. A matched isolated-pair (no-context) staircase at each D therefore directly tests whether tcoh's roughly 0.4 x D growth is context (grouping) or pedestal. This is the cheapest, code-reusing option and may rescue the existing tcoh data for the talk.

4. ZERO-PEDESTAL TEST PAIR AFTER CONTEXT OF COHERENCE D (Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010 logic; this is essentially tsync): keep, with two corrections. (a) Remove the justification that 'capture persists across 80-ms gaps (Holmes & Roberts 2006)'. Those authors argue that effect is inhibition, NOT grouping, and Holmes & Roberts (2011) found some listeners lose the precursor effect with any gap. (b) Cite Christiansen & Oxenham (2014) instead as the verified precedent for a synchronous test event after offset context, and add post-cursor context around the test pair. Use a cap above 100 ms or constant stimuli (Micheyl 2010 hit ceiling around 44-50 ms). Note that off-frequency captors raised thresholds slightly in Micheyl 2010 Exp. 1, so the off-frequency control is not perfectly neutral.

5. PSYCHOMETRIC FUNCTIONS PLUS PER-TRIAL ORGANISATION REPORT (bistability): keep, now better supported. Verified: auditory streaming is bistable (Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006). Objective performance is better on trials reported as integrated, beyond stimulus codependence (Billig & Carlyon 2016). In Micheyl 2013, synchronous 15-st tones were mostly heard as two streams (about 0.76) with large individual differences, and some listeners showed step-like jumps from 0 to 35 ms. Bregman & Pinker (1978) found asynchrony effects strongest where competition is balanced. Implications: use constant stimuli with lapse and guess terms, consider mixture (grouped vs ungrouped) models of per-trial Pc, collect a 1-vs-2 report after each trial on a subset, and choose ΔF in the ambiguous regime rather than 15 st.

6. MATCHED COMPLEMENTARY-TASK DESIGN (added; Micheyl & Oxenham 2010 JARO template): pair the grouping-helps task with a segregation-helps task on near-identical stimuli in the same listeners (e.g. Micheyl 2013 Exp. 3 level-increment detection as the segregation-helps arm). The prediction is crossing functions of D, a cleaner ARO/JASA figure than either function alone. Template verified; the specific pairing with these stimuli is untested.

7. NOT RECOMMENDED: mistuned-harmonic pitch (Darwin & Ciocca 1992; Hukin & Darwin 1995) needs 80-300 ms or more. Vowel or captor paradigms are confounded by inhibition (Roberts & Holmes 2006-2011). Bregman & Pinker richness and stream ratings are subjective only.

8. OPTIONAL EEG COMPANION, downgraded: the ORN DECREASED from 40 to 500 ms asynchrony (Weise et al. 2012), so it is not a monotonic segregation index over D, and the ORNm evidence uses 160-ms delays (Lipp et al. 2010). Percept-locked decoding of bistable streaming (Billig, Davis & Carlyon 2018, MEG) is a better-grounded neural target if EEG is used at all.
evidence.angle_summary:
I checked all 18 cited papers on PubMed, and all 18 exist with correct DOIs. I read the full text where I could get it: Turgeon 2005, Bregman & Pinker 1978, Micheyl 2010, Micheyl 2013 and Elhilali 2009, plus PMC text for Christiansen & Oxenham 2014 and Wojtczak 2012 and 2013. The rest were checked against abstracts only.

Nothing is fabricated, but five corrections matter for the design:

1. **Christiansen & Oxenham 2014 is a context-only design.** The flanker-masker offset applied only to the precursor bursts. The burst carrying the target was always synchronous, so D was not held "throughout the sequence". At 60 ms, CMR was reduced but still significant in Experiments 1 and 2; it was no longer significant only in Experiment 3, where context came both before and after the target. This makes it a published JASA precedent for tsync's own logic: a synchronous test event after D-offset context, scored in dB. That includes the "anomalous ending".

2. **Wojtczak 2012 supports the tcoh grouping account more than reported.** For pairs where the high tone leads (tcoh's direction), isolated-pair thresholds stayed roughly flat for standards from 0 to 40 ms. So tcoh's growth of about 0.4 x D is unlikely to be pure Weber. The matched no-context control is cheap and decisive.

3. **Turgeon 2005's ceiling at 0 ms may not carry over to pure tones.** Pc was 0.99-1.00 at 0 ms, but the distractor and captor tones were interleaved odd and even harmonics of the same F0 in the same spectral region. The intermediate Pc values come from figures only. Harmonicity did have a small but significant effect.

4. **The Holmes & Roberts gap result was misapplied.** It describes inhibition, which those authors explicitly argue is not grouping. It cannot justify claiming that stream capture survives a gap.

5. **The ORN is not a simple index of D.** It got smaller as asynchrony grew from 40 to 500 ms.

Minor fixes:
- In Micheyl 2010 the staircase started at 50 ms, not 100 ms.
- In Micheyl 2010 Experiment 1, off-frequency captors raised thresholds slightly but significantly.
- The Bregman & Pinker lead-direction asymmetry is about A-B segregation and is explained by "good continuation". It is not evidence about asynchrony sensitivity.

On the bistability question, I added papers the colleague missed. The most important is Micheyl 2013 Experiment 1: at 15 semitones, synchronous A and B tones were reported as two streams about 76% of the time, with large individual differences. In Experiment 3, two listeners' d' jumped abruptly between D = 0 and 35 ms. So at 15 st grouping is weak and ambiguous even at D = 0, which squeezes the range of any task where grouping helps. Bistable or mixed organisation is plausible. The other additions are Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006, Billig & Carlyon 2016 (concurrent subjective and objective measures), Thompson et al. 2011, Micheyl & Oxenham 2010 (matched tasks where integration or segregation helps), Billig et al. 2018, and Elhilali 2009 itself. In Elhilali, the asynchronous controls were rate mismatches, not fixed lags.

What this means for the design:
- Pilot a smaller frequency separation (about 6-9 st).
- Use constant stimuli with mixture or lapse models, and per-trial 1-vs-2-stream reports on some trials.
- Put context both before and after the test event.
- Strongest figure for the talk: functions of D that cross, from a grouping-helps task and a segregation-helps task run on matched stimuli in the same listeners.

FACT-CHECK RESULT: all 23 cited papers exist. Each DOI matched its PubMed record (PMIDs found by citation lookup). I checked every abstract. Where full text was reachable (PMC/BioC/PMC HTML) I also checked the numbers: Micheyl 2013, Elhilali 2009, Micheyl 2010, Christiansen & Oxenham 2014, Micheyl/Kreft 2013, Teki 2013 and Wojtczak 2012. None of the colleague's findings is refuted. Most are accurate. The corrections are about detail.

(1) Micheyl 2013 Exp 3 (n=7: L1-L6, L8).
- The individual trend was 'more marked' for L4, L6 and L8. The colleague left out L4. It was weaker for L1, L2 and L5. L3 stayed near chance.
- Two differences were significant: 0 vs 100 ms (MAP 1.10, 95% CR [0.03, 2.05]) and 0 vs 50 ms (0.65 [0.04, 1.42]).
- The A distractors were 420.4 Hz, 15 semitones below the 1000-Hz targets.
- The abrupt 0-to-35-ms jump in L6 and L8 is in the text. The authors attribute the inter-individual variability to cross-frequency neural delays, citing Wojtczak 2012.
- Exp 1 had n=7. Group P('2 streams') for synchronous tones went from 0.29 (1 st) to 0.76 (15 st); alternating went from 0.11 to 0.97. Alternating-minus-synchronous was 0.23 at 9 st and 0.19 at 15 st, both credible. L7 reversed, possibly because of beats.
- 'Bistab' does not appear in the text.
- I could not verify '104-216 trials/condition' or '28 presentations'. Test blocks had 51-52 trials, after extensive practice, so these listeners were trained, not naive.

(2) Elhilali 2009.
- Psychophysics: n=9 experienced listeners. A = 1000 Hz; B 0.5, 0.75 or 1.25 octaves above (6/9/15 st). 100-ms tones, 10-ms ramps, 50-ms gaps. 5 precursor pairs plus a target pair. 2I-2AFC, '3-down/1-up' (79.4%), at least 4 runs.
- Thresholds were 2-4 ms for synchronous sequences and 10-20 ms for the 30/70-ms A-gap (tempo-mismatch) controls, F(1,10)=7.39. I did not find a separate number for B-alone in the text.
- The paper does state that an alternating sequence with 40-ms onset asynchrony (about 50% overlap) is 'usually heard like the non-overlapping' (segregated) sequence. This is informal, not measured.
- The physiology used 75-ms tones.

(3) Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010.
- Exp 1: n=6, lead/lag discrimination symmetric about 0 (the difference between intervals is 2Δt). Exp 2: n=8, detection. Exp 3: 4 listeners per part.
- Captors: 5 before and 2 after the target, 50-ms gaps, at 1000 Hz or 594.6 Hz. Δt was capped at 100 ms.
- On-frequency captor thresholds were about 43 ms (6 st) and 50 ms (15 st) in Exp 1, and about 44 ms in Exp 2. The authors say these may be ceiling values.
- Ear of entry: no disruption when the target pair was in the ear opposite the captors, or when the captors shared frequency but not ear with a target tone. Disruption occurred only when frequency AND ear were shared.

(4) Christiansen & Oxenham 2014 (n = 7, 10 and 8 for Exps 1-3). All numbers confirmed, including the ±30-ms jitter null result and p=0.10 at 60 ms in Exp 3.

(5) Micheyl/Kreft 2013. All statistics confirmed (n=8; 100 trials/condition; ±2% shift; 4% mistuning; Async = background 40 ms before 60-ms targets).

(6) Teki 2013.
- The AXB experiment is odd-figure IDENTIFICATION with coherence fixed at 6, not detection. The 4-chord d' of 0.31 was not different from 0 (p=0.12).
- 25-ms chords: 92±3% hits at the best coherence/duration. Noise gaps: robust up to 300 ms; d'=1.00 at 500 ms.

My PubMed search found no auditory study that staggers SFG figure components by an onset delay, which supports the 'split-figure is new' claim (search was limited).

IMPORTANT MISSED PAPERS (verified):
(a) Wojtczak, Beim, Micheyl & Oxenham 2012 (JASA 131:363). This bears directly on the Weber worry about tcoh. Asynchrony discrimination between isolated 40-ms tones (250 Hz plus 1-6 kHz) at reference asynchronies of 0-40 ms did NOT follow Weber's law. Thresholds rose with the reference only for low-frequency-leading pairs and stayed flat for high-frequency-leading pairs. Detection was better when the low tone led. So the tcoh rise (about 0.4 x D) is not automatically Weber. The way to resolve it is to measure the context-free pedestal function in the same listeners.
(b) Wojtczak, Mehta & Oxenham 2017 (PNAS 114:1201). There is a robust asymmetry: listeners tolerate a delay of the LOW tone relative to the high tone better than the reverse. tcoh has A (low) lagging B, which is the tolerant direction, so the sign of D must be stated, counterbalanced or chosen on purpose.
(c) Micheyl & Oxenham 2010 (JARO 11:709). This is the direct template for the user's 'mirror' goal: two complementary temporal-gap tasks with nearly identical stimuli in the same listeners, one where integration helps and one where segregation helps, plus subjective judgments.
(d) Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006 (Curr Biol 16:1351). Verified: auditory streaming is bistable, with dynamics like visual bistability and limited volitional control.
(e) Shamma, Elhilali & Micheyl 2011 (TINS 34:114). Verified: binding requires attention to one feature.
(f) Bregman & Pinker 1978 (Can J Psychol 32:19). Exists. It is the classic captor (A) vs simultaneous-fusion (B-C asynchrony) paradigm; asynchrony favours capture. Exact values were not checked.
(g) Christiansen, Jepsen & Dau 2014 (JASA 135:323). A temporal-coherence model plus data on grouping by onset/offset synchrony. Abstract only.
(h) Lee & Oxenham 2024 (JASA 156:3285). Speech bands desynchronised by 0-120 ms: intelligibility fell, but the fall was no greater with a talker masker than with noise. This cautions against assuming coherence drives segregation in every domain.
(i) Neilans & Dent 2015b (J Comp Psychol 129:174). Segregation thresholds were lower for complex signals than for pure tones.

BISTABILITY VERDICT: plausibly yes, and the support is solid. Moore & Gockel 2012, Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006 and Bendixen 2010 show switching under constant stimulation. Micheyl 2013 shows step-like individual delay functions and an ambiguous D=0 percept (76% 'two streams'). None of the cited papers tests bistability as a function of A-B onset delay, so that experiment is open.

verified.citation: Turgeon M, Bregman AS, Ahad PA (2002). Rhythmic masking release: contribution of cues for perceptual organization to the cross-spectral fusion of concurrent narrow-band noises. J Acoust Soc Am 111(4):1819-1831 (PMID 12002866)
verified.corrected_claim:
Confirmed from the abstract.
- RMR with brief narrow-band noise bursts; 2-AFC rhythm identification plus clarity ratings.
- Synchrony fully fuses bursts across frequency and space. 20-40 ms asynchrony gives no fusion; 10-20 ms gives partial fusion, where other cues decide.
- Frequency and spatial separation reduced fusion but did not abolish it. Onset asynchrony was the dominant cue, with additive effects of the other cues.
- Burst durations and accuracy values were not checked (no full text).
verified.relevance: The closest grouping-helps template whose judged quantity (which rhythm) does not depend on D. It predicts the steep fall between about 10 and 40 ms. Note that it used noise bursts, not pure tones.

verified.citation: Turgeon M, Bregman AS, Roberts B (2005). Rhythmic masking release: effects of asynchrony, temporal overlap, harmonic relations, and source separation on cross-spectral grouping. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 31(5):939-953 (PMID 16262490)
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract. The stimuli are described as brief TONES with identical distractors, captured by temporally overlapping captors. Fusion depended primarily on onset asynchrony and degree of temporal overlap. Harmonic relations had some influence. Only dichotic presentation was an effective spatial cue. Both preattentive and attention-driven processes were involved. Micheyl 2013 cites it for about 30-ms onset asynchronies promoting segregation.
verified.relevance: Supports porting RMR to tones. Onset asynchrony and overlap must be separated, because with fixed-duration tones D changes both.

verified.citation: Christiansen SK, Oxenham AJ (2014). Assessing the effects of temporal coherence on auditory stream formation through comodulation masking release. J Acoust Soc Am 135(6):3520-3529 (PMID 24907815, PMC4048442)
verified.corrected_claim:
Confirmed from full text.
- Design: 187.5-ms bursts with 20-ms ramps at a 250-ms onset interval. 1-kHz tone target in a 20-Hz masker band at 1 kHz. Flankers at 0.25, 0.5, 2 and 4 kHz, 60 dB SPL per band. 3I-3AFC, 2-down/1-up (70.7%), 4 estimates per condition.
- Exp 1 (n=7 analysed of 8; 4 precursors plus target): offsets of 0, 20, 40 and 60 ms. CMR was significantly reduced at 40 and 60 ms but not at 20 ms. Rate mismatch (200 or 300 vs 250 ms) also reduced it. ±30-ms uniform jitter did NOT differ from baseline. CMR remained significant in every condition (t(6)>4.46).
- Exp 2 (n=10): CMR persisted at 60 ms (t(9)=2.39, p=0.02).
- Exp 3 (n=8; 10 bursts with postcursors): CMR at 60 ms was not different from 0 (t(7)=1.42, p=0.10).
- CMR values in dB appear only in the figures.
verified.relevance: A grouping-helps index that falls with a fixed lag. The jitter null result means irregular timing alone does not break binding. It is too costly as the main task.

verified.citation: Grose JH, Hall JW (1993). Comodulation masking release: is comodulation sufficient? J Acoust Soc Am 93(5):2896-2902 (PMID 8315153)
verified.corrected_claim:
Confirmed from the abstract.
- Exp 1: CMR could be completely abolished when the on-signal and flanking bands were 50 ms or more asynchronous.
- Exp 2: a streaming paradigm disrupted CMR significantly, but a substantial CMR remained.
- Exp 3: a harmonic-series manipulation had a small effect, not attributed to parsing.
verified.relevance: Independent grouping-helps evidence that the benefit is gone by about 50 ms.

verified.citation: Micheyl C, Hanson C, Demany L, Shamma S, Oxenham AJ (2013). Auditory stream segregation for alternating and synchronous tones. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 39(6):1568-1580 (PMID 23544676, PMC3973443)
verified.corrected_claim:
Checked against full text.
- Exp 1 (n=7, L1-L7): MAP P('2 streams') for synchronous tones rose from about 0.29 (1 st) to about 0.76 (15 st); for alternating tones from about 0.11 to about 0.97. Alternating minus synchronous was credible only at 9 st (0.23 [0.03, 0.40]) and 15 st (0.19 [0.03, 0.44]). L7's P('2 streams') fell with separation, possibly because of beats.
- Exp 3 (n=7, L1-L6 and L8): 15 st, with A distractors 15 st BELOW the 1000-Hz B targets (420.4 Hz). Delays of 0, 35, 50, 71 and 100 ms, in randomised order. Group mean d' went from about 1.48 (0 ms) to 2.43 (100 ms).
- Credible differences: 0 vs 100 ms (1.10 [0.03, 2.05]) and 0 vs 50 ms (0.65 [0.04, 1.42]); no other pairs.
- The trend was 'more marked' for L4, L6 and L8 (the colleague omitted L4) and weaker for L1, L2 and L5. L3 was near chance.
- L6 and L8 showed an abrupt improvement from 0 to 35 ms. The authors cite 20-40 ms as typically enough, and speculate that the individual variability reflects cross-frequency neural delays (citing Wojtczak 2012).
- The paper does not mention bistability.
- Listeners had a practice phase (at least 100 trials per block) and were tested in blocks of 51-52 trials. I could not verify the '104-216 trials/condition' and '28 presentations' figures.
verified.relevance: The reference curve. Ambiguous synchronous percepts and step-like individual functions support a bistable, mixture interpretation. Individual functions and fixed-level d' should be reported.

verified.citation: Elhilali M, Ma L, Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ, Shamma SA (2009). Temporal coherence in the perceptual organization and cortical representation of auditory scenes. Neuron 61(2):317-329 (PMID 19186172, PMC2673083)
verified.corrected_claim:
Checked against full text.
- Psychophysics: n=9 listeners with extensive experience. A = 1000 Hz; B 0.5, 0.75 or 1.25 octaves above. 100-ms tones, 10-ms ramps, 50-ms gaps. 5 precursor A/B pairs plus a target pair. 2I-2AFC tracking 79.4%, described as 3-down/1-up although the step rule says 'two consecutive correct'. Started at 20 ms; at least 4 thresholds per condition.
- Synchronous: 2-4 ms at all separations. 'Asynchronous' controls had A gaps of 30 or 70 ms against B gaps of 50 ms, i.e. a tempo mismatch, not a fixed lag: thresholds 10-20 ms (F(1,10)=7.39). The standard interval's final pair was synchronous.
- A B-alone control was run, but I did not find a separate value for it in the text.
- The paper states informally that an alternating sequence with 40-ms onset asynchrony (about 50% overlap) is 'usually heard like the non-overlapping' sequence. This was not measured psychophysically. The 40-ms overlap condition in the physiology used 75-ms tones.
verified.relevance: Confirms that Elhilali's asynchronous control was not a fixed lag, so a fixed-lag behavioural D curve is new. The 2-4 vs 10-20 ms contrast sets the expected size of the effect.

verified.citation: Micheyl C, Hunter C, Oxenham AJ (2010). Auditory stream segregation and the perception of across-frequency synchrony. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 36(4):1029-1039 (PMID 20695716, PMC4315665)
verified.corrected_claim:
Confirmed from full text.
- Stimuli: 100-ms tones (10-ms ramps), 60 dB SPL. A = 1000 Hz; B = 1414.2 Hz (6 st) or 2378.4 Hz (15 st). Captors: 5 before and 2 after the target A, 50-ms gaps, at 1000 Hz (on-frequency) or 594.6 Hz (9 st below).
- Exp 1 (n=6): 2I lead/lag discrimination (interval difference 2Δt). 3-down/1-up, Δt capped at 100 ms. On-frequency thresholds were about 43 ms (6 st) and 50 ms (15 st), possibly at ceiling. They were significantly higher than no-captor and off-frequency thresholds.
- Exp 2 (n=8): synchrony detection, about 44 ms at 15 st on-frequency (F(1,7)=33.4 vs no captor).
- Exp 3 (4 listeners per part): no disruption when the target pair was in the ear opposite the captors. Disruption occurred only when the captors shared both frequency AND ear with a target tone.
verified.relevance: Sequential capture impairs synchrony judgements, and lead/lag around zero has no pedestal. But on-frequency captors push thresholds near the 100-ms cap: a probe task after strong context risks ceiling.

verified.citation: Micheyl C, Kreft H, Shamma S, Oxenham AJ (2013). Temporal coherence versus harmonicity in auditory stream formation. J Acoust Soc Am 133(3):EL188-EL194 (PMID 23464127, PMC3579859)
verified.corrected_claim:
Confirmed from full text.
- Design: n=8 (from 14 screened). 9 targets per trial: 8 precursors and a test shifted ±2% (up/down judgement), 100 trials per condition, d'. Backgrounds: harmonic (F0 = f_ref/N, N = 3-6), log-spaced, or shifted by 25% of F0. Targets harmonic or mistuned by +4%. MBS = same N within a trial; MBD = N varies across bursts. Sync = 100-ms targets with the background; Async = background starts 40 ms before 60-ms targets, offsets aligned.
- Statistics: H-Sync MBD vs MBS, t(7)=3.23, p=0.014. S-Sync, p=0.09 (inconclusive). M-Sync vs H-Sync MBS, t(7)=6.88, p<0.0005. Async better in all comparisons (2.67<t<9.87, p≤0.032).
- d' values are only in Fig. 1B.
verified.relevance: Mistuning alone segregates temporally coherent tones. That 15 st (ratio 2.38, not a low-integer ratio) weakens binding at D=0 is the colleague's inference, not a result of this paper. It does justify a harmonic-ratio control.

verified.citation: Teki S, Chait M, Kumar S, Shamma S, Griffiths TD (2013). Segregation of complex acoustic scenes based on temporal coherence. eLife 2:e00699 (PMID 23898398, PMC3721234)
verified.corrected_claim:
Checked against full text.
- Stimulus: chords of 50 ms (25 ms in one experiment) with 10-ms ramps; on average 10 components (5-15) from 129 log-spaced frequencies between 179 and 7246 Hz (1/24-octave steps).
- Correction: the AXB experiment was odd-figure IDENTIFICATION/discrimination, not detection, with coherence fixed at 6. d' was 0.31±0.18 at 4 chords (not different from 0, p=0.12), 1.75±0.34 at 8 chords and 2.93±0.26 at 12 chords.
- 25-ms chords: 92±3% hits at the best coherence/duration.
- Ramped figures: maximum hit rates 0.97 (step 2) and 0.83 (step 5).
- Noise interruptions: robust up to 300 ms; d'=1.00±0.30 at 500 ms.
- No condition staggered figure components in time. A PubMed search (figure-ground AND asynchrony) returned no auditory study doing so.
verified.relevance: A robust coherence measure. A split-figure with onset delay D appears to be new.

verified.citation: Teki S, Chait M, Kumar S, von Kriegstein K, Griffiths TD (2011). Brain bases for auditory stimulus-driven figure-ground segregation. J Neurosci 31(1):164-171 (PMID 21209201)
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract. Introduced SFG, in which figure and background overlap and differ only in statistics of fluctuation. Behaviour was 'remarkably sensitive'. fMRI in naive listeners doing an irrelevant task showed IPS and STS activity and no significant primary auditory cortex activation.
verified.relevance: Founding SFG paper.

verified.citation: Teki S, Kumar S, Griffiths TD (2016). Large-scale analysis of auditory segregation behavior crowdsourced via a smartphone app. PLoS One 11(4):e0153916 (PMID 27096165)
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed: a modified SFG game in The Great Brain Experiment app, n = 5148. Performance was robust and consistent with the lab study (n = 10).
verified.relevance: SFG-type tasks survive consumer hardware.

verified.citation: Johns MA, Calloway RC, Phillips I, Karuzis VP, Dutta K, Smith E, Shamma SA, Goupell MJ, Kuchinsky SE (2023). Performance on stochastic figure-ground perception varies with individual differences in speech-in-noise recognition and working memory capacity. J Acoust Soc Am 153(1):286 (PMID 36732241)
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed: n = 37. Figures of 4, 6, 8 or 10 coherent tones; stimuli spectrally and temporally flat. More tones gave higher accuracy and faster RT. For 10 tones, faster RT went with better QuickSIN. Working memory and musicianship modulated these relationships.
verified.relevance: Graded coherence effect in a sample of naive-study size. Individual-difference covariates are worth logging.

verified.citation: Tóth B, Kocsis Z, Háden GP, Szerafin Á, Shinn-Cunningham BG, Winkler I (2016). EEG signatures accompanying auditory figure-ground segregation. NeuroImage 141:108-119 (PMID 27421185)
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed: detection improved with coherence and duration. ORN and P400 amplitudes grew with both. Only P400 amplitude correlated with detection performance. Both components had generators inside and outside auditory cortex.
verified.relevance: Gives EEG markers for a split-figure or D manipulation.

verified.citation: O'Sullivan JA, Shamma SA, Lalor EC (2015). Evidence for neural computations of temporal coherence in an auditory scene and their enhancement during active listening. J Neurosci 35(18):7256-7263 (PMID 25948273)
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed: SFG with stochastically varying coherence and a regression (TRF) approach. Passive coherence effect at about 115-185 ms; larger and lasting to about 265 ms during active listening.
verified.relevance: Template for an EEG regression on D.

verified.citation: Thompson SK, Carlyon RP, Cusack R (2011). An objective measurement of the build-up of auditory streaming and of its modulation by attention. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 37(4):1253-1262 (PMID 21480747)
verified.corrected_claim:
Confirmed:
- ABA triplets: 50-ms tones, 75-ms gaps.
- Detecting a delay of B relative to the preceding A was better early than late in the sequence, and better at Δf = 4 than 8 st, consistent with subjective judgements.
- A competing task in the other ear for the first 10 s improved detection at 12.5 s into a 13.5-s sequence.
- Build-up impairs performance, and listeners cannot prevent it.
verified.relevance: Context length and probe position are factors in any integration-helps design.

verified.citation: Roberts B, Glasberg BR, Moore BCJ (2008). Effects of the build-up and resetting of auditory stream segregation on temporal discrimination. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 34(4):992-1006 (PMID 18665740)
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed: a 2.0-s fixed-frequency inducer, then a 0.6-s test of 3 L-H cycles. Listeners discriminated an isochronous sequence from one with delayed H tones, at H-L separations of 0-12 st. Every inducer-vs-L-tone difference tested (frequency, number of onsets, tone:silence ratio, level, lateralisation) moved thresholds toward the no-inducer value, so abrupt changes reset segregation.
verified.relevance: tsync's anomalous ending may itself reset streaming, with an effect that grows with D. A matched-change control is needed.

verified.citation: Hukin RW, Darwin CJ (1995). Comparison of the effect of onset asynchrony on auditory grouping in pitch matching and vowel identification. Percept Psychophys 57(2):191-196 (PMID 7885817)
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed. The 80-ms onset (contribution to pitch starts falling) and 300-ms zero point are PRIOR results for pitch, summarised in the abstract. The roughly 40-ms value for vowel identity also comes from prior work. This paper's three experiments show the difference comes from the task, not the stimulus structure: the asynchrony that removes a harmonic from pitch is the same for a vowel and for a flat-spectrum complex, and is much larger than the one that removes it from vowel quality.
verified.relevance: The binding window depends on the measure. Avoid claiming one universal window.

verified.citation: Bendixen A, Denham SL, Gyimesi K, Winkler I (2010). Regular patterns stabilize auditory streams. J Acoust Soc Am 128(6):3658-3666 (PMID 21218898)
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed: continuous integrated/segregated reporting; perception switched in all conditions. Regular patterns in one or both streams prolonged two-stream phases and left one-stream phases unchanged. The colleague's step to 'isochronous A and B with a fixed D should give long segregated phases' is an extrapolation, not tested.
verified.relevance: Bistability under constant stimulation. Regularity stabilises segregation.

verified.citation: Szalárdy O, Bendixen A, Böhm TM, Davies LA, Denham SL, Winkler I (2014). The effects of rhythm and melody on auditory stream segregation. J Acoust Soc Am 135(3):1392-1405 (PMID 24606277)
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed: two interleaved sequences overlapping in pitch range and differing in ITD/ILD, built from different songs, with notes or timing scrambled or isochronous. Continuous reporting. Temporal overlap between tones of the two streams was the strongest segregation cue. Tonality and familiarity also had effects.
verified.relevance: D changes overlap as well as onset asynchrony; the two should be separated.

verified.citation: Winkler I, Denham S, Mill R, Bohm TM, Bendixen A (2012). Multistability in auditory stream segregation: a predictive coding view. Phil Trans R Soc B 367(1591):1001-1012 (PMID 22371621)
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed: a review and model. Alternative organisations are represented in parallel and compete for awareness; predictive processing stabilises them.
verified.relevance: Theoretical basis for treating intermediate-D trials as a mixture of states.

verified.citation: Moore BCJ, Gockel HE (2012). Properties of auditory stream formation. Phil Trans R Soc B 367(1591):919-931 (PMID 22371614)
verified.corrected_claim:
Confirmed:
- Large differences give fission and very small ones fusion. Intermediate differences give irregular flips between one and several streams (bistability).
- Segregation builds up and is reset by sudden changes or attention switches.
- Regularity stabilises streams.
verified.relevance: Predicts bistability at intermediate D. The link to the noisy tpair staircases is the colleague's inference.

verified.citation: Lu K, Xu Y, Yin P, Oxenham AJ, Fritz JB, Shamma SA (2017). Temporal coherence structure rapidly shapes neuronal interactions. Nat Commun 8:13900 (PMID 28054545)
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed: in ferret A1, synchronous sequences rapidly enhanced responses, sensitivity and presumed connectivity, and alternating sequences suppressed them, but ONLY when the animals were engaged in the task and attentive.
verified.relevance: Behavioural tasks should be active. Passive EEG D effects may be small.

verified.citation: Neilans EG, Dent ML (2015). Temporal coherence for pure tones in budgerigars (Melopsittacus undulatus) and humans (Homo sapiens). J Comp Psychol 129(1):52-61 (PMID 25419717)
verified.corrected_claim: Abstract confirms: same procedures for synchronous, asynchronous and partially overlapping pure tones. Humans were more apt to FUSE partially overlapping tones, whereas budgerigars segregated them. Temporal cues mattered most for overlapping sounds. Budgerigars, not humans, followed streaming-model predictions. Overlap values and task details were not checked.
verified.relevance: Partial overlap may still be heard as fused in humans, consistent with a weak subjective D effect.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Wojtczak M, Beim JA, Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ (2012). Perception of across-frequency asynchrony and the role of cochlear delays. J Acoust Soc Am 131(1):363-377 (PMID 22280598, PMC3272712)
verified.corrected_claim:
From the abstract and PMC full text:
- A 250-Hz tone was paired with a 1, 2, 4 or 6 kHz tone (40-ms tones, 10-ms ramps), n=6.
- Subjective synchrony peaked at physical synchrony, with a steeper slope on the low-leading side. Asynchrony detection was better for low-leading pairs.
- Discrimination at reference asynchronies of 0, 10, 20, 30 and 40 ms: thresholds rose overall with the reference but did NOT follow Weber's law. They rose for low-leading pairs and stayed roughly flat for high-leading pairs; the two converged at larger references. Values are only in Fig. 6.
- Micheyl 2013 cites this paper to explain individual differences.
verified.relevance: Bears directly on the Weber objection to tcoh. Isolated-pair pedestal discrimination is not proportional to the pedestal. Measure the context-free pedestal function in the same listeners: grouping is shown only if thresholds after context exceed it.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Wojtczak M, Mehta AH, Oxenham AJ (2017). Rhythm judgments reveal a frequency asymmetry in the perception and neural coding of sound synchrony. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 114(5):1201-1206 (PMID 28096408)
verified.corrected_claim: From the abstract: behaviour and EEG show no low-frequency timing advantage, but a robust asymmetry. Listeners were more sensitive to timing differences when the high tone FOLLOWED the low tone than vice versa, i.e. more tolerant of delays of the low tone relative to the high tone.
verified.relevance: The sign of D matters. tcoh's 'A (low) lags B' is the delay direction listeners tolerate more, which may prolong binding and flatten the D curve. Counterbalance the sign or choose it on purpose.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ (2010). Objective and subjective psychophysical measures of auditory stream integration and segregation. J Assoc Res Otolaryngol 11(4):709-724 (PMID 20658165)
verified.corrected_claim: From the abstract: two complementary temporal-gap discrimination tasks with similar stimuli and procedures, one helped by integration and one by segregation, tested in the same listeners. Frequency separation, rate and sequence length were varied, and subjective judgements were collected. The results mostly fit segregation helping one task and hurting the other.
verified.relevance: The closest published template for the user's 'mirror of Micheyl 2013' aim: an integration-helps and a segregation-helps task on near-identical stimuli in the same listeners.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Pressnitzer D, Hupé JM (2006). Temporal dynamics of auditory and visual bistability reveal common principles of perceptual organization. Curr Biol 16(13):1351-1357 (PMID 16824924)
verified.corrected_claim: From the abstract: auditory streaming is bistable, with percepts alternating spontaneously. Alternation dynamics and susceptibility to volitional control resemble visual plaids. Individual biases did not correlate across modalities.
verified.relevance: The bistability reference the user named. Supports continuous-report measurement and treating states as a mixture.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Shamma SA, Elhilali M, Micheyl C (2011). Temporal coherence and attention in auditory scene analysis. Trends Neurosci 34(3):114-123 (PMID 21196054)
verified.corrected_claim: From the abstract: stream formation depends primarily on temporal coherence among feature-encoding responses. Binding of the coherent features into a stream happens when attention is directed to one feature.
verified.relevance: Theory paper cited by the project. Together with Lu 2017, it argues for active tasks.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Bregman AS, Pinker S (1978). Auditory streaming and the building of timbre. Can J Psychol 32(1):19-31 (PMID 728845)
verified.corrected_claim: Exists (no PubMed abstract). Secondary sources describe a repeating cycle of a pure tone A alternating with a B+C pair. Listeners judged whether B was captured into a stream with A, and the timbre of C. More B-C asynchrony gave more streaming and less fusion. Exact asynchrony values and data were not checked.
verified.relevance: The classic paradigm pitting sequential capture against simultaneous synchrony, and the conceptual ancestor of tsync and RMR. Cite it as the origin.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Christiansen SK, Jepsen ML, Dau T (2014). Effects of tonotopicity, adaptation, modulation tuning, and temporal coherence in 'primitive' auditory stream segregation. J Acoust Soc Am 135(1):323-333 (PMID 24437772)
verified.corrected_claim: From the abstract: a Dau-model front end with a temporal-coherence back end, simulating (i) streaming vs repetition time and Δf, and (ii) grouping of distant components by onset/offset synchrony. Adaptation and modulation filtering may increase sensitivity to onset asynchrony. Data details were not checked.
verified.relevance: A computational model that could be used to predict D curves for candidate stimuli before testing.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Lee J, Oxenham AJ (2024). Testing the role of temporal coherence on speech intelligibility with noise and single-talker maskers. J Acoust Soc Am 156(5):3285-3297 (PMID 39545746)
verified.corrected_claim: From the abstract: speech filtered into 8 bands and desynchronised by 0-120 ms. Intelligibility fell with asynchrony, but the fall was similar for a noise masker and a single-talker masker, and depended mainly on target (not masker) asynchrony.
verified.relevance: A recent caution: coherence may matter less for speech segregation than for tones. Useful for the JASA discussion and for framing D effects as stimulus-specific.

candidate_measures: A. Pure-tone rhythmic masking release with D-delayed captors (Turgeon 2002; Turgeon 2005; origin in Bregman & Pinker 1978). Kept, all supporting findings verified. Grouping helps, and the judged rhythm does not depend on D. Predicted fall at about 10-40 ms. Caveat: the 2002 study used noise bursts; the 2005 study used tones. Pilot the captor frequency ratio and separate onset asynchrony from overlap (fix the overlap or the captor duration).

B. Split-figure SFG with the high half delayed by D (new; no prior auditory study found in PubMed). Kept. Teki 2013's robustness numbers verified. Correction: the AXB d' values (0.31, 1.75, 2.93) come from figure IDENTIFICATION at coherence 6, not detection. Risk: integration survives 300-ms noise gaps, so the effect of D is uncertain.

C. Lead/lag (±Δ) discrimination of a probe pair after a D-context (Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010). Kept, with a new caution. With on-frequency captors, thresholds reached about 43-50 ms, near the 100-ms cap, so a strong D-context risks ceiling. Use fixed Δ levels and a matched-change control (Roberts et al. 2008 reset).

D. CMR with D-offset flanking bands (Christiansen & Oxenham 2014; Grose & Hall 1993). Kept only as a citation for the shape of the falloff (all numbers verified: reduced at 40 and 60 ms, not at 20 ms; ±30-ms jitter had no effect). Too costly as the main task.

E. Fixed-level constant stimuli at 5-6 D values with a one-bit percept report after each trial; d' conditioned on percept; per-listener logistic/mixture fit giving D50. Kept. Supported by verified Micheyl 2013 individual data (step-like jumps in L6 and L8; ambiguous D=0 percept) and by the bistability literature.

F. Continuous one-vs-two report at several D values, 30-60 s per sequence, about 5 min in total (Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006; Bendixen 2010; Moore & Gockel 2012). Kept. It answers the bistability question directly. No cited paper has measured bistability as a function of A-B onset delay, so this is a new result in itself.

G. Harmonic vs inharmonic A:B ratio control (Micheyl, Kreft, Shamma & Oxenham 2013). Kept, but the claim that 15 st weakens D=0 binding is the colleague's inference, not a reported result. Limit to 2-3 D values.
H. EEG delay-TRF (O'Sullivan 2015), or ORN/P400 to split-figure events (Tóth 2016), during active listening (Lu 2017). Kept as secondary.
I. Context-length and probe-position factor (Thompson 2011; Roberts 2008). Kept, all verified.

J. [NEW] Rescue tcoh with a context-free pedestal control (Wojtczak et al. 2012). In the same listeners, measure asynchrony discrimination for an isolated A-B pair (or after a B-alone context) at the same pedestals D, and compare with thresholds after the coherent context. Wojtczak 2012 found that isolated-pair pedestal discrimination does NOT follow Weber's law (rising only for low-leading pairs), so a context-minus-isolated threshold ratio separates grouping from pedestal effects. This reuses existing tcoh code, and the one listener's curve (3.5 to 22 ms) can be re-tested quickly.

K. [NEW] Set the sign of D on purpose or counterbalance it (Wojtczak, Mehta & Oxenham 2017). Listeners tolerate the low tone lagging more than the high tone lagging. tcoh's A (low) lags B is the tolerant direction, which may delay the loss of binding. Running B lagging A as well (or matching Micheyl 2013's direction) tests the asymmetry and protects the comparison with Micheyl 2013.

L. [NEW] A matched pair of integration-helps and segregation-helps tasks on near-identical stimuli in the same listeners (Micheyl & Oxenham 2010 JARO template). For example, Micheyl 2013's increment-detection task (segregation helps) beside a grouping-helps task (RMR, or level-increment detection where A and B share the increment), both with the same D values and tone parameters. This gives a within-listener crossover plot, the mirror the talk needs.

verified.citation: Micheyl C, Hanson C, Demany L, Shamma S, Oxenham AJ (2013). Auditory stream segregation for alternating and synchronous tones. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 39(6):1568-1580. PMID 23544676, PMC3973443
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the PMC full text. Exp. 1: 7 listeners. B = 1000 Hz; A sits 1, 3, 6, 9 or 15 semitones lower (943.9 down to 420.4 Hz). 100-ms tones with 20-ms ramps, 100-ms gaps, 12 A + 12 B tones (2.3 s synchronous, 2.4 s alternating). Nominal 60 dB SPL, A roved ±4 dB, and a 4-dB B increment on 50% of trials (never in the first 4 B tones). 28 presentations per condition, alternating blocks first. Listeners were told the percept 'could change during the course of the sequence' and to report it toward the end. Group MAP P('2 streams'): alternating about 0.11 (1 st) to 0.97 (15 st); synchronous about 0.29 to 0.76. Alternating minus synchronous was significant only at 9 st (0.23 [0.03, 0.40]) and 15 st (0.19 [0.03, 0.44]). Synchronous curves: L1-L4 rose, L5-L6 rose weakly, L7 fell; the authors suggest beats at small spacings for L7. All 7 listeners rose with spacing for alternating tones. Caveat about pitch-separation responding confirmed. Exp. 3: 7 listeners (one, L3, near chance), 15 st, D = 0, 35, 50, 71, 100 ms. d' about 1.48 at D=0 and 2.43 at D=100; credible differences only for 0 vs 100 (1.10 [0.03, 2.05]) and 0 vs 50 (0.65 [0.04, 1.42]). L6 and L8 showed an abrupt gain between 0 and 35 ms; the authors say 35 ms 'seems to be enough to break' binding. The paper reports NO switching or bistability data. 'Bistable' is our inference from mixed trial-level reports, not the authors' claim.
verified.relevance: Every number the colleague cites checks out. Two additions matter. (a) The abrupt 0 to 35 ms gain in some listeners means a grouping-helps D function will probably saturate early, so D should be sampled densely below 35-40 ms. (b) Exp. 1 shows trial-level percept variability, but it is not evidence of within-trial bistable alternation.

verified.citation: Billig AJ, Carlyon RP (2016). Automaticity and primacy of auditory streaming: Concurrent subjective and objective measures. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 42(3):339-353. PMID 26414168, PMC4763253
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the PMC full text. 12 listeners (I could not confirm they were naive). ABA- triplets: 50-ms tones with 10-ms ramps, 75-ms gaps within a triplet, 200 ms between triplets, one triplet every 500 ms. A roved over one octave around 800 Hz; B 4 or 8 st above. 55 dB SPL, with an ignored noise in the contralateral ear. 35-39 triplets per sequence (17.5-19.5 s). Deviants delay B by 50 ms; positions early (6th triplet), middle or late. Exp. 2: 48 trials (24 per spacing), 2-s gaps between trials. CORRECTION: the session lasted about 30 min including training, NOT about 90 min. d' was higher during integrated reports: t(11)=4.15, p=.002, d=1.80. Criterion was more conservative when segregated: t(11)=8.93, d=2.93. Adding percept to the spacing+position logistic model: chi2(1)=77.40; adjusted count pseudo-R2 rose from .22 to .36. Segregated percept at the deviant: early 2%, middle 41%, late 64%. Worst condition (8 st, late, about 80% segregated) still had d' about 2. Dual-task cost: d' fell by 0.59 compared with Exp. 1 (F(1,11)=12.10), more at 8 st and for late deviants.
verified.relevance: Supports the percept-contingent analysis (candidate 3). Fix the session length: concurrent reporting is cheaper than stated (about 30 min for 48 long trials). Also remember Psi_seg is far above chance, since within-stream cues survive segregation.

verified.citation: Micheyl C, Hunter C, Oxenham AJ (2010). Auditory stream segregation and the perception of across-frequency synchrony. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 36(4):1029-1039. PMID 20695716, PMC4315665
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the PMC full text. A = 1000 Hz; B 6 or 15 st higher (the Fig. 1 legend says 6 and 9, the text says 6 and 15). 100-ms tones with 10-ms ramps, 60 dB SPL. Captors: 5 before and 2 after target A, 50-ms gaps, either on-frequency (1000 Hz) or off-frequency (594.6 Hz). 3-down-1-up staircase, delta-t capped at 100 ms. Exp. 1 (order, 6 listeners): on-frequency thresholds about 43 ms (6 st) and 50 ms (15 st), which the authors call near the 100-ms ceiling. Exp. 2 (detection, 8 listeners): on-frequency at 15 st about 44 ms, with some runs above 70 ms. Off-frequency was not different from no captors in Exp. 2 (p=.49), and slightly worse in Exp. 1. CORRECTION on the ideal-observer comparison: in the 4 shared listeners, ORDER thresholds were 1.84 times LARGER than detection thresholds, whereas the ideal observer predicted order thresholds about 2.91 times SMALLER than detection thresholds. The data run in the opposite direction from the prediction, so order thresholds were 'about five times larger than expected'. The colleague's wording ('against a prediction of 2.91') hides that the predicted direction is reversed. Exp. 3A: captors in the opposite ear from both targets abolished the captor effect. Exp. 3B (B tone in the opposite ear) still showed elevation. Exp. 3C (A tone in the opposite ear): no captor effect.
verified.relevance: Strong support for using synchrony detection near 0 ms as a grouping-sensitive readout that has no Weber confound. It also documents the staircase ceiling problem when capture dominates. 'Removed the effect' applies only to Exp. 3A, not to every ear manipulation.

verified.citation: Elhilali M, Ma L, Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ, Shamma SA (2009). Temporal coherence in the perceptual organization and cortical representation of auditory scenes. Neuron 61(2):317-329. PMID 19186172, PMC2673083
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the PMC full text. Psychophysics: 9 experienced listeners. A = 1000 Hz, B 6, 9 or 15 st higher. 100-ms tones (10-ms ramps). Only 5 precursor A and 5 precursor B tones, then the target pair. B-B gaps were 50 ms (150-ms SOA, 6.7 Hz). A-A gaps were 50 ms (synchronous) or 30/70 ms (asynchronous controls); the colleague called these 'inter-tone intervals', but they are silent gaps. 2I-2AFC with a 500-ms gap between intervals; the last B was shifted by delta-T; 3-down-1-up staircase. Thresholds were about 2-4 ms with synchronous precursors at every spacing, and about 10-20 ms in the asynchronous controls; B-alone did not differ from the asynchronous controls. There was NO formal subjective streaming experiment. The text does say 'synchronous tone sequences are always heard as one stream', but the Fig. 1 caption says they 'usually evoke' a single stream. So the claim rests on informal listening. Neural: 75-ms tones with 5-ms ramps; 40-ms onset asynchrony (about 50% overlap) for the overlapping condition; Exp. I spacings 0.25, 0.5 and 1 octave.
verified.relevance: Theoretical anchor; the colleague's description is accurate. The tension with Micheyl 2013 Exp. 1 is real, but it sets an informal claim against a formal measurement, and the behavioural task used only about 1.5-s sequences (5 precursor pairs).

verified.citation: Pressnitzer D, Hupé JM (2006). Temporal dynamics of auditory and visual bistability reveal common principles of perceptual organization. Curr Biol 16(13):1351-1357. PMID 16824924
verified.corrected_claim: The abstract confirms: bistable perception occurs in auditory streaming; the temporal dynamics of alternations and the susceptibility to volitional control are strongly similar to visual plaids; subject-specific biases did not correlate across modalities. I could NOT verify from accessible text the specific claims about the exclusivity, inevitability and randomness criteria, or that build-up is an artefact of averaging switches. The attribution of the latter to 'Denham & Winkler 2006' is a separate, unchecked reference. Hupé & Pressnitzer (2012) does describe build-up as arising from the first-percept bias plus later alternation.
verified.relevance: Valid as the citation establishing auditory bistability. The 'build-up is an averaging artefact' point should be cited to Hupé & Pressnitzer 2012, or verified in the full text, before it goes into a talk.

verified.citation: Rankin J, Sussman E, Rinzel J (2015). Neuromechanistic model of auditory bistability. PLoS Comput Biol 11(11):e1004555. PMID 26562507, PMC4642990
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the PMC full text. ABA- triplets of 125-ms tones, 0.5-s triplets (8 Hz tone rate), 240-s trials. 8 spacings (1-15 st); equidominance at 5 st. 16 recruited, 15 analysed, three 8-trial blocks (24 trials per subject). At 5 st (normalised, pooled over 45 trials, 1575 durations): mean 7.7 s, CV 0.83, log-normal fit and not gamma. Pilot (6 subjects): 4.3 s, CV 0.73. Model: 5.1 s, CV 0.72. Cites published means of about 4-9 s. Build-up takes 'a few to ten seconds' at intermediate spacings, tens of seconds at small spacings, and is near-instant at large ones. tau_a = 1.4 s; NMDA-like tau_e = 70 ms. Generalised Levelt II: durations of the stronger percept change more.
verified.relevance: Supports the timescale argument: a trial of about 2.4 s falls inside a typical first phase, so the mixture across trials dominates over switches within a trial.

verified.citation: Rankin J, Osborn Popp PJ, Rinzel J (2017). Stimulus pauses and perturbations differentially delay or promote the segregation of auditory objects. Front Neurosci 11:198. PMID 28473747, PMC5397483
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the PMC full text. ABA_ with 100-ms tones and 10-ms ramps, 400-ms triplets, 4, 7 or 10 st. A roved 420-1060 Hz, 65 dB SPL, 5-s gaps between trials. The percept of the final triplet was reported. Pause experiment: 7 context triplets, a 300 or 600 ms pause, then 3 test triplets; both pauses gave a partial reset toward integration of similar size (F(2,14)=5.13). Distractor/deviant experiments: 6 triplets, with the perturbation after the 3rd. The distractor was a 50-ms tone at A-2, A, (A+B)/2, B, B+2, B+4, B+8 or B+15 st; the deviant was B raised by 2 st. Perturbations at or between A and B PROMOTED segregation (F(3,21)=5.80, largest at small spacing). Perturbations above B or below A had no effect (F=2.15, p=.125); B+15 had no effect (data not shown). 8 subjects per experiment, 17 in total. MINOR: 'three triplets is enough' is the authors' design choice justified by citing earlier studies; they did not test it.
verified.relevance: Direct warning for tsync's anomalous ending. It also supports short trials with end-of-trial reports and gaps of at least 5 s between trials.
