verified.citation: Thompson SK, Carlyon RP, Cusack R (2011). An objective measurement of the build-up of auditory streaming and of its modulation by attention. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 37(4):1253-1262. PMID 21480747
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: ABA triplets of 50-ms tones with 75-ms gaps, 4 vs 8 st. Detection of a single lengthened B-after-A gap was better early than late and at 4 st than at 8 st. Exp. 2: a delay 12.5 s into a 13.5-s sequence was detected better when listeners did a competing other-ear task for the first 10 s. Listeners could not prevent build-up even though it hurt performance. There are three experiments, of which the colleague described two.
verified.relevance: As stated: in a grouping-helps task, performance depends on context duration and attention, so these must be held constant across D.

verified.citation: Carlyon RP, Cusack R, Foxton JM, Robertson IH (2001). Effects of attention and unilateral neglect on auditory stream segregation. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 27(1):115-127. PMID 11248927
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: build-up was greatly reduced or absent while listeners attended a competing contralateral task; neglect patients showed less segregation for left-ear sequences. The DOI resolves with the standard form 10.1037/0096-1523.27.1.115; PubMed lists 10.1037//0096-1523.27.1.115.
verified.relevance: As stated: keep attentional load constant across D.

verified.citation: Cusack R, Deeks J, Aikman G, Carlyon RP (2004). Effects of location, frequency region, and time course of selective attention on auditory scene analysis. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 30(4):643-656. PMID 15301615
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract (Exps. 3-4): after even short physical gaps or brief attention switches, streaming is reset. A hierarchical decomposition model is proposed. Exps. 1-2 show that attention effects are not a general suppression by side or frequency region.
verified.relevance: Supports dropping 2I-2AFC in favour of single-interval trials, because the gap between intervals partly resets the percept.

verified.citation: Billig AJ, Davis MH, Carlyon RP (2018). Neural decoding of bistable sounds reveals an effect of intention on perceptual organization. J Neurosci 38(11):2844-2853. PMID 29440556, PMC5852662
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: 27 listeners (15 M, 12 F), HLH- sequences, continuous reports during MEG. A classifier separated integrated from segregated periods during neutral listening. Trying for a percept increased the time it was reported. Auditory-cortex responses resembled the segregation signature more when listeners tried to segregate than when they tried to integrate.
verified.relevance: As stated: listeners motivated to integrate really change their perception, so instructions must be identical across D. Also shows that percept can be decoded from M/EEG.

verified.citation: Hupé JM, Pressnitzer D (2012). The initial phase of auditory and visual scene analysis. Philos Trans R Soc Lond B 367(1591):942-953. PMID 22371616, PMC3282313
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: at onset, both streaming and plaids start with a bias toward grouping, and the first percept lasts longer ('inertia'). The two properties are independent: removing depth ambiguity in plaids removed inertia but not the bias. In audition, level differences between streams left both inertia and first-percept bias intact. The abstract states that build-up of the probability of segregation results from these two properties.
verified.relevance: Correct. It is also the better citation for 'build-up reflects the first-percept bias plus alternation'. The inference that short trials compress a grouping-helps D effect is the colleague's, not the paper's.

verified.citation: Denham SL, Gyimesi K, Stefanics G, Winkler I (2013). Perceptual bistability in auditory streaming: How much do stimulus features matter? Learning & Perception 5(Suppl 2):73-100
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed via the REAL repository record and the Consensus abstract (not in PubMed, so the colleague's Consensus link was the only pointer; the DOI is 10.1556/LP.5.2013.Suppl2.6). With longer-than-usual two-tone sequences, listeners hold the first percept for a relatively long time and then switch between two or more organisations, each held for much shorter durations. Stimulus parameters affect the quality and duration of the first percept far more than later percepts. Full-text numbers not checked.
verified.relevance: As stated: short fresh-start trials sample the regime most sensitive to the stimulus parameter (D).

verified.citation: Denham S, Bõhm TM, Bendixen A, Szalárdy O, Kocsis Z, Mill R, Winkler I (2014). Stable individual characteristics in the perception of multiple embedded patterns in multistable auditory stimuli. Front Neurosci 8:25. PMID 24616656
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: after training on all length-4 embedded patterns, listeners reported many more patterns than integrated or segregated. Individual switching patterns were idiosyncratic, more similar within a person across sessions than between people, and preserved a year later.
verified.relevance: As stated: expect stable individual differences; use per-listener slopes or a mixed model.

verified.citation: Farkas D, Denham SL, Bendixen A, Winkler I (2016). Assessing the validity of subjective reports in the auditory streaming paradigm. J Acoust Soc Am 139(4):1762. PMID 27106324
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: catch trials promoting each percept were used to exclude listeners who misunderstood the instructions. Explicit-bias instructions and a random-response condition gave markedly different behaviour from neutral instructions. Social desirability was unrelated to perceptual measures. Conclusion: reports are valid.
verified.relevance: As stated: add catch trials if one-vs-two-stream reports are collected.

verified.citation: Spielmann MI, Schröger E, Kotz SA, Pechmann T, Bendixen A (2013). Using a staircase procedure for the objective measurement of auditory stream integration and segregation thresholds. Front Psychol 4:534. PMID 23970873
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: the staircase varied either the ISI or the spacing with the other held fixed. The integration task (cross-stream temporal judgment) gave consistent thresholds and related significantly to subjective thresholds; the segregation task (within-stream deviance detection) was less suited to staircases. Staircasing D itself was NOT tested; that is the colleague's extrapolation.
verified.relevance: Supports a cross-stream timing task, and the idea of staircasing the stimulus parameter at a fixed judged quantity. State clearly that applying it to D is new.

verified.citation: Turgeon M, Bregman AS, Roberts B (2005). Rhythmic masking release: effects of asynchrony, temporal overlap, harmonic relations, and source separation on cross-spectral grouping. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 31(5):939-953. PMID 16262490
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: listeners identified which of 2 rhythms was played; accuracy and rated clarity indexed fusion of distractors with captors. Fusion depended mainly on onset asynchrony and temporal overlap; harmonic relations had some influence; only an extreme spatial difference (dichotic) was effective; both preattentive and attentional processes were involved. The colleague says 'only dichotic presentation among spatial cues was effective', which matches. The stimuli appear to be complex tones (2002 used noise bursts). I could NOT retrieve the full text (the McGill PDF host is discontinued), so 'varies smoothly with onset asynchrony' and all parameter values are unverified. Fusion in the companion 2002 paper (below) is abolished by 20-40 ms asynchrony, which suggests the RMR function is steep rather than smooth over a 0-100 ms D range.
verified.relevance: A valid template for a grouping-helps, Weber-free task. Its useful D range is probably about 0-40 ms, not Micheyl's 0-100 ms.

verified.citation: Byrne Á, Rinzel J, Rankin J (2019). Auditory streaming and bistability paradigm extended to a dynamic environment. Hear Res 383:107807. PMID 31622836
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: for fixed ABA- stimuli, switches occur at random every 2-15 s. With slow periodic modulation of features, switches become entrained to the rising and falling phases, depending on the modulation period and each listener's intrinsic switching.
verified.relevance: As stated: an interesting slow-sweep design for EEG, not the primary measure.

verified.citation: Winkler I, Denham S, Mill R, Bohm TM, Bendixen A (2012). Multistability in auditory stream segregation: a predictive coding view. Philos Trans R Soc Lond B 367(1591):1001-1012. PMID 22371621
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: a review and theory paper. Alternative descriptions are represented in parallel and compete for awareness; predictive processing stabilises continuing patterns and signals new sources.
verified.relevance: Framing, as stated.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Christiansen SK, Oxenham AJ (2014). Assessing the effects of temporal coherence on auditory stream formation through comodulation masking release. J Acoust Soc Am 135(6):3520-3529. PMID 24907815, PMC4048442
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the PMC full text. Task: detect a 1-kHz tone in a 20-Hz-wide masker band at 1 kHz, with comodulated flanking bands at 0.25, 0.5, 2 and 4 kHz. Bursts of 187.5 ms (20-ms ramps), 250-ms onset interval, 60 dB SPL per band. 3I-3AFC, 2-down-1-up. Exp. 1 (7 listeners): a fixed flanker-masker onset offset of 0, 20, 40 or 60 ms; CMR was significantly reduced at 40 and 60 ms (no significant effect reported at 20 ms), and also reduced with different burst rates, but CMR stayed significant in every condition. Exp. 3 (ten bursts, target at burst 5-7): CMR significant at 0 ms (t(7)=14.1), not significant at 60 ms (t(7)=1.42). Caveats from the authors: short sequences may limit build-up; within-channel and peripheral contributions not fully excluded.
verified.relevance: The most important paper the colleague missed. It is a published GROUPING-HELPS measure in which performance falls with a FIXED onset offset between streams, and the judged quantity (tone detection) is identical at every offset, so there is no Weber confound. It is a direct counterpart to Micheyl 2013 Exp. 3 by the same lab. It also suggests the effect emerges between 20 and 40 ms.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Turgeon M, Bregman AS, Ahad PA (2002). Rhythmic masking release: contribution of cues for perceptual organization to the cross-spectral fusion of concurrent narrow-band noises. J Acoust Soc Am 111(4):1819-1831. PMID 12002866
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: synchrony fully fuses short noise bursts across frequency and space; an asynchrony of 20-40 ms produces no fusion; 10-20 ms produces partial fusion. Onset asynchrony was the dominant cue, with additive effects of other cues.
verified.relevance: Gives the asynchrony scale for cross-spectral fusion of brief sounds: fusion is lost by about 20-40 ms. Together with Micheyl 2013 (abrupt 0 to 35 ms gains) and Christiansen & Oxenham 2014 (effect at 40 ms or more), it argues for sampling D densely in the 0-40 ms range.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Micheyl C, Kreft H, Shamma S, Oxenham AJ (2013). Temporal coherence versus harmonicity in auditory stream formation. J Acoust Soc Am 133(3):EL188-EL194. PMID 23464127, PMC3579859
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: a performance-based measure in which listeners discriminated frequency shifts in a regular sequence of target tones within a constant or randomly varying multi-tone background. Targets were temporally coherent or incoherent with the background, and harmonically or inharmonically related to it. Temporal incoherence facilitated segregation, and inharmonicity could too, even with coherent timing.
verified.relevance: Another objective temporal-coherence measure from the same group (segregation-helps). It shows that harmonicity is a confound to control if A and B frequencies are changed, for example when reducing the spacing.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Bregman AS, Pinker S (1978). Auditory streaming and the building of timbre. Can J Psychol 32(1):19-31. PMID 728845
verified.corrected_claim: Existence confirmed in PubMed (no abstract available). The paper is widely cited as the classic A-BC capture paradigm, in which the onset asynchrony of B and C trades off against sequential capture of B by A. I did not verify its specific numbers.
verified.relevance: The historical precedent for competition between sequential capture and simultaneous grouping as a function of onset asynchrony. Cite it for background only, after checking the full text.

verified.citation: [ADDED] O'Sullivan JA, Shamma SA, Lalor EC (2015). Evidence for neural computations of temporal coherence in an auditory scene and their enhancement during active listening. J Neurosci 35(18):7256-7263. PMID 25948273
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: EEG with stochastic figure-ground stimuli in which figure coherence was modulated stochastically, analysed with temporal response functions. A coherence response appeared about 115-185 ms during passive listening and was larger and longer (up to about 265 ms) during active listening.
verified.relevance: An EEG temporal-coherence readout that needs no reports. It is relevant to candidate 9 and to the lab's ongoing figure-ground EEG work.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Lu K, Xu Y, Yin P, Oxenham AJ, Fritz JB, Shamma SA (2017). Temporal coherence structure rapidly shapes neuronal interactions. Nat Commun 8:13900. PMID 28054545
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract: in ferret A1, synchronous tone sequences rapidly enhanced responses, receptive-field sensitivity and spiking correlations, and alternating sequences suppressed them, but only when the animals were engaged in the task and attending.
verified.relevance: Neural evidence that the effects of temporal coherence depend on attention. It supports keeping the task and attention identical across D.

candidate_measures: 1. KEEP. Fixed target size, constant stimuli, d' or proportion correct vs D, mirroring Micheyl 2013 Exp. 3. CHANGE: sample D densely below about 40 ms (e.g., 0, 10, 20, 35, 50, 100). Fusion of brief sounds is lost by 20-40 ms (Turgeon et al. 2002), some Micheyl listeners jumped from 0 to 35 ms, and CMR fell at 40 ms or more (Christiansen & Oxenham 2014). The colleague's cost estimate (about 25-30 min for 5 D values) is plausible but was not checked against data.

2. KEEP. Make the judged quantity synchrony detection near 0 ms at every D (Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010; Elhilali 2009), with a matched-displacement control at every D. Note that in Micheyl 2010 order thresholds were 1.84 times LARGER than detection thresholds, the reverse of the ideal-observer prediction, so prefer detection (sync vs async) over order judgments.

3. KEEP, with a corrected cost. Percept-contingent hybrid (Billig & Carlyon 2016): the concurrent report cost about 0.59 d' units there, and the whole Exp. 2 took about 30 min, not 90. A GLMM plus a mixture model with Farkas-style catch trials stands.

4. KEEP. Stand-alone subjective p(2 streams | D) using Micheyl 2013 Exp. 1's protocol (about 2.4 s, report at the end). Neither Micheyl 2013 nor Elhilali 2009 has behavioural percept data for partly overlapping D (Elhilali's 'always one stream' was informal, and her Fig. 1 caption says 'usually'). The colleague's claim that no one has measured long-run switching for synchronous or overlapping sequences was not falsified by a quick search, but it is not proven.

5. KEEP, but treat as second line. Rhythmic masking release (Turgeon et al. 2005; 2002). The 2005 parameters could not be verified in the full text; the 2002 data show fusion gone by 20-40 ms, so the task will saturate early in D. New code and training needed.

5b. NEW, high priority. CMR-based grouping-helps measure (Christiansen & Oxenham 2014). Detect a tone in a narrowband masker whose comodulated flanking band(s) lag by a fixed D. The release from masking falls as D grows (significant at 40 and 60 ms), the judged quantity (tone detection) is identical at every D (no Weber confound), there is no anomalous ending, and the lab has published a clean D manipulation. A pure-tone A/B analogue (e.g., the target embedded in the B channel and A-channel flanking tones comodulated with the masker) would need piloting. Risk: CMR was not fully abolished in their Exps. 1-2, and within-channel cues must be controlled.
6. KEEP as second choice. Across-stream vs within-stream Weber-normalised timing ratio.

7. KEEP. Reduce A-B spacing to raise p_int. Micheyl 2013 Exp. 1 confirms synchronous P(2 streams) of about 0.76 at 15 st, and alternating vs synchronous differed only at 9 and 15 st. At 6 st the two did not differ (0.11 [-0.10, 0.33]), so 9 st may be a better compromise than 6 st. Watch harmonicity (Micheyl, Kreft et al. 2013) and beats at small spacings.
8. KEEP. Single-interval trials with at least 2-5 s between trials (Rankin et al. 2017 used 5 s; Billig & Carlyon used 2 s), and a fixed context length (Thompson et al. 2011; Cusack et al. 2004).
9. KEEP. EEG as a no-report check: MEG decoding (Billig et al. 2018) and EEG temporal-coherence TRFs (O'Sullivan et al. 2015) both have precedent.

Probably-fail list: KEEP (staircases on asynchrony at fixed D; whole-pair jitter at fast rates; minutes-long continuous reports as the primary measure). Note that the claim that the mixture-induced ceiling explains tpair's noisy or ceiling thresholds is a plausible hypothesis, not a demonstrated fact.
evidence.angle_summary: VERDICT: all 19 papers the colleague cited exist; 18 have DOIs that resolve in PubMed, and Denham et al. 2013 Learning & Perception was confirmed via the REAL repository (DOI 10.1556/LP.5.2013.Suppl2.6). The numbers for Micheyl 2013, Billig & Carlyon 2016, Micheyl 2010, Elhilali 2009, Rankin 2015 and Rankin 2017 were checked against the PMC full texts, and nearly all match. CORRECTIONS: (1) Billig & Carlyon 2016 Exp. 2 took about 30 min (48 trials), not about 90 min. (2) Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010: order thresholds were 1.84 times LARGER than detection thresholds, while the ideal observer predicted them 2.91 times SMALLER, so the result runs opposite to the prediction. The colleague's wording obscured this. Exp. 3's ear manipulation removed the captor effect only when the captors were in the ear opposite both targets. (3) Elhilali 2009 has no formal subjective streaming data. 'Always heard as one stream' is in the text, but the Fig. 1 caption says 'usually', the behavioural sequences had only 5 precursor pairs, and the A-stream controls differ in gap (30/70 ms), not interval. (4) Micheyl 2013 itself reports no switching. 'Bistable' is our inference from trial-level mixtures in Exp. 1, though the instructions did tell listeners the percept 'could change'. (5) Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006: the core bistability claim is verified, but 'build-up is an averaging artefact' should be cited to Hupé & Pressnitzer 2012, and the 'Denham & Winkler 2006' attribution was not checked. (6) Turgeon et al. 2005 parameters could not be retrieved; only the abstract was verified. (7) Spielmann 2013 never staircased onset delay; that is an extrapolation. ANSWER TO 'IS IT BISTABLE?': plausibly yes at the level of the trial-to-trial percept mixture (Micheyl Exp. 1: synchronous P(2 streams) about 0.76 at 15 st, with large and even reversed individual differences). No study measured switching dynamics for synchronous or partly overlapping sequences, so a long-run claim is untested. The mixture-model framing and the advice to use constant stimuli instead of staircases stand. KEY MISSED PAPER: Christiansen & Oxenham 2014 JASA, a grouping-helps CMR measure in which release from masking falls with a FIXED flanker-masker onset offset (significant at 40 and 60 ms, not reported at 20 ms), with the judged quantity identical across offsets. It is a direct, Weber-free counterpart to Micheyl 2013 Exp. 3 from the same lab. Also added: Turgeon, Bregman & Ahad 2002 (fusion abolished by 20-40 ms asynchrony) and Micheyl Exp. 3's abrupt 0 to 35 ms gains, which together say a grouping-helps D function will likely saturate by about 35-40 ms, so D should be sampled densely below 40 ms rather than at Micheyl's 0-100 ms. Further additions: Micheyl, Kreft et al. 2013 (harmonicity confound), O'Sullivan et al. 2015 (EEG coherence TRF) and Lu et al. 2017 (coherence effects depend on attention).

verified.citation: Bregman AS, Ahad PA, Crum PA, O'Reilly J (2000). Effects of time intervals and tone durations on auditory stream segregation. Percept Psychophys 62(3):626-636
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed by the PubMed abstract (PMID 10909253). Listeners rated on a 7-point scale how hard it was to hear one coherent stream in HLH- gallops. Onset-to-onset time, tone duration, the ISI between same-frequency tones and frequency separation were varied. The speed effect on segregation is 'primarily due to its effect on the ISI between tones in the same frequency region'. The claim that 5 Hz/100-ms and 6.7 Hz/75-ms are close in streaming terms is the colleague's inference, not a result from the paper.
verified.relevance: Supports matching Micheyl's 5 Hz/100-ms geometry, since the same-frequency gap (100 ms) is the parameter that controls streaming.

verified.citation: Moore BCJ, Gockel HE (2012). Properties of auditory stream formation. Phil Trans R Soc B 367(1591):919-931
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract and the PMC full text (PMC3282308). Build-up is rapid over about 10 s and continues more slowly up to at least 60 s. Haywood & Roberts (2010) is cited: one deviant final inducer tone (frequency, duration, or silence) gives substantial resetting, and resetting is graded rather than all-or-none. Roberts et al. (2008) is cited for 'a large variety of types of abrupt changes'. At intermediate separations the percept flips irregularly, and instructions shift the proportions. The TCB rises markedly with repetition period while the FB changes only slightly. Bendixen et al. (2010): regularities prolong two-stream phases and leave one-stream phases unchanged. The review gives no stimulus parameters for Pressnitzer & Hupé (2006). Caveat the colleague missed: the reset evidence cited comes from constant-frequency inducers (see Haywood & Roberts 2013 below).
verified.relevance: Authoritative support that ABA-type sequences are bistable at intermediate settings and that build-up and reset exist. Applies to tsync's short (about 2.4 s) contexts.

verified.citation: Pressnitzer D, Hupé JM (2006). Temporal dynamics of auditory and visual bistability reveal common principles of perceptual organization. Curr Biol 16(13):1351-1357
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract (PMID 16824924). Auditory streaming shows true bistability: spontaneous alternations whose temporal dynamics and susceptibility to volitional control resemble visual plaids, and subject-specific biases do not correlate across modalities. Stimulus parameters are NOT confirmed. Later reanalyses of the Hupé/Pressnitzer data describe 4-min ABA- runs at 5 semitones (not about 7) with 110-120 ms onset-to-onset intervals, but this is unverified for the 2006 paper itself. The 'averaging stochastic switches produces smooth build-up' claim belongs to Denham & Winkler (2006), verified separately below.
verified.relevance: Directly answers the user's question: yes, ABA streaming is bistable. Intermediate D in an A/B-delay paradigm should produce trial-to-trial and listener-to-listener percept mixtures.

verified.citation: Denham SL, Winkler I (2006). The role of predictive models in the formation of auditory streams. J Physiol Paris 100(1-3):154-170
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract (PMID 17084600). It reports a perceptual experiment confirming that streaming is bistable, and supports the proposal that the gradual build-up of streaming 'may be an artefact of averaging across many subjects' (citing Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006).
verified.relevance: Explains why group D-curves can look graded while individuals (e.g., Micheyl's L6 and L8) switch abruptly. Supports per-listener and percept-conditioned analysis.

verified.citation: Micheyl C, Hanson C, Demany L, Shamma S, Oxenham AJ (2013). Auditory stream segregation for alternating and synchronous tones. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 39(6):1568-1580
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the PMC full text (PMC3973443). Exp. 1: 7 listeners; 24 tones (12 A + 12 B); 100-ms tones with 20-ms ramps; 100-ms gaps between same-frequency tones; 2.3 s (synchronous) or 2.4 s (alternating); separations of 1, 3, 6, 9 and 15 semitones. Correction: P(2 streams) at 15 semitones (about 0.97 alternating vs about 0.76 synchronous) are group averages, not modal values. The difference was credible only at 9 semitones (0.23 [0.03, 0.40]) and 15 semitones (0.19 [0.03, 0.44]). Exp. 3: 7 listeners, 15 semitones, D = 0/35/50/71/100 ms. Group MAP d' was about 1.48 at 0 ms and 2.43 at 100 ms (35/50/71 ms values appear only in Fig. 7). Credible differences: 0 vs 100 ms (1.10 [0.03, 2.05]) and 0 vs 50 ms (0.65 [0.04, 1.42]). L6 and L8 improved abruptly between 0 and 35 ms. Listeners ran 104-216 trials per condition (more than 200 in 86% of cases). The first 4 B tones never changed. The increment was 4 dB (64 vs 60 dB SPL), and the A rove was ±4 dB.
verified.relevance: This is the segregation-helps reference curve. The mirror experiment should copy its geometry and its constant-stimuli d' metric.

verified.citation: Elhilali M, Ma L, Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ, Shamma SA (2009). Temporal coherence in the perceptual organization and cortical representation of auditory scenes. Neuron 61(2):317-329
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the PMC full text (PMC2673083). 9 non-author listeners described as having 'extensive experience' with the procedure. 100-ms tones, 10-ms ramps; A = 1000 Hz; B 0.5, 0.75 or 1.25 octaves above. 5 A + 5 B precursors, then a target pair. Synchronous condition: 50-ms gaps (150-ms cycle). Asynchronous condition: B gaps 50 ms, A gaps 30 or 70 ms, so the two streams run at different rates rather than with a fixed lag. 2I-2AFC, 3-down-1-up, 500 ms between sequences, left earpiece only. Synchronous thresholds were about 2-4 ms at all separations. Asynchronous thresholds were about 10-20 ms and did not differ from B-alone. The 40-ms onset asynchrony was used only in the ferret physiology.
verified.relevance: The baseline the lab's tcoh copies. The synchronous advantage may reflect an across-channel synchrony cue rather than streaming per se.

verified.citation: Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ (2010). Objective and subjective psychophysical measures of auditory stream integration and segregation. J Assoc Res Otolaryngol 11(4):709-724
verified.corrected_claim: Checked against the PMC full text (PMC2975891). B = 1000 Hz; A 0-15 semitones below; 20-ms ramps; T = 50 or 100 ms; N = 1, 2, 4 or 8. Integration task (Exp. 2, 7 listeners): AB-A vs A-BA, with triplet onsets jittered ±T. Segregation task (Exp. 3): last B early or late, with B-B interval 6T, A shifted ±T, N = 2/4/8, and a no-A condition. 2-down-1-up (70.7%). Exp. 2: Δf F(5,30)=21.47; N F(3,18)=23.38; rate F(1,6)=6.33. Exp. 3: Δf F(4,24)=8.94; rate F(1,6)=44.45; N n.s. Slow/fast ratios without A were 1.82, 1.35 and 1.20 (N = 2, 4, 8), used to correct for Weber; a rate effect remained after correction. Mean Spearman rho was 0.61-0.69 (integration) and -0.46 to -0.59 (segregation). Individual correlations were inconsistent. The 0-semitone N effect at the fast rate was attributed tentatively to precursor distraction.
verified.relevance: The template for matched integration- and segregation-helps tasks with explicit Weber and no-A baselines.

verified.citation: Thompson SK, Carlyon RP, Cusack R (2011). An objective measurement of the build-up of auditory streaming and of its modulation by attention. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 37(4):1253-1262
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract (PMID 21480747). ABA triplets of 50-ms tones with 75-ms gaps. Detecting a short increase in the B-preceding-A gap was better early than late in the sequence and better at Δf 4 than 8 semitones, consistent with subjective judgements. Exp. 2: a competing task in the other ear for the first 10 s improved detection of a delay 12.5 s into a 13.5-s sequence. Build-up is not fully under voluntary control. Exact early/late probe times for Exp. 1 were not verified.
verified.relevance: A validated integration-helps objective task that indexes build-up. Its judged quantity is still A-B timing, so it needs the same-frequency control.

verified.citation: Roberts B, Glasberg BR, Moore BCJ (2008). Effects of the build-up and resetting of auditory stream segregation on temporal discrimination. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 34(4):992-1006
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract (PMID 18665740). A 2.0-s FIXED-FREQUENCY inducer, then a 0.6-s test of 3 L-H cycles at 0-12 semitones; listeners judged isochronous vs delayed H. Every inducer-test difference tested (frequency, number of onsets, tone:silence ratio, level, lateralization) moved thresholds toward the no-inducer value. Caveat: the inducer was a constant-frequency sequence, not an alternating or AB context like tsync's.
verified.relevance: A reset warning for 'context then deviant ending' designs. How far it transfers to tsync's AB context is uncertain (see Haywood & Roberts 2013).

verified.citation: Haywood NR, Roberts B (2010). Build-up of the tendency to segregate auditory streams: resetting effects evoked by a single deviant tone. J Acoust Soc Am 128(5):3019-3031
verified.corrected_claim: Verified (PMID 21110597). This paper was cited only second-hand by the colleague. The inducer was 10 identical L tones. A single deviant final inducer (frequency, level, duration, or silence) reduced reported segregation, often substantially. The effect was partly replicated with a temporal-discrimination measure. Resetting grew only gradually with the size of the frequency change and began once the change was noticeable.
verified.relevance: Shows that one deviant can reset build-up, but only for constant-frequency inducers.

verified.citation: Haywood NR, Roberts B (2013). Build-up of auditory stream segregation induced by tone sequences of constant or alternating frequency and the resetting effects of single deviants. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 39(6):1652-1666 [ADDED; missed by colleague]
verified.corrected_claim: Verified (PMID 23688330). Constant-frequency inducers reach maximum effect after only 3 tones and promote segregation much more than alternating inducers, an advantage lasting about 10 s. Resetting by a single deviant (a longer tone) occurred ONLY with constant-frequency inducers, not with alternating ones. The authors interpret this as the deviant disrupting 'capture' into a pre-established stream.
verified.relevance: Weakens the colleague's claim that tsync's re-synchronised ending necessarily resets segregation, since tsync's context is an alternating/AB sequence. The anomalous-ending objection to tsync still stands on other grounds (D-dependent displacement, Weber), but 'reset' is not established for this kind of context.

verified.citation: Turgeon M, Bregman AS, Roberts B (2005). Rhythmic masking release: effects of asynchrony, temporal overlap, harmonic relations, and source separation on cross-spectral grouping. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 31(5):939-953
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract (PMID 16262490). Identify 1 of 2 rhythms masked by identical irregular distractors. Fusion of distractors with temporally overlapping captors releases the rhythm. Fusion depended primarily on onset asynchrony and temporal overlap. Harmonicity had some influence. Only dichotic presentation was effective spatially. Both preattentive and attention-driven processes contributed. Per-condition accuracies were not verified.
verified.relevance: The closest published grouping-helps task where accuracy falls with asynchrony and the judgement (rhythm identity) is not timing. It indexes concurrent fusion.

verified.citation: Turgeon M, Bregman AS, Ahad PA (2002). Rhythmic masking release: contribution of cues for perceptual organization to the cross-spectral fusion of concurrent narrow-band noises. J Acoust Soc Am 111(4):1819-1831
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract (PMID 12002866); the correct DOI is 10.1121/1.1453450 (the colleague gave a Lancaster eprint URL). Brief narrow-band noise bursts. Synchrony fully fuses across frequency and space. A 20-40 ms asynchrony produces no fusion; 10-20 ms produces partial fusion, where other cues become critical. Onset asynchrony was dominant; frequency and spatial separation reduced fusion additively but did not abolish it.
verified.relevance: Predicts that an RMR-style grouping-helps curve collapses by about 20-40 ms, much steeper than Micheyl's 0-100 ms segregation curve.

verified.citation: Friberg A, Sundberg J (1995). Time discrimination in a monotonic, isochronous sequence. J Acoust Soc Am 98(5):2524-2531
verified.corrected_claim: Not in PubMed; verified through web sources and the abstract. 30 listeners adjusted the 4th of 6 tones toward isochrony, with IOIs of 100-1000 ms. The absolute JND was about 6 ms for IOIs below about 240 ms (the full text says about 250 ms), and the relative JND about 2.5% above that. The colleague's claim that musical training had no effect was NOT verified. The DOI was missing in the colleague's entry.
verified.relevance: The single-stream timing floor from a method-of-adjustment task. Forced-choice limits (Hirsh 1990) are larger.

verified.citation: Hirsh IJ, Monahan CB, Grant KW, Singh PG (1990). Studies in auditory timing: 1. Simple patterns. Percept Psychophys 47(3):215-226
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract (PMID 2326145). In 6- or 10-tone isochronous sequences, delay thresholds were 6-8% at IOI 200 ms, 11-12% at 100 ms and almost 20% at 50 ms. Position did not matter at 100 and 200 ms; at 50 ms, final positions were best. There was 'some evidence' (at 200 ms) of poorer discrimination for a tone of different frequency, and discrimination was poorer around a doubled interval.
verified.relevance: The forced-choice single-stream anisochrony limit, about 12-16 ms at Micheyl's 200-ms cycle. This is consistent with the tcoh plateau and with Elhilali's asynchronous/B-alone thresholds (an inference).

verified.citation: Ehrlé N, Samson S (2005). Auditory discrimination of anisochrony: influence of the tempo and musical backgrounds of listeners. Brain Cogn 58(1):133-147
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract (PMID 15878734). Adaptive 2AFC; IOI 80-1000 ms. JNDs grow linearly and proportionally with IOI (Weber) except at 80 ms. Percussionists are more sensitive than non-musicians and other instrumentalists.
verified.relevance: Supports Weber scaling of single-stream timing, and recording percussion training as a covariate.

verified.citation: Zera J, Green DM (1993a). Detecting temporal onset and offset asynchrony in multicomponent complexes. J Acoust Soc Am 93(2):1038-1052; Zera J, Green DM (1993b). Detecting temporal asynchrony with asynchronous standards. J Acoust Soc Am 93(3):1571-1579
verified.corrected_claim: Both confirmed from abstracts (PMIDs 8445115, 8473611). (a) Onset-asynchrony thresholds in harmonic complexes had a minimum of 0.2 ms at a 1-ms rise time. Offset thresholds were 0.45-1.3 ms, about 10 times the onset thresholds. Log-spaced complexes were nearly two orders of magnitude worse in some conditions. Detection relies on across-channel comparison. (b) An asynchronous standard greatly increased the difficulty of detecting onset asynchrony of one component; offset detection was little affected.
verified.relevance: The mechanism behind the reference-asynchrony confound in tcoh and tsync: the synchronous reference has a privileged cue. Note these are multicomponent complexes, not two pure tones 15 semitones apart.

verified.citation: Wojtczak M, Beim JA, Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ (2013). Effects of temporal stimulus properties on the perception of across-frequency asynchrony. J Acoust Soc Am 133(2):982-997
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract and PMC full text (PMC3574076). 250-Hz tone plus a 1/2/4/6-kHz tone; 500 ms; 10-ms ramps. 3I-3AFC, 2-down-1-up; 5 listeners in Exp. 2. Detection was better with the low-frequency tone leading. The asymmetry held only for standard asynchronies of 20 ms or less. At 20 dB SL, low-leading thresholds 'varied little with the standard asynchrony' up to 20 ms, then the two directions converged. At 85 dB SPL, thresholds rose up to 20 ms and then stayed 'relatively constant' from 20 to 100 ms. There is no Weber-law description; numeric values are in figures only. Onsets dominate.
verified.relevance: Asynchrony discrimination does not follow a clean Weber law; it plateaus. tcoh lags A (low) behind B, which is the less sensitive (high-leading) direction. Counterbalance it.

verified.citation: Vliegen J, Moore BCJ, Oxenham AJ (1999). The role of spectral and periodicity cues in auditory stream segregation, measured using a temporal discrimination task. J Acoust Soc Am 106(2):938-945
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract (PMID 10462799). ABA ABA sequences; B either at the midpoint between As or slightly delayed. Pure tones (A = 300 Hz) or filtered complexes (F0 100 Hz) differing in F0 only or in passband only. Intervals of 1-18 semitones. Shift thresholds rose with interval in all conditions, most for spectral differences.
verified.relevance: A classic integration-helps objective streaming task. Its same-frequency baseline logic carries over to a D-manipulation.

verified.citation: Fishman YI, Arezzo JC, Steinschneider M (2004). Auditory stream segregation in monkey auditory cortex: effects of frequency separation, presentation rate, and tone duration. J Acoust Soc Am 116(3):1656-1670
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract (PMID 15478432). Awake macaque A1 with ABAB sequences. Higher rates attenuated off-BF B responses more than A responses, and longer tone durations facilitated this differential attenuation, paralleling psychoacoustics.
verified.relevance: Background on rate and duration (a forward-suppression account). Not decisive for the D design.

verified.citation: Micheyl C, Kreft H, Shamma S, Oxenham AJ (2013). Temporal coherence versus harmonicity in auditory stream formation. J Acoust Soc Am 133(3):EL188-EL194
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract (PMID 23464127). Listeners discriminated frequency shifts in a regular target pure-tone sequence within a constant or random multi-tone background. Temporal incoherence facilitated segregation, and inharmonicity facilitated it even when targets and masker were temporally coherent.
verified.relevance: A segregation-helps measure with a non-temporal judgement. The 'grouping-helps conjunction' mirror proposed by the colleague is untested.

verified.citation: Neilans EG, Dent ML (2015; epub 2014). Temporal coherence for pure tones in budgerigars and humans. J Comp Psychol 129(1):52-61
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed from the abstract (PMID 25419717). With the same procedures, humans were more apt to fuse partially overlapping tones, while budgerigars segregated them. Budgerigars matched temporal-coherence model predictions and humans did not. Percent-overlap values were not verified.
verified.relevance: Humans may integrate partially overlapping A/B (D < tone duration) more than temporal-coherence models predict, so the human D-curve may be shallower or shifted.

verified.citation: van Noorden LPAS (1975). Temporal coherence in the perception of tone sequences. Doctoral dissertation, Eindhoven University of Technology / Institute for Perception Research
verified.doi_or_url: https://research.tue.nl (search title); colleague's URL is WRONG
verified.corrected_claim: The thesis exists and its TCB/FB concepts are confirmed through Moore & Gockel (2012): the TCB rises markedly with repetition period and the FB changes only slightly. However, the colleague's URL (web.pa.msu.edu/acoustics/vani.pdf) is a DIFFERENT document, titled 'Temporal predictability as a grouping cue in the perception of auditory streams', not van Noorden's thesis. The thesis itself was not read. The claim that 15 semitones at 5 Hz is above the TCB for alternating tones is an inference, and it is consistent with Micheyl's P(2 streams) of about 0.97.
verified.relevance: The conceptual basis for an ambiguous (bistable) region between the FB and the TCB.

verified.citation: Micheyl C, Hunter C, Oxenham AJ (2010). Auditory stream segregation and the perception of across-frequency synchrony. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 36(4):1029-1039 [ADDED; important omission]
verified.corrected_claim: Verified from the PubMed abstract (PMID 20695716) and the PMC full text (PMC4315665). A = 1000 Hz; B 6 or 15 semitones above; 100-ms pure tones with 10-ms ramps at 60 dB SPL. Captors: 5 before and 2 after the target A, at the A frequency (on) or 9 semitones below (off), with 50-ms gaps (150-ms cycle, as in Elhilali). Exp. 1 (6 listeners): 2I-2AFC lead-vs-lag discrimination, 3-down-1-up. On-frequency captors raised thresholds to about 43 ms (6 semitones) and about 50 ms (15 semitones), significantly above the no-captor and off-frequency conditions (no-captor values in figures only). Exp. 2 (8 listeners): synchrony detection; about 44 ms with on-frequency captors, and off-frequency captors did not differ from no captors. Exp. 3: contralateral captors removed the effect. Captor number and rate were not varied.
verified.relevance: The closest published grouping-helps paradigm. Sequential capture of A away from B strongly impairs across-frequency synchrony and temporal-order judgements, with remote-frequency captors as a built-in non-streaming control. A lead/lag discrimination is symmetric about synchrony, which sidesteps the reference-asynchrony (Weber/Zera-Green) problem.

verified.citation: Christiansen SK, Oxenham AJ (2014). Assessing the effects of temporal coherence on auditory stream formation through comodulation masking release. J Acoust Soc Am 135(6):3520-3529 [ADDED; important omission]
verified.corrected_claim: Verified from the PubMed abstract (PMID 24907815) and PMC4048442. Narrowband (20-Hz) noise bursts: masker at 1 kHz, flankers at 0.25/0.5/2/4 kHz; 187.5-ms bursts; 250-ms onset interval. Fixed flanker-masker offsets of 0/20/40/60 ms were applied to precursor (and postcursor) bursts only; the target burst was always synchronous. Different rates (200/300 vs 250 ms) were also tested. CMR (Exp. 1, 7 listeners analysed) fell significantly at 40 and 60 ms offsets and with mismatched rates; ±30-ms jitter had no significant effect. In Exp. 3 (10-burst sequences, 8 listeners), CMR was significant at 0 ms but not at 60 ms. The effect was not larger than in Exp. 1. CMR values are in figures only (a few dB).
verified.relevance: A published grouping-helps performance measure where the A-B offset D is manipulated in the context and the judgement (tone detection in noise) is not timing, so there is no Weber confound. It is the strongest existing template for the user's goal.

verified.citation: Shamma SA, Elhilali M, Micheyl C (2011). Temporal coherence and attention in auditory scene analysis. Trends Neurosci 34(3):114-123 [theory reference in task; verified]
verified.corrected_claim: Verified (PMID 21196054). It argues that stream formation depends primarily on temporal coherence between feature-encoding responses, with attention to one feature binding the coherent features.
verified.relevance: The theory frame for the talk and paper.

candidate_measures: CMR-based grouping measure (NEW; strongest; built on Christiansen & Oxenham 2014). Detect a B-band target in a B-band masker whose amplitude envelope is comodulated with A-band flankers. Precursor and postcursor flanker bursts run at onset delay D relative to the B-band bursts, and the target burst itself is always synchronous, so the final event is identical across D. Grouping (D = 0) gives CMR; asynchrony segregates the flankers and abolishes CMR. Performance should fall with D, and the judged quantity (tone detection) is not timing. Published effect: significant CMR loss at 40-60 ms. Risks: noise bands rather than pure tones, effects of a few dB, a long-ish onset interval (250 ms); pilot it at Micheyl's 5 Hz.

Captor/lead-lag task (NEW; Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010). Judge whether the final A-B pair is A-leading or B-leading by a fixed small asynchrony (constant stimuli). The reference is symmetric about synchrony, so it does not grow with D. The context A/B relation (D) determines whether A is captured into its own stream. Remote-frequency captors (published) or a 0-semitone version serve as the non-streaming control. Effect size in the original was large (about 44-50 ms with on-frequency captors). Caveat: the final pair differs from the context when D > 0, so pilot whether a constant final-pair deviation contaminates it.

Rhythmic-masking-release analogue (kept; Turgeon et al. 2002, 2005 verified). A B-band target rhythm plus irregular B-band distractors, each paired with an A captor at delay D. Fusion releases the rhythm, so accuracy should fall with D. No Weber confound. Expect the curve to collapse by about 20-40 ms (concurrent-fusion window), much steeper than Micheyl's 0-100 ms. Level-rove the captors.

Fixed-level (constant-stimuli) trials with a one-key trial-by-trial 1-vs-2-stream report and percept-conditioned d' (kept). Bistability is verified (Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006; Moore & Gockel 2012; Denham & Winkler 2006), as are abrupt individual jumps (Micheyl 2013: L6, L8). Model performance as P(integrated|D) x d'_int + (1 - P) x d'_seg with mixed models. Caveat: individual subjective-objective correlations are unreliable (Micheyl & Oxenham 2010).

Same-frequency (0-semitone) or no-A control at every D (kept; Micheyl & Oxenham 2010 used no-A ratios of 1.82/1.35/1.20 to correct for Weber; Vliegen et al. 1999). Report the 15-semitone minus control difference as the grouping effect.

Context-free asynchrony-discrimination baseline at 3-4 reference D values with matched tones and lead direction (kept). Wojtczak et al. 2013 verified that thresholds plateau beyond about 20 ms at high level and vary little up to 20 ms at low level, so the tcoh 0.4 x D fit should be tested against a measured baseline, not assumed to be Weber. This could rescue the existing tcoh data.

Thompson/Carlyon-style cross-stream gap detection with early vs late probes (kept; verified). Integration helps and build-up is indexed objectively, but the judgement is A-B timing, so it needs the 0-semitone control, and trials are long.
Conjunction/interval-change task (kept but flagged UNTESTED). Inspired by Micheyl, Kreft et al. 2013, which is a segregation-helps task; no published grouping-helps version was found.

Parameter guidance (kept with correction). Use Micheyl's 5 Hz, 100-ms tones, 20-ms ramps, 15 semitones; express D as cycle phase and overlap; use constant stimuli and d'; counterbalance lead direction (Wojtczak 2013); record percussion and musical training (Ehrlé & Samson 2005). Avoid D-dependent anomalous endings mainly because of the Weber and displacement confounds. 'Reset by a single deviant' is established only for constant-frequency inducers (Roberts 2008; Haywood & Roberts 2010, 2013); Haywood & Roberts 2013 found no single-deviant reset after alternating inducers, so reset is a possible but not established threat to tsync.
evidence.angle_summary:
I checked all 19 of the colleague's citations (PubMed metadata or abstracts, plus PMC full text for Micheyl 2013, Elhilali 2009, Micheyl & Oxenham 2010, Moore & Gockel 2012 and Wojtczak 2013). All 19 exist and none is refuted. The corrections are:

(1) Micheyl 2013 Exp. 1: the P(2 streams) values (about 0.97 alternating, 0.76 synchronous) are group averages, not modal values. Exp. 3 details are confirmed (d' 1.48 to 2.43; credible differences for 0 vs 50 and 0 vs 100 ms; L6 and L8 jumped abruptly).
(2) The van Noorden URL points to a different paper ('Temporal predictability as a grouping cue...'). The thesis exists but was not read.
(3) Turgeon 2002: correct DOI is 10.1121/1.1453450. Friberg & Sundberg: DOI is 10.1121/1.413218; the cutoff is 240 ms in the abstract and about 250 ms in the full text; 'musical training had no effect' is unverified.
(4) Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006: stimulus parameters are unverified. Later reanalyses of their data describe 5 semitones and 4-min runs, not 7 semitones. The 'build-up is an artefact of averaging' claim belongs to Denham & Winkler 2006, now verified.
(5) Wojtczak 2013: the plateau is confirmed at 85 dB SPL (rise to 20 ms, then flat to 100 ms). At 20 dB SL thresholds varied little up to 20 ms. So asynchrony discrimination is not cleanly Weber.
(6) Important nuance on the reset critique of tsync. Roberts 2008 and Haywood & Roberts 2010 used constant-frequency inducers. Haywood & Roberts 2013 found single-deviant resetting ONLY after constant-frequency inducers, not alternating ones. So 'tsync's ending resets segregation' is plausible but unestablished. tsync's stronger problems are the D-dependent displacement and the Weber/Zera-Green reference confound.

Bistability: yes, it is supported by verified sources (Moore & Gockel 2012; Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006; Denham & Winkler 2006) and by Micheyl's step-like individual curves. Intermediate D likely sits in an ambiguous region, which argues for constant stimuli, a trial-wise percept report and percept-conditioned or mixture analysis instead of staircases.

Two important papers the colleague missed, both verified:
- Micheyl, Hunter & Oxenham 2010 (JEP:HPP 36:1029). On-frequency captors raise A-B lead/lag and synchrony thresholds to about 43-50 ms; remote captors serve as a control. This is a grouping-helps task with a reference symmetric about synchrony.
- Christiansen & Oxenham 2014 (JASA 135:3520). Comodulation masking release is lost when precursor flankers are offset by 40-60 ms from the masker band, while the target burst stays synchronous. This is a grouping-helps performance measure with D manipulated in context, a non-timing judgement and no anomalous ending, which makes it the best template for the user's goal.

The colleague's other candidate measures stand. The conjunction task remains untested.

I checked all 20 of the colleague's papers against PubMed records, and against the PMC full text where it exists. All 20 exist. Most claims hold, but there are some errors, listed first.

ERRORS:
(a) "Vliegen & Oxenham 1999, shift thresholds rose with A-B interval" is misattributed. Vliegen & Oxenham 1999 (JASA 105:339) used subjective ABA reports and interleaved-melody recognition. The shift-threshold result is from Vliegen, Moore & Oxenham 1999 (JASA 106:938, doi 10.1121/1.427140).
(b) The Teki 2016 entry should use doi 10.1093/cercor/bhw173, Cereb Cortex 26(9):3669-80, not the Consensus link.
(c) Micheyl & Oxenham 2010 is in PMC as open full text (PMC2975891), contrary to the colleague's note.
(d) Calling Denham & Winkler 2006 a "companion review" to Pressnitzer & Hupé is unsupported. The only match is J Physiol Paris 100:154, on predictive models. I could not confirm the claim that build-up averaging comes from it.
(e) Spielmann 2013's session length is 60-80 min in the Discussion (75-90 min was the stated target), and 20 blocks in total.
(f) Elhilali, Xiang et al. 2009: the 20 training trials belong to the 9-listener psychoacoustic study. The 14 listeners were the MEG study (18 recruited).
(g) Billig et al. 2018 itself reports the segregation positivity at 66-138 ms after the L tone, not "about 60-100 ms from earlier studies".

CONFIRMED with exact numbers: Billig & Carlyon 2016 Exp 2. Twelve listeners, 48 sequences, about 30 min. Better deviant sensitivity during integrated reports: t(11)=4.15, d=1.80. Adding percept to the model gave chi2(1)=77.40 overall and 73.47 with early deviants excluded. Deviants in segregated phases: 2%, 41% and 64% for early, middle and late. More conservative responding during segregation: t(11)=8.93. Dual-task cost of 0.59 d'. Also confirmed: Micheyl 2013 Exp 3 (d' 1.48 to 2.43; L6 and L8 jump abruptly between 0 and 35 ms; in Exp 1, L7's reports may reflect beats) and Elhilali 2009 (9 experienced listeners; 100-ms tones with 50-ms gaps; A gaps of 30 or 70 ms; thresholds 2-4 ms versus 10-20 ms).

FLAW IN THE TOP PICK: displacing B "relative to its own B rhythm" also changes the B-B intervals. That is a within-stream cue, and Micheyl & Oxenham 2010 Exp 3 shows segregation helps that kind of judgement. So the deviant would carry both an integration-helped cue and a segregation-helped cue. The fix: jitter the B-B (or pair-to-pair) intervals so that only the A-B relation is informative. Micheyl & Oxenham 2010 jittered inter-triplet gaps by ±T for this reason. Percept-conditioning at a fixed D does remove the Weber confound for the percept contrast, but a d'-versus-D curve still carries it.

IMPORTANT PAPERS THE COLLEAGUE MISSED (verified):
- Christiansen & Oxenham 2014, JASA 135:3520. Comodulation masking release (CMR) fell when flanker and masker precursor bursts had a fixed onset offset of 40-60 ms (tested at 0, 20, 40 and 60 ms). The target interval was always synchronous, so the listener detects a tone and makes no timing judgement. This gives a grouping-helps, Weber-free performance measure as a function of D.
- Rhythmic masking release: Turgeon, Bregman & Ahad 2002 (JASA 111:1819) and Turgeon, Bregman & Roberts 2005 (JEP:HPP 31:939). Rhythm identification depends on distractors fusing with synchronous captors. Synchrony gives full fusion, 10-20 ms partial fusion, and 20-40 ms none.
- Denham et al. 2014 (Front Neurosci 8:25) and Farkas et al. 2016 (PLoS One): individual switching patterns are idiosyncratic and stable for up to a year.
- Rankin, Sussman & Rinzel 2015 (PLoS Comput Biol): a mechanistic model of auditory bistability.

On bistability: the evidence that ABA streaming is bistable (Pressnitzer & Hupé; Gutschalk; Billig 2018) is solid. Applying it to synchronous-versus-delayed A/B is still an inference. I found no paper that measured bistable switching as a function of onset delay, which makes that a novel contribution.

verified.citation: Billig AJ, Carlyon RP (2016). Automaticity and primacy of auditory streaming: Concurrent subjective and objective measures. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 42(3):339-353 (epub 2015)
verified.corrected_claim: The colleague's summary is accurate. Stimuli: 50-ms tones with 10-ms ramps, 75-ms within-triplet and 200-ms between-triplet gaps, one triplet per 500 ms, 35/37/39 triplets (17.5-19.5 s). Delta-f was 4 or 8 semitones, with A roved around 800 Hz over one octave. Triplets went to one ear and 400-ms noise bursts to the other. The deviant was a B tone 50 ms late, at the 6th triplet, the 18th from last, or the 7th from last. The same 12 listeners did both experiments. Exp 2 had 48 trials in 4 blocks and took about 30 min including training. Sensitivity was higher during integrated than segregated reports: t(11)=4.15, p=.002, d=1.80. Adding percept to the mixed model gave chi2(1)=77.40, or 73.47 with early deviants excluded; pseudo-R2 rose from .22 to .36. Deviants falling in segregated phases: 2% early, 41% middle, 64% late. Responding was more conservative during segregated phases: t(11)=8.93, d=2.93. The effect was carried by hits, not false alarms. Dual-task cost: d' fell 0.59 from Exp 1 to Exp 2, F(1,11)=12.10. I did not check the 90-min length of Exp 1. Caveat: the deviant changes both A-B and B-B timing.
verified.relevance: This is the template for percept-conditioned d' at a fixed stimulus, which removes the Weber confound from the percept contrast. Its feasibility numbers (12 listeners, about 30 min) are confirmed.

verified.citation: Micheyl C, Hanson C, Demany L, Shamma S, Oxenham AJ (2013). Auditory stream segregation for alternating and synchronous tones. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 39(6):1568-1580
verified.corrected_claim: Exp 1 had 7 listeners. Tones were 100 ms with 20-ms ramps, B at 1000 Hz, A 1-15 semitones lower, A levels roved ±4 dB, 28 presentations per condition. P(two streams), alternating: about 0.11 at 1 semitone to 0.97 at 15. Synchronous: about 0.29 to 0.76. Sync and alternating differed significantly only at 9 semitones (0.23) and 15 semitones (0.19). Four listeners' 'two streams' reports rose with separation and two rose more weakly. L7's fell, and the authors suggest L7 linked beats in the synchronous tones to the 'two streams' response. Exp 3 had 7 listeners (L1-L6, L8), D = 0/35/50/71/100 ms, and a 60-to-64-dB increment. Group d' (MAP) went from about 1.48 to 2.43. The 0-vs-100 ms difference was 1.10, CR [0.03, 2.05]; 0 vs 50 ms was 0.65. L3 stayed near chance. L6 and L8 improved abruptly between 0 and 35 ms. The analysis was a hierarchical Bayesian probit model.
verified.relevance: This is the anchor paper. The abrupt individual jumps and the heterogeneous subjective reports fit a threshold-like or bistable organisation. The authors themselves say 35 ms or less may 'break' binding.

verified.citation: Elhilali M, Ma L, Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ, Shamma SA (2009). Temporal coherence in the perceptual organization and cortical representation of auditory scenes. Neuron 61(2):317-329
verified.corrected_claim: The psychophysics is confirmed. Nine listeners with extensive experience; A at 1000 Hz, B 6, 9 or 15 semitones above. Tones were 100 ms with 10-ms ramps. There were 5 precursor tones per stream and then a target pair. Synchronous: 50-ms gaps throughout. Asynchronous: B gaps 50 ms, A gaps 30 or 70 ms, so the streams ran at different tempi (a drifting asynchrony, not a constant lag). 2I-2AFC, 3-down-1-up, 79.4% correct. Thresholds were 2-4 ms synchronous and 10-20 ms asynchronous, not different from B alone; the paper gives no B-alone number in the text. The reported statistic F(1,10)=7.394, p<0.001 is internally inconsistent; that F gives p of about .02. The claim that the model predicts a 'graded transition as asynchrony grows' was not verified.
verified.relevance: Confirms that Elhilali's asynchronous condition was drifting, not a constant D, so it never faced tcoh's D versus D+delta Weber problem.

verified.citation: Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ (2010). Objective and subjective psychophysical measures of auditory stream integration and segregation. J Assoc Res Otolaryngol 11(4):709-724
verified.corrected_claim: Full text is in PMC (PMC2975891), contrary to the colleague's note. Integration task: shift of the last B within an ABA triplet (AB-A versus A-BA). Seven listeners; B at 1000 Hz; delta-f 0-15 semitones; T = 50 or 100 ms; N = 1-8 triplets; inter-triplet gap jittered by ±T; 2-down-1-up. Thresholds rose with delta-f, F(5,30)=21.47, and with N (build-up). Segregation task: the final B-B interval, 6T ± Δt, with the A tones made uninformative. Thresholds fell with delta-f. Subjective-objective correlations: rho = 0.69 for the integration task and -0.46 for the segregation task at the group level. They were weak at the individual level.
verified.relevance: Precedent for matched integration-helps and segregation-helps tasks. Two practical points: jitter between triplets is used to stop the within-stream rhythm being informative, and the B-B interval task shows that a within-B-stream timing deviant is segregation-helped. That matters for the design of the top-pick deviant.

verified.citation: Thompson SK, Carlyon RP, Cusack R (2011). An objective measurement of the build-up of auditory streaming and of its modulation by attention. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 37(4):1253-1262
verified.corrected_claim: The abstract confirms it. ABA triplets of 50-ms tones with 75-ms gaps. Detection of a lengthened A-to-B gap was better early than late, and better at delta-f 4 than 8, consistent with subjective judgements. In Exp 2, detection of a delay 12.5 s into a 13.5-s sequence improved when listeners did a competing task in the other ear for the first 10 s. Build-up is not fully under voluntary control. I did not check the full text, so I could not confirm the delay size.
verified.relevance: Supports using deviant position (early versus late) as a within-D build-up factor in fixed-stimulus designs.

verified.citation: Pressnitzer D, Hupé JM (2006). Temporal dynamics of auditory and visual bistability reveal common principles of perceptual organization. Curr Biol 16(13):1351-1357
verified.corrected_claim: The abstract confirms bistable streaming, with switch dynamics and susceptibility to volitional control similar to visual plaids, and no cross-modal correlation of subject-specific biases. The claim that a companion review by Denham & Winkler (2006) argues build-up reflects averaging over switching is unsupported. The only match is Denham SL & Winkler I (2006), J Physiol Paris 100:154-170, on predictive models, which is not a companion piece. I could not verify that attribution.
verified.relevance: The core evidence that ABA streaming is bistable. Extending it to synchronous-versus-delayed A/B is an inference; I found no study of switching as a function of onset delay.

verified.citation: Gutschalk A, Micheyl C, Melcher JR, Rupp A, Scherg M, Oxenham AJ (2005). Neuromagnetic correlates of streaming in human auditory cortex. J Neurosci 25(22):5382-5388
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed. Alternating pure tones. In Exp 1, long-latency activity (>60 ms, probably non-primary cortex) correlated with percept as parameters varied. In Exp 2, an ambiguous sequence gave a bistable percept, and that activity covaried with spontaneous switches while the stimulus stayed constant.
verified.relevance: Percept-locked neural markers at a fixed stimulus. A feasible EEG companion at one ambiguous D.

verified.citation: Billig AJ, Davis MH, Carlyon RP (2018). Neural decoding of bistable sounds reveals an effect of intention on perceptual organization. J Neurosci 38(11):2844-2853
verified.corrected_claim: Paradigm confirmed. 27 listeners (25 in the booth, 24 in MEG, 23 in the neural analyses). HLH- triplets of 100-ms tones with 10-ms ramps, 50-ms within-triplet and 200-ms between-triplet gaps, H at 1000/1017 Hz, delta-f 4 or 6 semitones. Sequences of 250 triplets lasted 150 s. Classifier epochs were 600 ms, excluding epochs within 1.5 s of a button press. Correction: this paper itself finds the segregated response more positive at 216-288 ms after triplet onset, which is 66-138 ms after L-tone onset. That is not a '60-100 ms' value from earlier studies.
verified.relevance: The same tone duration as Micheyl 2013 and a similar rate. Shows percept decoding is possible, and that intention biases organisation, so neutral instructions are needed.

verified.citation: O'Sullivan JA, Shamma SA, Lalor EC (2015). Evidence for neural computations of temporal coherence in an auditory scene and their enhancement during active listening. J Neurosci 35(18):7256-7263
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed. EEG with SFG stimuli whose figure coherence was modulated stochastically, analysed by linear regression (TRF). Passive listening gave an effect at about 115-185 ms; active listening a larger one lasting to about 265 ms.
verified.relevance: A TRF approach to varying D within long sequences. Acoustic onset regressors would be needed as nuisance terms. Directly compatible with the lab's SFG EEG pipeline.

verified.citation: Elhilali M, Xiang J, Shamma SA, Simon JZ (2009). Interaction between attention and bottom-up saliency mediates the representation of foreground and background in an auditory scene. PLoS Biol 7(6):e1000129
verified.corrected_claim: Mostly correct, with these fixes. The psychoacoustic study had 9 listeners. The MEG study had 18 recruited and 14 analysed, at the 8-semitone protection region only. The target repeated at 4 Hz, 250-500 Hz in 2-semitone steps. Maskers were 50 tones/s over 5 octaves. Tasks: a 2-semitone target frequency shift versus a masker duration lengthening (75 to 400 ms). Training: a 20-trial block (psychoacoustics) or a 12-sound block (MEG). d' was about 3 at 8 semitones in MEG. Attention-related power and phase enhancement was only at 4 Hz. Within-participant neural-behavioural build-up slopes were positive (mean angle about 34 degrees); no r value is given.
verified.relevance: Frequency tagging needs a stream-specific rate. A and B at a shared 5 Hz make the tag confounded with D.

verified.citation: Sussman E, Ritter W, Vaughan HG Jr (1999). An investigation of the auditory streaming effect using event-related brain potentials. Psychophysiology 36(1):22-34
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed. No MMN at the slow pace. At the fast pace, an MMN for the low-stream deviant only; the high deviant elicited none. Both deviants elicited MMNs when the across-stream deviance interval exceeded 250 ms (Exp 2).
verified.relevance: MMN logic for streaming. EEG-heavy and segregation-helps, so not a fit for the primary behavioural measure.

verified.citation: Szalárdy O, Winkler I, Schröger E, Widmann A, Bendixen A (2013). Foreground-background discrimination indicated by event-related brain potentials in a new auditory multistability paradigm. Psychophysiology 50(12):1239-1250
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed. An ERP modulation from about 70 ms tracked whether a sound was in the reported foreground or background, with no extra integrated-versus-segregated effect. MMN-indexed grouping did not correspond to reported grouping. Companion caution also verified: Paavilainen et al. 2018, Heliyon 4:e00608 (doi 10.1016/j.heliyon.2018.e00608). There, MMN to abstract-regularity violations appeared irrespective of pace, that is, whether one stream or two was perceived.
verified.relevance: A caution that MMN may not index conscious organisation.

verified.citation: Spielmann MI, Schröger E, Kotz SA, Pechmann T, Bendixen A (2013). Using a staircase procedure for the objective measurement of auditory stream integration and segregation thresholds. Front Psychol 4:534
verified.corrected_claim: 50-ms tones; low stream fixed at 250 Hz; ISI 50/100/150/200 ms. Integration task: a rhythm regular/irregular judgement on 12-tone sequences. Segregation task: a louder low-tone deviant (80 dB) among high tones at random levels (65/75/85 dB). Weighted staircases with 1-unit and 3-unit steps: 1/3 semitones, or 10/30 ms for ISI. The Methods also say '3 up-1 down', which is inconsistent. Runs ended after 14 reversals. There were 12 objective and 8 subjective blocks (20 in total) plus training, each about 1-5 min. Session length: about 60-80 min per the Discussion; 75-90 min was the target. N = 19 analysed. The integration staircase worked; the segregation staircase did not.
verified.relevance: Confirms that the integration-helps direction suits adaptive tracking. Each condition costs a few minutes.

verified.citation: Teki S, Barascud N, Picard S, Payne C, Griffiths TD, Chait M (2016). Neural correlates of auditory figure-ground segregation based on temporal coherence. Cereb Cortex 26(9):3669-3680
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed, but the DOI should replace the Consensus link. MEG in naive, distracted listeners. Evoked responses began about 150 ms after figure onset. Sources were in the planum temporale and intraparietal sulcus.
verified.relevance: A pre-attentive coherence marker in the same family as the lab's figure-ground EEG.

verified.citation: Lu K, Xu Y, Yin P, Oxenham AJ, Fritz JB, Shamma SA (2017). Temporal coherence structure rapidly shapes neuronal interactions. Nat Commun 8:13900
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed (ferret A1). Response rates, STRF sensitivity and spiking correlations were rapidly enhanced by synchronous sequences and suppressed by alternating ones, only when the animals were engaged and attentive.
verified.relevance: Supports active-listening behavioural measures. Passive EEG may underestimate the D effect.

verified.citation: Bey C, McAdams S (2003). Postrecognition of interleaved melodies as an indirect measure of auditory stream formation. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 29(2):267-279
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed; the DOI replaces the Consensus link. Recognition was impossible with the same mean frequency and maximal contour crossing. It improved with frequency separation and timbre dissimilarity, and was unaffected by the silent interval before the probe. The companion paper Bey & McAdams 2002, Percept Psychophys 64:844 (doi 10.3758/bf03194750), is also confirmed: a probe before the mixture improved performance and reduced 'same' bias.
verified.relevance: Segregation-helps, so it fits our need weakly.

verified.citation: Lipp R, Kitterick P, Summerfield Q, Bailey PJ, Paul-Jordanov I (2010). Concurrent sound segregation based on inharmonicity and onset asynchrony. Neuropsychologia 48(5):1417-1425
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed. The third harmonic was mistuned 8% or delayed 160 ms. Both cues gave behavioural segregation, an ORNm and a P230m. The P75m was specific to mistuning. The ORNm looked automatic; the P230m was attention-sensitive, especially for inharmonicity. The suggestion that ORN amplitude grows with D for isolated pairs is untested speculation.
verified.relevance: A possible cheap EEG companion. It indexes simultaneous, not sequential, grouping.

verified.citation: Snyder JS, Alain C, Picton TW (2006). Effects of attention on neuroelectric correlates of auditory stream segregation. J Cogn Neurosci 18(1):1-13
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed. ABA- patterns repeated for 10.8 s with a 100-ms SOA, A at 500 Hz and B at 500, 625, 750 or 1000 Hz. The B-tone P1-N1-P2/N1c enhancement varied with delta-f and correlated with streaming. A positivity at 150-250 ms grew over the trial and was smaller when tones were ignored. Right-hemisphere dominance; sources in Heschl's gyrus.
verified.relevance: B-evoked responses are confounded by inter-onset interval when D varies. Use them only conditioned on percept at a fixed D.

verified.citation: Roberts B, Glasberg BR, Moore BCJ (2002). Primitive stream segregation of tone sequences without differences in fundamental frequency or passband. J Acoust Soc Am 112(5):2074-2085
verified.corrected_claim: The Roberts result is confirmed: 60-ms tones, 40-ms gaps, progressive delay of B, 70 dB SPL in pink noise. Passband or phase differences raised thresholds and also raised the proportion of time segregated. MISATTRIBUTION: the cited 'Vliegen & Oxenham 1999, shift thresholds rose with A-B interval' is wrong. Vliegen & Oxenham 1999 (JASA 105:339) used subjective reports and interleaved melodies. The shift-threshold result is from Vliegen J, Moore BCJ, Oxenham AJ (1999), JASA 106:938-945, doi 10.1121/1.427140: in ABA sequences with B at the midpoint or delayed, shift thresholds rose with the A-B interval (1-18 semitones).
verified.relevance: Precedent for integration-helps timing tasks matching subjective segregation. The Weber caveat applies if D is the variable.

verified.citation: Farkas D, Denham SL, Bendixen A, Winkler I (2016). Assessing the validity of subjective reports in the auditory streaming paradigm. J Acoust Soc Am 139(4):1762
verified.corrected_claim: Confirmed. Catch trials identified listeners who misunderstood the instructions. Neutral instructions did not show systematic voluntary biasing, compared with explicit-bias and random-response conditions. Social desirability was unrelated to the reports. Companion paper verified: Farkas, Denham, Bendixen, Tóth, Kondo & Winkler 2016, PLoS One 11:e0154810 (doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0154810), on idiosyncratic switching patterns related to executive function and ego-resiliency. The colleague's 'Denham 2014' is Denham et al. 2014, Front Neurosci 8:25 (doi 10.3389/fnins.2014.00025): individual switching patterns stayed stable after a year.
verified.relevance: The recipe for validating percept reports from naive listeners, and support for treating individual differences as stable traits.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Christiansen SK, Oxenham AJ (2014). Assessing the effects of temporal coherence on auditory stream formation through comodulation masking release. J Acoust Soc Am 135(6):3520-3529
verified.corrected_claim: Task: detect a 1-kHz tone in a 20-Hz-wide masker band, with four comodulated or random flanker bands at 0.25, 0.5, 2 and 4 kHz. Bursts were 187.5 ms with 20-ms ramps, with 4 precursor bursts at a 250-ms onset interval. Procedure: 3AFC, 1-up-2-down. Fixed flanker-masker onset offsets in the precursors were 0, 20, 40 and 60 ms. CMR fell significantly at 40 and 60 ms (no significant reduction reported at 20 ms). It also fell with different flanker and masker rates, but not with jitter alone. In Exp 3, CMR was absent at 60 ms (t(7)=1.42) and robust at 0 ms. The target burst itself was always synchronous. Seven, ten and eight listeners in Exps 1-3.
verified.relevance: The closest published solution to the lab's problem. It is a performance measure where grouping helps (CMR needs flankers and masker in one stream), driven by a constant precursor onset offset. The judged quantity is tone detection, not timing, so there is no Weber confound. A pure-tone analogue would use Micheyl-like A/B context at delay D followed by a synchronous test pair.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Turgeon M, Bregman AS, Ahad PA (2002). Rhythmic masking release: contribution of cues for perceptual organization to the cross-spectral fusion of concurrent narrow-band noises. J Acoust Soc Am 111(4):1819-1831; and Turgeon M, Bregman AS, Roberts B (2005). Rhythmic masking release: effects of asynchrony, temporal overlap, harmonic relations, and source separation on cross-spectral grouping. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 31(5):939-953
verified.corrected_claim: Task: 2AFC identification of which rhythm was played, plus clarity ratings, with the rhythm masked by irregular identical distractors. The rhythm is released when distractors fuse with synchronous flankers or captors in another frequency region. In 2002, synchrony fully fused bursts across frequency and space, 10-20 ms asynchrony gave partial fusion, and 20-40 ms gave none. In 2005, fusion depended mainly on onset asynchrony and temporal overlap; harmonicity had some effect and only dichotic separation mattered.
verified.relevance: A classic grouping-helps, fixed-stimulus d' measure whose dependent variable is rhythm identity, not a timing judgement. Fusion falls over 0-40 ms of asynchrony, the same range where Micheyl's L6 and L8 jump.

verified.citation: [ADDED] Rankin J, Sussman E, Rinzel J (2015). Neuromechanistic model of auditory bistability. PLoS Comput Biol 11(11):e1004555
verified.corrected_claim: A network model with mutual inhibition, adaptation, noise and slow NMDA excitation reproduces ABA integrated/segregated alternations. It predicted, and psychoacoustics confirmed, that delta-f mainly changes the dominance durations of the stronger percept (a Levelt-type property).
verified.relevance: A framework for the bistability question. Prediction: as D grows, mainly the durations of 'one stream' dominance phases should shorten. That would be a testable, novel D-based result.

candidate_measures: TOP PICK, kept with a correction: a dual-report design at fixed D with fixed-size deviants, after Billig & Carlyon 2016 Exp 2 (verified: 12 listeners, 48 sequences, about 30 min; integrated-report sensitivity higher, t(11)=4.15; percept added to the model chi2=77.4, or 73.5 without early deviants; listeners more conservative while segregated). Use long Micheyl-type A/B sequences at 3 D values, continuous one/two-stream buttons and a deviant key. CORRECTION: a B shift 'relative to its own B rhythm' also creates a within-B-stream interval cue, which segregation helps (Micheyl & Oxenham 2010 Exp 3). Jitter the pair-to-pair interval, as in Micheyl & Oxenham 2010 (±T between triplets), so that only the A-B relation is informative. Analyse with SDT or a mixed model, because of the criterion shift. Percept-conditioned d' at a fixed D is Weber-free. A d'-versus-D curve is not.

NEW, strongest Weber-free option (verified precedent: Christiansen & Oxenham 2014): CMR-style or masking-release probe after a coherent versus delayed context. Context: A and B sequences at delay D (pure tones, or narrowband noise as in the original). Test: a synchronous final pair, where the listener detects a target that is only easy if A and B are grouped. Examples are a comodulation cue, or a probe tone in B whose detection benefits from A being in the same stream. The judged quantity is a detection threshold or fixed-level d', not timing. Christiansen & Oxenham found CMR reduced at 40-60 ms offsets and abolished at 60 ms in Exp 3.

NEW, rhythmic masking release adapted to A/B pairs (verified: Turgeon et al. 2002, 2005). The B-band rhythm is masked by irregular B distractors. Distractors that are synchronous with A captors fuse and release the rhythm. Vary the captor-distractor delay D over 0-40 ms or more. The dependent variable is 2AFC rhythm identification (fixed stimuli, d'), with no cross-stream timing judgement. Note: here grouping of distractor with captor helps the B-target rhythm, so in this framing performance falls with D. Fusion was full at 0 ms, partial at 10-20 ms and absent at 20-40 ms for noise bursts. Needs a pure-tone pilot at a 15-semitone separation.

Method of constant stimuli replacing staircases (kept). Fix the deviant size per listener at about 75-80% at D = 0, then run fixed trials at each D. On its own this does not remove Weber's law. Combine it with a per-trial percept report for percept-conditioned d'.
Non-timing conjunction or coherent-level-change deviant (kept as a pilot idea; no direct precedent verified). Risk: an ideal observer can combine both channels regardless of grouping.

Cross-stream relational pitch (interval) deviant with common transposition (kept as a pilot idea). The cue type changes from harmonic dyad to melodic interval as D grows, so an isolated-pair control is required.

Percept-only measure: P(one stream), dominance durations and first-switch latency versus D (Pressnitzer & Hupé 2006; Rankin et al. 2015; Farkas et al. 2016 JASA catch-trial controls). Rankin's model predicts that D should mainly shorten the dominance of the stronger 'one stream' percept. No study of bistability as a function of onset delay was found, so this would be a novel ARO result. Pair it with an objective task.

Build-up probe (early versus late deviant position) as a free factor (Thompson et al. 2011; Billig & Carlyon 2016: only 2% of early deviants fell in segregated phases). Prediction: the late-minus-early d' difference grows with D.
EEG option 1: TRF or regression of EEG on stochastically varying D within long sequences (O'Sullivan et al. 2015: passive about 115-185 ms, active to about 265 ms), with onset nuisance regressors.
EEG option 2: percept-locked responses at one ambiguous D (Gutschalk 2005; Billig 2018, which found the segregated response more positive 66-138 ms after the middle tone, from 150-s sequences).
EEG option 3: MMN to cross-stream deviants. Not recommended as primary: needs many deviants, and MMN can dissociate from reported organisation (Szalárdy 2013; Paavilainen 2018, verified).
EEG option 4: intermodulation frequency tagging. Speculative; I did not verify whether an auditory-streaming precedent exists. Pilot only.
Interleaved-melody identification: weak fit (segregation-helps, Bey & McAdams 2003). Not recommended.
